scenarios.title: Pricing the Pig Launcher Tie-In Bill of Quantities
scenarios.project_type: Pig launcher skid tie-in on a desert crude gathering line
scenarios.summary: Price a six-line civil and mechanical bill of quantities for a pig launcher skid tie-in, then report the bill total, the line count and the plain mean of the unit rates.
scenarios.brief: A desert crude gathering line is being extended with a new pig launcher skid, and the tie-in package has just come back from the estimating team as a short bill of quantities. The construction manager wants a quick independent check of the priced bill before it is issued for subcontractor pricing. She also asks for the plain average of the quoted rates so she can sanity-check the rate spread across trades. Your job is to reprice the bill line by line and report the headline figures.
objectives: Extend each bill of quantities line as quantity multiplied by unit rate
Aggregate line extensions into a total priced bill value
Count bill lines correctly as a discrete control measure
Compute the plain arithmetic mean of unit rates and distinguish it from a quantity-weighted average
Apply stated rounding conventions to reported quantity surveying outputs
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic guided lab on bill of quantities pricing.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, quantities and rates are synthetic and simplified for training use only.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Extend each line as qty x rate:
B1: 120 x 15 = 1800
B2: 40 x 25 = 1000
B3: 24 x 150 = 3600
B4: 18 x 200 = 3600
B5: 32 x 50 = 1600
B6: 250 x 8 = 2000

Step 2 - Total = sum of extensions:
1800 + 1000 + 3600 + 3600 + 1600 + 2000 = 13600.00

Step 3 - Line count = number of bill lines = 6.

Step 4 - Average rate = plain mean of the rates, NOT weighted by quantity:
(15 + 25 + 150 + 200 + 50 + 8) / 6 = 448 / 6 = 74.666... = 74.67

Teaching point: the quantity-weighted average rate would be total value divided by total quantity = 13600 / (120 + 40 + 24 + 18 + 32 + 250) = 13600 / 484 = 28.10. The plain mean of 74.67 is far higher because the high-rate, low-quantity items (concrete at 200 and welds at 150) carry the same weight as the 250 m2 of coating priced at 8. Reporting a plain mean as if it were an average cost per unit of work would overstate the bill by more than double.

Final answers: total = 13600.00, line_count = 6, average_rate = 74.67

scenarios.title: Hardened USV Maintenance Jetty — Bill of Quantities Roll-Up
scenarios.summary: Price a measured bill of quantities for a hardened unmanned-vessel jetty, then contrast the plain mean of rates against what the bill actually costs.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic defence agency is building a hardened maintenance jetty for a squadron of unmanned surface vessels at a coastal support facility. objectives: Extend each bill line as quantity x rate and total a 14-line bill of quantities to two decimal places
Report the line count of a bill accurately as a control check on completeness
Compute the plain arithmetic mean of the rate column without weighting it by quantity
Explain why an unweighted mean rate is distorted by low-quantity, high-rate items
Identify which measure is appropriate when benchmarking bill rates against cost per unit of work
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic quantity-surveying exercise; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, quantities and rates are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, organisation or price book.
scenarios.worked_solution: Method. 1) Extend every line: amount = qty x rate. B1 48500 x 62.40 = 3,026,400.00; B2 12750 x 138.75 = 1,769,062.50; B3 3620 x 845.00 = 3,058,900.00; B4 2840 x 1265.50 = 3,594,020.00; B5 960 x 412.25 = 395,760.00; B6 415 x 2380.00 = 987,700.00; B7 268 x 5640.00 = 1,511,520.00; B8 96 x 8125.00 = 780,000.00; B9 5400 x 96.80 = 522,720.00; B10 7250 x 41.35 = 299,787.50; B11 12 x 74500.00 = 894,000.00; B12 340 x 3180.00 = 1,081,200.00; B13 24 x 18650.00 = 447,600.00; B14 6 x 96400.00 = 578,400.00. 2) total = sum of extensions = 18,947,070.00. 3) line_count = 14. 4) average_rate = (sum of the 14 rates) / 14 = 211,737.05 / 14 = 15,124.08 (15,124.075 unrounded). Teaching point: the quantity-weighted rate is total / total qty = 18,947,070.00 / 82,481 = 229.72, about one sixty-fifth of the plain mean. B11, B13 and B14 carry rates in the tens of thousands on quantities of 12, 24 and 6, so they dominate the unweighted mean while contributing under 11 percent of the money. Quote the plain mean only where the ask says so, never as a cost-per-unit benchmark.

scenarios.title: Cash Flow Watch: Milldale Flood Levee Early Works
scenarios.project_type: Rural flood levee and pump station upgrade
scenarios.summary: Track cumulative cash position on a flood levee early-works contract where milestone receipts lag site spend, and find the peak funding the contractor must carry.
scenarios.brief: Your firm holds the early-works contract for the Milldale flood levee and pump station upgrade. Mobilisation, sheet piling and earthworks bills arrive from month one, but the client only certifies milestone payments after embankment sections pass survey, so receipts trail spend in the opening months. The commercial manager wants to know how deep the cash hole gets before the certificates catch up, and where the account lands at the end of the six-month early-works window.
objectives: Compute period net cash flow and the running cumulative cash position from inflow and outflow data
Identify peak funding as the deepest cumulative deficit, expressed as a positive funding requirement
Interpret the closing cumulative position as the project's net cash outcome over the reporting window
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or contract.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Net cash flow per period: net = inflow − outflow.
P1: 0 − 40 = −40
P2: 20 − 50 = −30
P3: 60 − 45 = +15
P4: 70 − 40 = +30
P5: 80 − 35 = +45
P6: 60 − 30 = +30

Step 2 — Cumulative position: running sum of period nets.
After P1: −40
After P2: −40 + (−30) = −70
After P3: −70 + 15 = −55  ← cumulative position at end of period 3
After P4: −55 + 30 = −25
After P5: −25 + 45 = +20
After P6: +20 + 30 = +50

Step 3 — Peak funding: the deepest cumulative deficit is −70 (end of period 2), so the peak funding requirement, stated as a positive number, is 70. This is the most cash the contractor must finance before milestone certificates begin to close the gap.

Step 4 — Final position: the closing cumulative net after period 6 is +50.

Answers: cumulative_3 = −55; peak_funding = 70; final_position = 50.

scenarios.title: Flare Gas Recovery Retrofit — Contractor Cash Flow and Peak Funding
scenarios.project_type: Flare gas recovery unit retrofit at a gas processing plant
scenarios.summary: Track a retrofit contractor's monthly cash position across eight periods, find the deepest funding deficit, and resist a change order that looks approved but was rejected.
scenarios.brief: Your firm holds the mechanical-and-piping contract for a flare gas recovery unit retrofit inside a live onshore gas processing plant. Milestone billings lag heavy early spending on compressor skids, tie-in spools, and shutdown labour, so the treasury team needs to know how deep the cash hole gets and where the job lands at completion. A confusing email thread about a change order is muddying the numbers, and you must work strictly from the approved commercial register.
objectives: Compute period-by-period cumulative net cash position from inflow and outflow data
Identify peak funding requirement as the deepest cumulative deficit, expressed as a positive number
Distinguish approved commercial data from rejected change documentation when assembling a cash forecast
Interpret the closing cumulative position as the project's final cash outcome
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, facility, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Net cash per period: net_t = inflow_t − outflow_t.
P1: 0 − 180 = −180; P2: 40 − 260 = −220; P3: 120 − 310 = −190; P4: 280 − 300 = −20; P5: 420 − 290 = +130; P6: 510 − 240 = +270; P7: 460 − 180 = +280; P8: 380 − 120 = +260.

Step 2 — Cumulative position: C_t = C_(t−1) + net_t.
C1 = −180.00; C2 = −400.00; C3 = −590.00; C4 = −610.00; C5 = −480.00; C6 = −210.00; C7 = +70.00; C8 = +330.00.

Step 3 — Handle the twist: change order CO-07 (a 95 receipt supposedly landing in period 2) appears "approved" in an email chain, but the change register shows it REJECTED. The table already excludes it — add nothing. Including it would understate peak funding by 95 and overstate the final position.

Step 4 — Answers.
cumulative_3 = C3 = −590.00.
peak_funding = deepest cumulative deficit expressed as a positive number = |−610.00| at period 4 = 610.00.
final_position = C8 = 330.00.

scenarios.title: Tidal Sluice Gate Replacement: Peak Funding Under Milestone Lag
scenarios.summary: Expert guided lab on a 10-period infrastructure cash curve where a strong closing balance hides a deep late trough. Learners derive cumulative positions, closing position and peak funding.
scenarios.brief: A joint venture is replacing four tidal sluice gates on an estuary flood-defence barrier, working to fixed tidal closure windows. The client certifies milestones on a lag, so heavy early mobilisation and gate fabrication are financed by the contractor before receipts arrive. A partial recovery mid-programme tempts the treasury team into declaring the worst behind them, just as the second gate lift and coffer works reload the outflow. Your job is to build the cumulative cash curve and size the true financing line.
objectives: Build a period-by-period cumulative cash position from inflow and outflow data with a zero opening balance
Compute the closing cash position at programme end and distinguish it from the financing requirement
Identify the peak funding requirement as the deepest cumulative shortfall across all period ends, not the first trough
Read intermediate cumulative positions at nominated periods to trace the shape of the cash curve
Explain why a healthy final position can coexist with a large mid-programme funding need
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; synthetic infrastructure cash-flow pattern built to expose double-trough funding curves.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, organisation or financing arrangement.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: net_p = inflow_p - outflow_p; cumulative_p = cumulative_(p-1) + net_p, with cumulative_0 = 0. final_position = cumulative_10. peak_funding = absolute value of the minimum cumulative_p when that minimum is negative.

Net by period: P1 400-2150 = -1750; P2 900-2480 = -1580; P3 1250-2690 = -1440; P4 3400-2910 = +490; P5 3650-2760 = +890; P6 1150-3240 = -2090; P7 1480-3020 = -1540; P8 4900-2340 = +2560; P9 5600-1780 = +3820; P10 4260-1220 = +3040.

Cumulative curve: P1 -1750.00; P2 -3330.00; P3 -4770.00; P4 -4280.00; P5 -3390.00; P6 -5480.00; P7 -7020.00; P8 -4460.00; P9 -640.00; P10 +2400.00.

Answers: cumulative_3 = -4770.00; cumulative_5 = -3390.00; cumulative_7 = -7020.00; cumulative_9 = -640.00; final_position = 2400.00; peak_funding = 7020.00.

Trap: periods 4-5 lift the curve from -4770 to -3390, so an analyst anchoring on the first visible dip reports peak funding as 4770. The deepest point is period 7 at -7020, after the P6-P7 reload. Equally, the positive closing balance of 2400 says nothing about the financing line needed to reach it. Check: total inflow 26990 - total outflow 24590 = 2400, matching cumulative_10.

scenarios.title: Coastal Shield Landing Craft Mid-Life Upgrade — Cost Breakdown Roll-Up
scenarios.project_type: amphibious landing craft mid-life upgrade programme
scenarios.summary: Roll up a defence refit cost breakdown structure, compute programme-level actuals and variance, and isolate a hidden favourable variance the sponsor has overlooked.
scenarios.brief: You are the cost controller on Programme Coastal Shield, a mid-life upgrade of a fleet of amphibious landing craft. The refit yard has just submitted period actuals, and the programme sponsor is alarmed by headline overspend chatter from the hull shop. Before the steering board meets, you must roll the cost breakdown structure up from leaf work packages to programme level and show where money is truly being lost — and where one work package is quietly returning budget.
objectives: Compute roll-up totals for budget and actual cost from leaf work packages to the programme root of a CBS.
Compute cost variance (budget minus actual) at leaf, parent, and root levels.
Distinguish an unfavourable (overspend) variance from a favourable (opportunity) variance within the same structure.
Interpret a parent-level variance as the sum of its children's variances rather than a directly booked value.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real programme, fleet, or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up the budget. Only leaves carry values: 1.1.1 (4200) + 1.1.2 (1800) + 1.2 (6500) + 1.3 (3900) + 1.4 (1600) = 18000. Parent 1.1 budget = 4200 + 1800 = 6000.

Step 2 — Roll up the actuals (root_actual). 1.1.1 (4650) + 1.1.2 (2140) + 1.2 (7020) + 1.3 (3510) + 1.4 (1750) = 19070. So root_actual = 19070.00.

Step 3 — Programme variance (root_variance). Variance = budget − actual = 18000 − 19070 = −1070. So root_variance = −1070.00, an overall overspend.

Step 4 — Parent-level variance for Hull & Structural Refurbishment (variance_1.1). Node 1.1 carries no booked values of its own; roll up its children. Budget = 6000; actual = 4650 + 2140 = 6790. Variance = 6000 − 6790 = −790.00. Equivalently, sum the children's variances: (4200 − 4650) + (1800 − 2140) = −450 + (−340) = −790.

Step 5 — Leaf variance for Propulsion Overhaul (variance_1.3). Variance = 3900 − 3510 = +390.00. This is the favourable variance (opportunity): despite the programme's net overspend of 1070, the propulsion work package is returning 390 of budget, which partly offsets the hull and combat-systems overruns.

Final answers: root_actual = 19070.00; root_variance = −1070.00; variance_1.1 = −790.00; variance_1.3 = 390.00.

Report all values to 2 decimal places (sign: budget minus actual).

scenarios.title: Sterile Processing Refurbishment — Cost Breakdown Roll-Up
scenarios.summary: Roll up a four-package cost breakdown structure for a sterile processing refurbishment and report total budget, total actual, and the overall cost variance the sponsor is asking about.
scenarios.brief: A regional hospital is refurbishing its sterile processing department so surgical instrument turnaround can keep pace with a new operating theatre. The works were split into four cost packages: washer-disinfector replacement, clean-room partitioning, an instrument-tracking system, and technician training. With the final invoices now in, the clinical sponsor has heard rumours of an overspend on the washer-disinfectors and wants the roll-up confirmed before the close-out meeting.
objectives: Compute the total budget of a cost breakdown structure by rolling up leaf-level budgets to the root
Compute the total actual cost of a project from its leaf packages
Compute cost variance as budget minus actual and interpret its sign at project level
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up the budget. The root budget is the sum of the four leaf budgets: 42000 + 30000 + 18000 + 10000 = 100000. So root_budget = 100000.

Step 2 — Roll up the actuals. The root actual is the sum of the four leaf actuals: 45500 + 28000 + 19200 + 9300 = 102000. So root_actual = 102000.

Step 3 — Compute the cost variance. Variance = budget - actual = 100000 - 102000 = -2000. So root_variance = -2000.

Interpretation: the negative variance means the project finished 2000 over budget. Checking the leaves shows why: the washer-disinfector package overran by 3500 (42000 - 45500) and instrument tracking by 1200, while partitioning saved 2000 and training saved 700 — savings that only partly offset the equipment overrun the sponsor was worried about.

scenarios.brief: You are the project controls lead on a membrane filtration retrofit at a regional water reclamation works. scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures:

Step 1 — Screen the register by status. Only changes with status "approved" move the baseline. C1 (UV disinfection channel, +185000 cost, +3 weeks), C3 (pre-cast chlorine contact tank, -60000 cost, -2 weeks), and C5 (dewatering allowance, +38000 cost, +1 week) are approved. C2 (pipe gallery corrosion remediation, +240000, +4) is still pending — it is tempting because everyone expects it to pass, but it has not, so it is excluded. Step 3 — Approved schedule delta = 3 + (-2) + 1 = 2 weeks.

Step 4 — Revised BAC = baseline BAC + approved cost delta = 4200000 + 163000 = 4363000.

Step 5 — Revised duration = baseline duration + approved schedule delta = 40 + 2 = 42 weeks.

scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: Baseline BAC = 900000; baseline duration = 36 weeks.

Step 1 — Filter to approved changes only. C1 (approved) and C4 (approved) count. C2 is pending and C3 is rejected, so both are excluded — a pending change moves nothing until the board approves it, and a rejected change never does.

Step 2 — Approved cost delta = sum of approved cost deltas = 40000 + 10000 = 50000.00.

scenarios.summary: Rebuild the cost and schedule baseline of a silo-to-vertical-farm retrofit by isolating only board-approved change requests from a mixed log of approved, pending and rejected items.

scenarios.title: Restart Option Trade-Off at a Shut-In Sour Gas Gathering Station
scenarios.summary: A foundation guided lab in weighted decision analysis: score three restart options for a shut-in sour gas gathering station and identify the winning (lowest) penalty score.
scenarios.brief: Field Block Harrow-7 runs a small sour gas gathering station that has been shut in for five months after its single compressor train failed an integrity inspection. Three restart routes have been costed by the project controls team, each trading capital against time and technical uncertainty. Management wants a defensible weighted comparison rather than a gut call on headline price, so all three factors carry equal weight in the scoring model.
objectives: Compute a weighted penalty score from cost, schedule and risk inputs using equal weights
Apply the convention that the lowest weighted penalty score is the preferred option
Compare option scores to determine the best achievable score across the option set
Explain why the lowest-cost option is not automatically the preferred option
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic weighted-decision training case.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: Score = w_cost x |cost| + w_sched x |schedule| + w_risk x risk, with w_cost = w_sched = w_risk = 1. Cost is in millions, schedule in months, risk on a 0-10 scale, so the three terms are already on comparable scales and can be summed directly. Lower score is better (it is a penalty score).

O1 Modular Rental Compressor Skid: 6 + 4 + 5 = 15.00
O2 In-Situ Compressor Train Rebuild: 9 + 3 + 2 = 14.00
O3 Reroute Tie-In to the Northern Trunk: 5 + 7 + 3 = 15.00

Best score = min(15.00, 14.00, 15.00) = 14.00, achieved by O2.

Answers: score_O1 = 15.00, score_O2 = 14.00, best_score = 14.00.

Teaching point: O3 carries the lowest capital figure (5) but its seven-month schedule and moderate risk push its total to 15.00, so the highest-cost option wins once schedule and risk are weighted equally with cost.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: Score = w_cost x |cost| + w_sched x |schedule| + w_risk x risk, with w_cost = 1.0, w_sched = 0.8, w_risk = 1.5. Absolute values apply to cost and schedule, so an underrun or an early finish is penalised exactly like an overrun or a slip; risk is non-negative and enters directly. Lowest score wins.

O1: 12.00 + 0.8x4.0 (3.20) + 1.5x3.2 (4.80) = 20.00
O2: |-6.5| (6.50) + 0.8x9.0 (7.20) + 1.5x4.0 (6.00) = 19.70
O3: 28.00 + 0.8x|-3.0| (2.40) + 1.5x2.0 (3.00) = 33.40
O4: 9.50 + 0.8x|-7.5| (6.00) + 1.5x6.4 (9.60) = 25.10
O5: 4.00 + 0.8x11.5 (9.20) + 1.5x5.5 (8.25) = 21.45
O6: |-2.5| (2.50) + 0.8x2.5 (2.00) + 1.5x8.6 (12.90) = 17.40
O7: 15.00 + 0.8x1.0 (0.80) + 1.5x1.4 (2.10) = 17.90

Lowest score = 17.40 (O6), narrowly ahead of O7 at 17.90.

Trap: treating the negative cost and schedule figures as credits (signed arithmetic) would score O2 at 6.70 and O4 at 9.10, wrongly promoting them to the top of the ranking. The rule is absolute deviation, so favourable variances still cost points.

Each carries a cost variance (millions), a schedule variance (months) and a technical risk index (0-10). The board's rule penalises any deviation from baseline in either direction, using the absolute value of the variance.

Options as (cost, schedule, risk): O1 12.0, 4.0, 3.2; O2 -6.5, 9.0, 4.0; O3 28.0, -3.0, 2.0; O4 9.5, -7.5, 6.4; O5 4.0, 11.5, 5.5; O6 -2.5, 2.5, 8.6; O7 15.0, 1.0, 1.4. Weights: cost 1.0, schedule 0.8, risk 1.5.

Score = 1.0 x |cost| + 0.8 x |schedule| + 1.5 x risk, and a lower score is better. Report the weighted penalty scores for O2, O3, O4, O6 and O7, and the lowest score across all seven options. Round every answer to 2 decimals.

ask.label: Lowest (best) weighted penalty score across all options

scenarios.title: Cold-Chain Commissioning: Vaccine Fridge Log Quality Check
scenarios.summary: Audit the stabilisation temperature log from a ten-unit vaccine fridge commissioning run: score completeness, mean absolute error against setpoint, and out-of-band units.
scenarios.brief: A regional immunisation programme is commissioning ten modular vaccine refrigerators across newly fitted clinic rooms. Each unit was given a setpoint and left to stabilise overnight, and the commissioning technician recorded the settled temperature the next morning. One data logger dropped out and returned no reading at all, and the controls lead will not sign the handover certificate until the log itself is scored for quality. Your job is to grade the dataset before anyone argues about the fridges.
objectives: Compute completeness percentage from present versus total records in a commissioning log
Calculate mean absolute error of recorded values against their setpoints using present rows only
Identify how many present readings breach a stated deviation threshold
Explain why a missing reading is excluded from error maths but not from completeness
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic guided lab on data quality scoring.
scenarios.disclaimers: All units, setpoints and readings are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real facility or equipment.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - the log holds 10 unit rows; 9 carry a reading and unit U-05 has none.

Step 2 - completeness_pct = 100 x present / all = 100 x 9 / 10 = 90.00.

Step 3 - mean_abs_error = mean |value - expected| over PRESENT rows only. Deviations: U-01 0.2; U-02 0.2; U-03 0.9; U-04 0.1; U-06 0.4; U-07 0.0; U-08 0.6; U-09 0.2; U-10 0.1. Sum = 2.7. Mean = 2.7 / 9 = 0.30. U-05 contributes nothing because it has no reading.

Step 4 - anomaly_count = present rows whose deviation is strictly greater than the threshold 0.4. Only U-03 (0.9) and U-08 (0.6) exceed it; U-06 sits exactly at 0.4 and is not a breach. anomaly_count = 2.

Final: completeness_pct = 90.00, mean_abs_error = 0.30, anomaly_count = 2.

config.prompt: A regional immunisation programme is commissioning ten modular vaccine refrigerators. Each unit row below lists its setpoint temperature as "expected" and the settled overnight reading as "value". One unit's data logger failed and returned no reading, so that row carries no value at all. The commissioning threshold is 0.4 degrees: a reading counts as an anomaly only if its absolute deviation from setpoint is greater than the threshold. Using the log as given, report three figures: completeness percentage across all unit rows, mean absolute error against setpoint over rows that actually have a reading, and the count of readings breaching the threshold. Round the percentage and the mean absolute error to 2 decimal places; the anomaly count is a whole number.

scenarios.title: Hull Block Erection-Gap Scan: Dimensional Data Integrity Audit
scenarios.project_type: modular hull block dimensional control programme
scenarios.summary: Audit a 20-block laser-scan register of hull erection gaps where several readings never arrived, then report record count, completeness, mean absolute error and anomaly count.
scenarios.brief: A shipyard dimensional control cell laser-scans erection gaps on twenty pre-outfitted hull blocks staged for keel-up assembly. Several blocks sat under weather tarpaulin when the scan crew passed, so those rows carry a design gap but no reading at all. At least one scanned block sits just under the deviation threshold and reads as alarming without being an anomaly, while another clears it only narrowly. Grade the register honestly before the assembly sequence is locked.
objectives: Compute record count over every row in a partially populated measurement register
Derive completeness percentage as 100 x rows carrying a reading / all rows
Calculate mean absolute error over present readings only, excluding missing rows from the denominator
Count anomalies using a strict greater-than test against the deviation threshold
Distinguish near-threshold deviations from genuine threshold breaches
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic shipbuilding data-quality exercise; no external source data used.
scenarios.disclaimers: All blocks, identifiers and measurements are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real vessel, yard or survey record.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - record_count. Count every row regardless of whether a reading is present: 20 rows, so record_count = 20.

Step 2 - completeness_pct. Rows with a present reading = 20 - 3 missing (BK-103, BK-108, BK-114) = 17. completeness_pct = 100 x 17 / 20 = 85.00.

Step 3 - mean_abs_error. Compute |value - expected| for PRESENT rows only:
BK-101 0.4, BK-102 0.4, BK-104 3.2, BK-105 0.0, BK-106 1.4, BK-107 3.4, BK-109 0.2, BK-110 2.3, BK-111 0.0, BK-112 2.6, BK-113 0.5, BK-115 0.2, BK-116 0.4, BK-117 0.0, BK-118 4.6, BK-119 0.5, BK-120 1.1.
Sum = 21.2 over 17 present rows.
mean_abs_error = 21.2 / 17 = 1.2470588 -> 1.25.
The trap: dividing by all 20 rows gives 1.06, understating true scan error because missing rows contribute no error yet would inflate the denominator.

Step 4 - anomaly_count. Threshold = 2.5; a breach means deviation strictly greater than 2.5. Breaches: BK-104 (3.2), BK-107 (3.4), BK-112 (2.6), BK-118 (4.6) = 4. BK-110 at 2.3 is a near-miss and is NOT an anomaly. Missing rows are never anomalies.
anomaly_count = 4.

Final: record_count = 20, completeness_pct = 85.00, mean_abs_error = 1.25, anomaly_count = 4.

config.prompt: A shipyard dimensional control cell laser-scans erection gaps on twenty pre-outfitted hull blocks staged for keel-up assembly. Each row lists a block id, the design gap in millimetres as "expected", and the scanned gap as "value". Some blocks were still under weather tarpaulin when the scan crew passed, so those rows carry no reading at all. The deviation threshold is supplied with the data; a row is an anomaly only when its reading deviates from design by more than that threshold. From the figures below compute: the record count across all rows, the completeness percentage (100 x rows carrying a reading / all rows), the mean absolute error across rows that actually carry a reading, and the anomaly count. Round the percentage and the mean absolute error to two decimals; counts are whole numbers.

scenarios.title: Earned Schedule Check on a Drought-Resilience Intake Upgrade
scenarios.summary: Interpolate earned schedule from a cumulative PV curve for a water intake upgrade, strip out a rejected change from reported EV, and forecast time-based completion with SPI(t).
scenarios.brief: A regional utility is upgrading its raw-water intake and pre-treatment works as part of a drought-resilience program: a new low-level intake screen, twin sedimentation basins, and an interconnecting gravity main. The 8-month baseline is under pressure after river access restrictions slowed basin excavation. At the month-5 review, the contractor's progress report includes a scope change the change board actually rejected, so you must validate earned value before running the earned-schedule analysis the steering group has asked for.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by linear interpolation between two periods of a cumulative planned-value curve
Distinguish approved earned value from claimed earned value that includes a rejected change
Compute time-based schedule variance SV(t) and performance index SPI(t) from ES and actual time
Forecast a time-based estimate at completion EAC(t) using planned duration and SPI(t)
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, utility, or contractor.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Validate EV. The contractor's month-5 report claims cumulative earned value of 228, but this includes 28 earned against change request CR-14, which the change board REJECTED (the contractor's log is out of date). Validated EV = 228 - 28 = 200.

Step 2 — Earned schedule (ES). Find where EV = 200 sits on the cumulative PV curve. PV(3) = 160 and PV(4) = 240, so 160 < 200 < 240 and ES lies between periods 3 and 4. Interpolate: ES = 3 + (EV - PV(3)) / (PV(4) - PV(3)) = 3 + (200 - 160) / (240 - 160) = 3 + 40/80 = 3.50 months.

Step 3 — Time-based schedule variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 3.50 - 5 = -1.50 months. The project has earned only 3.5 months of the plan in 5 months of work — 1.5 months behind.

Step 4 — Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 3.50 / 5 = 0.70.

Step 5 — Time-based estimate at completion. EAC(t) = planned_duration / SPI(t) = 8 / 0.70 = 11.4286 ≈ 11.43 months, versus the 8-month baseline — about 3.4 months of forecast slip if performance does not improve.

Final answers: ES = 3.50; SV(t) = -1.50; SPI(t) = 0.70; EAC(t) = 11.43.

config.prompt: You are the project controls analyst on a regional utility's drought-resilience intake upgrade (new low-level intake screen, twin sedimentation basins, interconnecting gravity main), baselined at 8 months. Cumulative planned value by month: 40, 95, 160, 240, 330, 420, 490, 540 (final cumulative PV 540). It is the end of month 5 (AT = 5). The contractor reports cumulative earned value of 228, but that figure includes 28 earned against change request CR-14, which the change board rejected; only board-approved scope may earn value. Using the validated earned value, compute: 1) es — earned schedule ES, in months, interpolating linearly between the two months of the cumulative PV curve that bracket the validated EV; 2) sv_time — time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT, in months; 3) spi_time — schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT; 4) eac_time — time-based estimate at completion EAC(t) = planned duration / SPI(t), in months. Round all answers, including indices, to 2 decimal places.

scenarios.title: Earned Schedule Check: Seismic Instrumentation Refit
scenarios.summary: Convert earned value into earned schedule for a lagging seismic instrumentation refit at a nuclear station: interpolate ES on the cumulative PV curve, then derive SV(t) and SPI(t).
scenarios.brief: The station's outage readiness board has flagged the seismic instrumentation refit as a schedule concern. The cumulative planned-value curve for the six-period campaign was baselined before mobilisation, but containment access windows have been tighter than expected and earned value is lagging the plan. As the project controls analyst, you must translate the cost-based earned value into time-based measures using earned schedule, so the board sees slippage in periods rather than value units.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by linear interpolation on a cumulative planned-value curve
Compute time-based schedule variance SV(t) and interpret its sign in periods
Compute SPI(t) and explain why time-based indices outperform cost-based SV late in a project
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real facility, project, or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution: For the canonical figures: Cumulative PV curve is 100, 250, 450, 700, 900, 1000 over periods 1-6; AT = 4; EV = 350. Step 1 - locate EV on the PV curve: EV = 350 lies between PV(2) = 250 and PV(3) = 450, so ES is between periods 2 and 3. Step 2 - interpolate: ES = 2 + (EV - PV(2)) / (PV(3) - PV(2)) = 2 + (350 - 250) / (450 - 250) = 2 + 100/200 = 2.50 periods. Step 3 - schedule variance in time: SV(t) = ES - AT = 2.50 - 4 = -1.50 periods, meaning the work completed by period 4 was planned to be done by period 2.5, i.e. the campaign is 1.5 periods behind. Step 4 - time-based index: SPI(t) = ES / AT = 2.50 / 4 = 0.625, rounded to 0.63, confirming the project is progressing at roughly 63% of the planned rate. (For reference, a time forecast would be EAC(t) = planned_duration / SPI(t) = 6 / 0.625 = 9.6 periods.) Final answers: ES = 2.50, SV(t) = -1.50, SPI(t) = 0.63.

config.prompt: A twin-unit nuclear power station is running a six-period seismic instrumentation refit inside the reactor auxiliary building. The baseline cumulative planned value (PV) curve is: period 1 = 100, period 2 = 250, period 3 = 450, period 4 = 700, period 5 = 900, period 6 = 1,000. Planned duration is 6 periods. A status review is held at actual time AT = 4 periods, and the cumulative earned value achieved to date is the figure shown below. Using linear interpolation on the cumulative PV curve, compute: (1) the earned schedule ES in periods, (2) the schedule variance in time SV(t) = ES - AT in periods, and (3) the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT. Report ES and SV(t) in periods and round SPI(t) and ES to 2 decimal places. Do not use currency units; all values are in plain value units.

ask.label: Earned schedule ES (periods, to 2 decimal places)
Schedule variance in time SV(t) = ES - AT (periods)
Time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) (2 decimal places)

scenarios.title: Donor-Milk Cold-Chain Rollout: Earned Schedule at the Month-8 Gate
scenarios.summary: A nine-hospital neonatal donor-milk traceability programme reaches its month-8 sponsor gate. Convert a cumulative PV curve and earned value into ES, SV(t), SPI(t) and EAC(t) to forecast the real go-live.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic regional care network is deploying a shared donor-milk cold-chain traceability platform across nine hospital sites: chilled-transport sensors, bedside scanning at the cot, and a central pasteurisation batch registry. The 12-period plan was sold to the board on a fixed neonatal accreditation date, and cost variance alone has looked benign because unspent integration effort is masking slipped site cutovers. At the month-8 gate the sponsor wants the slip stated in months, not in value. Earned schedule converts the value curve into calendar language and produces a defensible finish-date forecast.
objectives: Locate the earned schedule interval by comparing earned value against the cumulative planned value curve
Interpolate ES linearly between two plan periods and express it in periods to four decimals
Compute SV(t) and SPI(t) and interpret each as calendar slip rather than value variance
Forecast EAC(t) from planned duration and SPI(t) and compare it to the committed 12-period plan
Explain to a sponsor why a time-based index changes the go-live conversation
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab from a synthetic multi-site healthcare deployment plan; no real organisation or dataset is represented.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they are not drawn from any real programme and are not benchmark data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: EV = 6320, AT = 8, PD = 12.
Step 1 - Bracket the earned value on the cumulative PV curve. The last period whose cumulative PV does not exceed EV is period 6 (PV6 = 5480); the next is period 7 (PV7 = 7060). So N = 6.
Step 2 - Interpolate. ES = N + (EV - PV_N) / (PV_(N+1) - PV_N) = 6 + (6320 - 5480) / (7060 - 5480) = 6 + 840 / 1580 = 6.5316 periods.
Step 3 - Schedule variance (time). SV(t) = ES - AT = 6.5316 - 8 = -1.4684 periods.
Step 4 - Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 6.5316 / 8 = 0.8165.
Step 5 - Time-based estimate at completion. EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) = 12 / 0.8165 = 14.6977 periods (equivalently PD x AT / ES = 96 / 6.5316).
Final values: es = 6.5316, sv_time = -1.4684, spi_time = 0.8165, eac_time = 14.6977.
Reading for the sponsor: eight months of calendar have bought roughly 6.53 months of plan, so the programme is about 1.47 months behind and earning schedule at about 82 percent of the planned rate. Held at that rate, the 12-period plan lands near period 14.70 - roughly 2.70 periods past the committed accreditation go-live, which is the number the board must either fund down or re-baseline.

config.prompt: Nine hospitals in a synthetic regional care network are deploying a shared donor-milk cold-chain traceability platform: chilled-transport sensors, bedside scanning at the cot, and a central pasteurisation batch registry. The plan runs 12 monthly periods, and the data date is the end of period 8. The cumulative planned value curve and the earned value at the data date are given in the figures below. Using earned schedule, compute: the earned schedule ES in periods; the schedule variance (time) SV(t) in periods; the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t); and the time-based estimate at completion EAC(t) in periods. Interpolate ES linearly between the two plan periods that bracket the earned value. Report every answer rounded to four decimal places.

scenarios.title: Footbridge Frame: First EVM Health Check
scenarios.summary: A prefabricated timber footbridge project is spending faster than it is earning. Compute SV, CV, and CPI from a single monthly snapshot to size the problem for the sponsor.
scenarios.brief: You are the junior project controller on a prefabricated cross-laminated timber footbridge being erected across a drainage canal. Wet weather has slowed panel deliveries, and the erection crane has been kept on standby at full day rate, so costs are running ahead of the work actually installed. The sponsor has asked for a one-page variance summary before approving the next drawdown, and you must produce the core earned value figures from this month's snapshot.
objectives: Compute schedule variance (SV) and cost variance (CV) from a single EVM snapshot
Compute the cost performance index (CPI) and round it to 2 decimal places
Interpret negative variances as behind-schedule and over-budget signals for a sponsor briefing
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project, company, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 400, EV = 360, AC = 450, BAC = 1200.

Step 1 — Schedule Variance: SV = EV − PV = 360 − 400 = −40. The project has earned 40 less than planned for this point, so it is behind schedule.

Step 2 — Cost Variance: CV = EV − AC = 360 − 450 = −90. The work earned cost 90 more than its budgeted value, confirming the sponsor's overspend concern.

Step 3 — Cost Performance Index: CPI = EV / AC = 360 / 450 = 0.80 (2 decimal places). Every unit spent is returning only 0.80 of budgeted work — the crane standby costs are eroding cost efficiency.

Final answers: SV = −40, CV = −90, CPI = 0.80.

config.prompt: You are the project controller on a prefabricated timber footbridge being erected across a drainage canal. Rain delays have held up panel deliveries while the erection crane sits on standby at full day rate, and the sponsor wants variance figures before releasing the next payment. Using the month-end figures shown below (planned value PV, earned value EV, actual cost AC, and budget at completion BAC), compute: (1) Schedule Variance SV = EV - PV, (2) Cost Variance CV = EV - AC, and (3) the Cost Performance Index CPI = EV / AC. Report variances as plain numbers (negative if unfavourable) and round the index to 2 decimal places.

scenarios.title: Busway Viaduct Overspend: CPI Forecast Under a Rejected Change
scenarios.summary: Month-8 cost health check on an elevated busway viaduct: compute CV, CPI, a CPI-based EAC, and VAC — while spotting that a rejected change request must not inflate the baseline.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls analyst on a 4.2 km elevated busway viaduct programme at its month-8 status snapshot. Girder erection has fallen behind the launch sequence while night-shift premiums and crane standby charges have pushed spending up, and the sponsor wants a defensible forecast before the next steering committee. Complicating matters, the contractor's monthly report presents change request CR-17 (value 60000, for utility relocation) as if it were approved — but the change board rejected it, so the performance measurement baseline is unchanged.
objectives: Compute cost variance and the cost performance index from a single EVM status snapshot
Forecast estimate at completion using the CPI-based method (EAC = BAC / CPI)
Compute variance at completion and interpret its sign for sponsor reporting
Distinguish a rejected change request from an approved baseline change when selecting BAC
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, organisation, or contract.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 300000, EV = 264000, AC = 292000, BAC = 720000. Change request CR-17 (60000) was rejected by the change board, so BAC remains 720000 — do not add CR-17 to any figure.

Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 264000 - 292000 = -28000. Negative, so the work performed cost more than its earned budget.

Step 2 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 264000 / 292000 = 0.90411... ≈ 0.90 (2 dp). Each unit spent is earning about 0.90 of value.

Step 3 — Estimate at completion (current cost performance continues): EAC = BAC / CPI = 720000 / 0.90411 = 796363.64. Use the unrounded CPI here — dividing by the rounded 0.90 would give 800000 and overstate the forecast.

Step 4 — Variance at completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 720000 - 796363.64 = -76363.64. A negative VAC means the project is forecast to finish about 76363.64 over budget if cost efficiency does not improve — the figure the sponsor needs for the steering committee.

Key trap: had you treated CR-17 as approved and used BAC = 780000, every forecast figure would be wrong. Only board-approved changes move the performance measurement baseline.

config.prompt: You are the controls analyst on an elevated busway viaduct programme at its month-8 snapshot. scenarios.title: Dehydration Skid Refurbishment: Reading the Month-4 EVM Snapshot
scenarios.summary: A gas terminal's dehydration skid refurbishment is burning cash faster than it earns value. Compute SV, CV, and CPI from a single monthly snapshot to size the problem.
scenarios.brief: A midstream operator is refurbishing the glycol dehydration skid at one of its inland gas processing terminals: new contactor internals, replacement reboiler tubes, and re-instrumented moisture analysers. At the month-4 progress review, the sponsor is uneasy — invoiced costs from the mechanical contractor look high against the work certified complete. As the project controls analyst, you must turn the snapshot figures into variances and a cost index the steering committee can act on.
objectives: Compute schedule variance (SV) and cost variance (CV) from a single EVM snapshot
Compute the cost performance index (CPI) and round it to 2 decimal places
Interpret negative variances and a CPI below 1.0 as signals of schedule slip and cost overrun
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, facility, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 10000, EV = 9000, AC = 12000, BAC = 45000.

Step 1 — Schedule Variance: SV = EV - PV = 9000 - 10000 = -1000. Negative, so the refurbishment has earned 1000 less value than planned to date: a modest schedule slip.

Step 2 — Cost Variance: CV = EV - AC = 9000 - 12000 = -3000. Negative, so the work certified complete has cost 3000 more than it is worth: this is the overspend the sponsor noticed.

Step 3 — Cost Performance Index: CPI = EV / AC = 9000 / 12000 = 0.75. Rounded to 2 decimal places: 0.75. Every unit spent is earning only 0.75 units of value, so cost efficiency — not schedule — is the dominant problem at month 4.

scenarios.title: Coastal Radar Mid-Life Upgrade — Cost Pressure at the Integration Gate
scenarios.project_type: Naval coastal surveillance radar mid-life upgrade
scenarios.summary: A defence radar mid-life upgrade is overspending during antenna integration while a rejected scope change still inflates the contractor's dashboard budget. Compute variances, CPI, EAC and VAC from the true baseline.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls analyst on a mid-life upgrade of a coastal surveillance radar chain: replacing the transmitter cabinets, re-blading the signal processors, and re-certifying the array on a live naval site. At the current reporting snapshot the integration work is running behind and over cost, and the sponsor wants a forecast before the next gate review. Complicating matters, the contractor's dashboard shows a budget that includes change request CR-114 (a 5000 uplift for spare transmitter modules) — but the change board REJECTED CR-114 last week, so the approved budget at completion remains as originally baselined.
objectives: Compute cost variance and CPI from a single EVM snapshot
Compute a CPI-based estimate at completion and the variance at completion
Distinguish the approved budget at completion from an unapproved (rejected) change-inflated figure
Interpret an unfavourable cost trend for a sponsor-facing gate review
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real programme, contractor, or defence organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution: For the canonical figures: PV = 15600, EV = 14100, AC = 16400, BAC = 42000. Note the twist first: CR-114 was rejected, so the dashboard figure of 47000 is NOT the budget — use the approved BAC of 42000 throughout. Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 14100 - 16400 = -2300. Work performed has cost 2300 more than it earned. Step 2 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 14100 / 16400 = 0.8598..., which rounds to 0.86. Every unit spent is earning about 0.86 of value. Step 3 — CPI-based estimate at completion: EAC = BAC / CPI. Use the unrounded CPI (equivalently EAC = BAC × AC / EV) = 42000 × 16400 / 14100 = 48851.06. Step 4 — Variance at completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 42000 - 48851.06 = -6851.06. Interpretation for the gate review: with SPI = 14100/15600 = 0.90 and CPI = 0.86, the project is behind schedule and over cost; if current cost efficiency persists, the upgrade will finish roughly 6851 over the approved baseline — and quoting the rejected-CR figure of 47000 would understate the overrun the sponsor actually faces.

scenarios.title: MRI Suite Fit-Out: Reading the First Cost and Schedule Signals
scenarios.project_type: Hospital MRI suite fit-out with magnetic shielding
scenarios.summary: A hospital imaging-wing MRI fit-out shows early signs of overspend on shielding work. Compute schedule variance, cost variance, and CPI from a single status snapshot.
scenarios.brief: A regional hospital is fitting out a new MRI suite: radiofrequency shielding, a quench vent, and a reinforced magnet slab. objectives: Compute schedule variance (SV) and cost variance (CV) from a single EVM snapshot
Compute the cost performance index (CPI) and round it to 2 decimal places
Interpret negative variances as behind-schedule and over-cost signals for a sponsor briefing

scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 400, EV = 360, AC = 450, BAC = 1600.

Step 1 — Schedule variance: SV = EV - PV = 360 - 400 = -40. The negative value means less work has been earned than was planned by this date: the fit-out is behind schedule.

Step 2 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 360 - 450 = -90. The negative value means the work earned so far cost more than it was budgeted to cost: the project is over cost, consistent with the board's concern about the shielding package.

Step 3 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 360 / 450 = 0.80 (2 decimal places). Every unit spent is returning only 0.80 units of budgeted work — a clear efficiency problem to raise at the Friday review.

Sanity check: both variances are negative and CPI < 1.0, so the cost and schedule stories agree with each other.

scenarios.title: Calder Vale Aquifer Recharge: Reading the Control Account Cold
scenarios.project_type: Managed aquifer recharge and injection wellfield programme
scenarios.summary: A water utility's aquifer recharge programme hits an unmapped fissure zone. Convert planned value, earned value, actual cost and budget at completion into the five indices and forecasts the programme board will ask for.
scenarios.brief: The Calder Vale Managed Aquifer Recharge Programme banks winter river flow underground for summer release through a 26-well injection field, a ceramic-membrane pretreatment train and 11 km of transfer main. Fourteen months in, two wells struck an unmapped fissure zone; grouting and re-drilling consumed float and cash at the same time. The control account now shows earned value trailing both plan and spend, and the board wants a defensible forecast rather than a narrative. Your job is to turn four raw figures into performance indices, a cost-based forecast to completion, and the efficiency the remaining work must achieve.
objectives: Compute SPI and CPI from planned value, earned value and actual cost and state what each says about the wellfield programme
Derive the CPI-based estimate at completion using EAC = BAC / CPI
Calculate variance at completion and interpret its sign as an overrun or underrun against the approved budget
Compute the to-complete performance index against the original budget and judge whether recovery is realistic
Round index and money results to the precision a programme board report requires
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic earned-value exercise; formulas follow standard earned value management practice.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, figures and site conditions in this scenario are synthetic and simplified for training; they are not drawn from any real project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 14860000, EV = 13275000, AC = 14410000, BAC = 26940000.

1) Schedule performance index: SPI = EV / PV = 13275000 / 14860000 = 0.893. Below 1, so earned progress trails the plan.

2) Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 13275000 / 14410000 = 0.921. About 0.92 of value returned per unit spent — the fissure-zone rework is being paid for without earning scope.

3) CPI-based estimate at completion: EAC = BAC / CPI = 26940000 / 0.921235 = 29243345 (nearest whole number). This assumes cost efficiency to date persists to the end of the programme.

4) Variance at completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 26940000 - 29243345 = -2303345. Negative, so the forecast is an overrun of roughly 2.3 million against the approved budget.

5) To-complete performance index against the original budget: TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = (26940000 - 13275000) / (26940000 - 14410000) = 13665000 / 12530000 = 1.091. Remaining work must run about 18 percent more cost-efficiently than performance to date (1.091 versus 0.921) to land on budget — the gap the board must either fund or descope.

Supporting reads: SV = EV - PV = -1585000; CV = EV - AC = -1135000; ETC = EAC - AC = 14833345.

scenarios.title: Three EACs, One Outage: Forecasting an RCP Seal-Package Replacement
scenarios.project_type: reactor coolant pump seal-package replacement outage
scenarios.summary: Expert guided lab on earned value and forecasting for a nuclear outage work package, where three legitimate EAC formulas disagree sharply and TCPI tests whether the plan is still reachable.
scenarios.brief: Unit 3 of a synthetic nuclear station is executing a reactor coolant pump seal-package replacement inside a fixed refuelling outage window. The containment-side path closed out early, so the outage director is briefing steady progress, while a parallel cable-tray re-route path quietly absorbs overtime crews. The learner works from cost-account totals in labour-hours and must produce variances, indices, three different estimates at completion, and the to-complete performance index. The tension is deliberate: the optimistic budget-rate forecast, the CPI-based forecast and the composite forecast diverge by a wide margin, and only one of them reflects the schedule pressure still in the system.
objectives: Compute schedule and cost variance and their matching performance indices from raw PV, EV, AC and BAC totals
Derive EAC three ways - CPI-based, composite CPI x SPI, and budget-rate - from one data set
Explain why the budget-rate EAC understates exposure when schedule pressure persists into remaining work
Calculate TCPI against BAC and judge whether the original budget is still achievable
Apply consistent rounding rules without propagating intermediate rounding
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original expert-level earned value and forecasting exercise; all figures constructed by the author.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, figures and outage details are entirely synthetic and simplified for training and represent no real facility or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 262500, EV = 241500, AC = 276000, BAC = 615000 labour-hours.

1. SV = EV - PV = 241500 - 262500 = -21000.00.
2. CV = EV - AC = 241500 - 276000 = -34500.00.
3. SPI = EV / PV = 241500 / 262500 = 0.9200.
4. CPI = EV / AC = 241500 / 276000 = 0.8750.
5. CPI-based EAC = BAC / CPI = 615000 / 0.875 = 702857.14.
6. Composite EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI). Remaining = 615000 - 241500 = 373500; CPI x SPI = 0.875 x 0.92 = 0.805; 373500 / 0.805 = 463975.16; EAC = 276000 + 463975.16 = 739975.16.
7. Budget-rate EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 276000 + 373500 = 649500.00. This is the trap: it assumes all remaining seal-package and cable-tray work runs exactly at plan rate despite CPI 0.875 and SPI 0.92 to date, flattering the outcome by about 53000 hours against the CPI-based view and about 90000 against the composite view.
8. TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 373500 / 339000 = 1.1018. Remaining work would have to run about 10.2 percent better than plan while performance to date is 12.5 percent worse than plan, so the budget is not credibly recoverable and the composite EAC is the defensible forecast to brief.

Round indices and TCPI to 4 decimals, hour amounts to 2 decimals, and do not round intermediate results.

1. Read the final month (period 10): EV = 41400, AC = 53200, PV = 48000 = BAC.
2. Final SPI = EV / PV = 41400 / 48000 = 0.8625.
3. Final CPI = EV / AC = 41400 / 53200 = 0.7782.

scenarios.summary: A guided lab on weighted portfolio scoring: normalise NPV, apply risk and fit weights, and rank four precast work packages where the biggest earner is not the best pick.
scenarios.brief: A precast concrete yard supplying deck panels for coastal causeway repairs has more bid invitations than casting-bed capacity for the coming season. Four candidate work packages differ sharply in cash value, delivery risk and how well they fit the yard's standard mould set. The selection committee uses a single weighted index so value, risk and strategic fit are traded off explicitly rather than argued informally. objectives: Normalise each candidate's NPV against the largest absolute NPV in the candidate set

Step 1 - Normalise NPV. The largest absolute NPV in the set is |800| = 800, so normalised NPV = npv / 800. P1: 1.00; P2: 0.75; P3: -0.25; P4: 0.50.

Step 2 - Apply score = 0.5 x (npv / max|npv|) + 0.2 x fit - 0.3 x risk.
P1 = 0.5(1.00) + 0.2(0.5) - 0.3(0.6) = 0.500 + 0.100 - 0.180 = 0.42
P2 = 0.5(0.75) + 0.2(0.8) - 0.3(0.2) = 0.375 + 0.160 - 0.060 = 0.475 (0.48 at 2 dp)
P3 = 0.5(-0.25) + 0.2(0.9) - 0.3(0.4) = -0.125 + 0.180 - 0.120 = -0.065
P4 = 0.5(0.50) + 0.2(0.6) - 0.3(0.3) = 0.250 + 0.120 - 0.090 = 0.28

Step 3 - Total portfolio NPV = 800 + 600 + (-200) + 400 = 1600.

Step 4 - Highest score in the set = P2 at 0.475.

Answers: total_npv = 1600; score_P1 = 0.42; top_score = 0.475.

Interpretation: P1 carries the largest NPV and so earns the maximum normalised value term, but its 0.6 risk costs 0.18 of score, while P2 pairs strong fit with the lowest risk and wins. P3 is value-destroying and scores negative despite the best fit rating.

P5: 0.5 x 0.202703 + 0.2 x 0.40 - 0.3 x 0.15 = 0.1364
P6: 0.5 x 0.445946 + 0.2 x 0.70 - 0.3 x 0.45 = 0.2280
P7: 0.5 x 0.682432 + 0.2 x 0.85 - 0.3 x 0.70 = 0.3412 + 0.1700 - 0.2100 = 0.3012
P8: 0.5 x 0.128378 + 0.2 x 0.30 - 0.3 x 0.20 = 0.0642

Step 3 - top_score = 0.4062 (P2). P7 holds the second-largest NPV yet its 0.70 risk index pushes it below P1's 0.3388.

Step 4 - total_npv = 420 + 610 + 285 - 740 + 150 + 330 + 505 + 95 = 1655.00.

Traps: normalising by 610 inflates every score, and excluding the mandated loss-maker overstates the total as 2395.

scenarios.title: Weighted Progress at the Reedmarsh Sludge Dewatering Upgrade
scenarios.summary: Roll up work-package percent complete into a single weighted progress figure for a water treatment sludge dewatering upgrade, and see why the sponsor's "it looks 75% done" impression is misleading.
scenarios.brief: The Reedmarsh water treatment works is replacing its ageing belt presses with two new centrifuge dewatering trains. The civil enabling works finished quickly and the site looks well advanced, so the programme sponsor believes the job is about three-quarters complete. As the project controls analyst, you must weight each work package by its budget share and report the true overall percent complete before the next steering meeting.
objectives: Compute overall percent complete as a budget-weighted average of work-package progress
Compute the total weighting basis used to normalise the roll-up
Interpret why unweighted or visual impressions of progress can overstate true completion
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or site.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Confirm the weighting basis. Total weight = 40 + 25 + 15 + 12 + 8 = 100.

Step 2 — Multiply each work package's weight by its percent complete:
- 1.1 Civil enabling works: 40 x 90 = 3600
- 1.2 Centrifuge train A installation: 25 x 60 = 1500
- 1.3 Centrifuge train B installation: 15 x 40 = 600
- 1.4 Polymer dosing system: 12 x 25 = 300
- 1.5 Commissioning and handover: 8 x 0 = 0

Step 3 — Sum the weighted contributions: 3600 + 1500 + 600 + 300 + 0 = 6000.

Step 4 — Divide by the total weight: overall percent complete = 6000 / 100 = 60.00%.

Interpretation: although the site visually looks about 75% done because the heavily weighted civil package is at 90%, the mechanical, dosing, and commissioning packages drag the true budget-weighted progress down to 60.00%. Total weight = 100.

scenarios.brief: Unit 2 of a twin-reactor station is running out of wet storage margin, so the owner is expanding the independent dry cask storage facility with a new pad, reinforced haul path, and transporter commissioning. Month-end progress is due to the oversight board tomorrow, but the civil contractor's submission includes an extra line item tied to change request CR-22 — a request the change board rejected two weeks ago. As the project controls analyst, you must produce the official weighted progress roll-up using only the approved control-account structure.
objectives: Compute a budget-weighted overall percent complete across multiple work packages
Distinguish approved scope from a rejected change request when assembling a progress roll-up
Interpret the effect of unauthorized scope on a weighted progress figure
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real facility, licensee, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Screen the scope. The contractor's report lists seven lines, but the seventh (weight 300, 80% complete) is tied to CR-22, which the change board REJECTED. Rejected changes carry no budget weight and must be excluded, leaving the six approved packages.

Step 2 — Total weight. Sum the approved weights:
420 + 260 + 310 + 195 + 145 + 170 = 1500.

Step 3 — Weighted contributions (weight x percent):
1.1 Pad civil works: 420 x 92 = 38640
1.2 Haul path reinforcement: 260 x 78 = 20280
1.3 Cask transporter commissioning: 310 x 55 = 17050
1.4 Security and monitoring integration: 195 x 40 = 7800
1.5 Licensing documentation package: 145 x 66 = 9570
1.6 Operator training and dry runs: 170 x 25 = 4250
Sum of contributions = 97590.

Step 4 — Overall percent complete = 97590 / 1500 = 65.06%.

Check the trap: including the rejected CR-22 line would give (97590 + 300 x 80) / (1500 + 300) = 121590 / 1800 = 67.55% — an overstated figure that would mislead the oversight board.

Final answers: total_weight = 1500; overall_percent = 65.06.

scenarios.title: Weighted Progress Roll-Up for a Live-Hospital MRI Suite Retrofit
scenarios.summary: Roll seven unevenly weighted work packages of a live-hospital MRI suite retrofit into one defensible weighted percent complete for a funding-tranche decision.
scenarios.brief: A live community hospital is converting shell space on its imaging floor into an interventional MRI suite while the adjacent surgical wing keeps operating. Seven work packages carry very different weights, and the loudest packages are not the heaviest ones. The sponsor must decide whether to release the next construction tranche and confirm the radiology staffing start date, so a single defensible weighted completion figure is needed rather than a simple average of package percentages.
objectives: Compute the total weight of a seven-package work breakdown from package-level weights
Convert each package's physical percent complete into earned weight units
Aggregate earned weight into an overall weighted percent complete, rounded to two decimals
Explain why a weighted roll-up differs from an unweighted average of package percentages
State the rolled-up completion figure in terms a funding sponsor can act on
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab using standard weighted-milestone progress measurement practice; all data invented.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, packages and the facility described are synthetic and simplified for training; they model no real project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Total weight. Sum every package weight: 148 + 63 + 87 + 126 + 94 + 112 + 71 = 701. total_weight = 701.

Step 2 - Earned weight per package, using earned = weight x percent / 100:
1.1: 148 x 0.925 = 136.90
1.2: 63 x 1.00 = 63.00
1.3: 87 x 0.74 = 64.38
1.4: 126 x 0.585 = 73.71
1.5: 94 x 0.41 = 38.54
1.6: 112 x 0.125 = 14.00
1.7: 71 x 0.00 = 0.00

Step 3 - Total earned weight: 136.90 + 63.00 + 64.38 + 73.71 + 38.54 + 14.00 + 0.00 = 390.53.

Step 4 - Overall weighted percent complete:
overall_percent = (total earned weight / total weight) x 100 = (390.53 / 701) x 100 = 55.7104... = 55.71 percent.

Sanity check for the sponsor: the unweighted average of the seven package percentages is (92.5 + 100 + 74 + 58.5 + 41 + 12.5 + 0) / 7 = 54.07 percent. The weighted figure is higher because the two heaviest packages (1.1 at 148 and 1.4 at 126) are further along than the light, late packages. The defensible number is 55.71 percent against 701 total weight units, with commissioning (1.7) not yet started and therefore fully at risk against the go-live date.

scenarios.title: Membrane Skid Late Delivery on the Aquifer Recharge Scheme
scenarios.project_type: Groundwater aquifer recharge treatment plant build
scenarios.summary: A late membrane skid delivery eats through a slim schedule buffer on a water recharge plant. Compute the critical delay, the revised project duration, and the float consumed.
scenarios.brief: The Harrow Vale Aquifer Recharge Scheme is building a nanofiltration plant that polishes river water before it is injected into a depleted chalk aquifer. The membrane skid is a critical-path item: nothing downstream can be commissioned until it is set on its plinth. The fabricator has just notified the delivery team that the skid will ship late, and the activity carries only a slim buffer. Translate the supplier's slip into schedule impact before the sponsor review.
objectives: Compute critical delay as the portion of a supplier slip that exceeds remaining float
Recalculate total project duration after a procurement delay hits the critical path
Quantify the float consumed by a late supplier delivery
Distinguish float erosion from genuine critical-path extension
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic guided lab on procurement delay impact.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures and entities are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, supplier or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Critical delay: critical_delay = max(0, supplier_delay_days - remaining_float) = max(0, 11 - 4) = 7 days. Only the slip beyond the buffer pushes the critical path.

Step 2 - New project duration: new_project_duration = project_duration + critical_delay = 180 + 7 = 187 days.

Step 3 - Float consumed: float_consumed = min(remaining_float, supplier_delay_days) = min(4, 11) = 4 days. The slip is larger than the buffer, so the entire remaining float is absorbed and the activity now has zero float.

Final answers: critical_delay = 7 days, new_project_duration = 187 days, float_consumed = 4 days. Interpretation: 4 of the 11 slipped days are absorbed by buffer, the other 7 extend the programme, and the skid delivery is now fully critical with no protection against any further supplier slip.

Using these figures, calculate: (1) the critical delay in days, (2) the new project duration in days, and (3) the float consumed in days. Report each answer as a plain number of days rounded to two decimal places.

scenarios.title: Forged Vessel Nozzle Slip: Critical-Path Procurement Impact
scenarios.project_type: small modular reactor vessel nozzle procurement package
scenarios.summary: A sole-source forging slip hits the critical path of a small modular reactor build. Convert the supplier delay into critical delay, revised duration and float consumed without being distracted by the non-binding paths.
scenarios.brief: A small modular reactor construction program buys its reactor-vessel penetration nozzles from a single qualified forge. The forge has notified a delivery slip, and the nozzle package is the driving activity on the approved critical path. A parallel steam-generator support-frame path carries far more float, and an unapproved change order for extra weld volumetric inspection is still with the change board. The controls team must translate the notified slip into schedule impact using only the critical-path figures.
objectives: Compute critical delay as max(0, supplier delay minus remaining float) on the driving activity
Derive the revised project duration by adding only the critical portion of a supplier slip
Quantify float consumed as min(remaining float, supplier delay) and distinguish it from the total slip
Exclude non-driving parallel paths and unapproved change orders from procurement impact analysis
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic sole-source procurement delay exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, entities and events are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, supplier or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: project_duration = 1460 days, remaining_float = 24 days, supplier_delay_days = 67 days.

Step 1 - Critical delay. Only the portion of the slip beyond the activity's remaining float pushes the end date. critical_delay = max(0, supplier_delay_days - remaining_float) = max(0, 67 - 24) = 43.00 days. The careless move is to add the full 67 days, or to let the parallel steam-generator path or the unapproved change order alter the arithmetic; neither is on the driving path and the change order is not approved, so both are excluded.

Step 2 - New project duration. Extend the approved duration by the critical portion only. new_project_duration = project_duration + critical_delay = 1460 + 43 = 1503.00 days.

Step 3 - Float consumed. Float can only be eaten up to what exists. float_consumed = min(remaining_float, supplier_delay_days) = min(24, 67) = 24.00 days. Self-check: float_consumed + critical_delay = 24 + 43 = 67, the full notified slip.

Answers: critical_delay = 43.00, new_project_duration = 1503.00, float_consumed = 24.00.

Using only the critical-path figures below - the approved project duration in days, the remaining float on the nozzle activity in days, and the notified supplier delay in days - compute the critical delay in days, the new project duration in days, and the float consumed in days. scenarios.title: Blast-Wall Pour Productivity Check: Harbour Grain Terminal
scenarios.summary: A foundation guided lab on unit-rate productivity: compute planned and actual cubic metres per labour hour for a marine grain terminal blast wall, then derive the performance factor.
scenarios.brief: You are the field controls analyst on a harbour grain terminal upgrade, where a reinforced concrete blast wall is being poured on night shifts squeezed between vessel berthings. Tide windows have been shortening, crews are breaking pours early, and the superintendent insists the package is only a little behind. The daily labour returns and the surveyed pour quantities tell a blunter story. Your job is to convert those raw figures into a unit rate the project team cannot argue with.
objectives: Compute planned productivity as planned quantity divided by planned labour hours
Compute actual productivity as earned quantity divided by actual labour hours
Derive the productivity factor as actual productivity divided by planned productivity
Interpret a productivity factor below 1.0 as labour under-performance against the estimate basis
Apply consistent rounding to three decimal places when reporting unit rates
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; synthetic construction labour-productivity dataset, no external source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and deliberately simplified for training; they do not represent any real project, crew or estimate.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: planned_qty = 480 m3, planned_hours = 600, earned_qty = 420 m3, actual_hours = 700.

Step 1 - Planned productivity = planned_qty / planned_hours = 480 / 600 = 0.800 m3 per labour hour. This is the estimate basis unit rate.

Step 2 - Actual productivity = earned_qty / actual_hours = 420 / 700 = 0.600 m3 per labour hour. Earned (surveyed in-place) quantity is the correct numerator, not claimed or forecast quantity.

Step 3 - Productivity factor = actual productivity / planned productivity = 0.600 / 0.800 = 0.750.

Interpretation: a factor of 0.750 means the crew achieves three quarters of the estimated output per labour hour. Supporting variances reinforce this: hours variance = 700 - 600 = +100 hours overspent, quantity variance = 420 - 480 = -60 m3 short. More hours burned for less wall in place. At the current rate the remaining 60 m3 would absorb roughly 100 further labour hours, so the shortened tide windows must be addressed rather than absorbed.

The latest cycle returns give the surveyed earned quantity placed and the actual labour hours charged. scenarios.title: Levee Corridor Cable Pull: Productivity Factor Under Standby Hours
scenarios.project_type: coastal levee HV cable duct-bank installation
scenarios.summary: Expert guided lab on cable-pulling productivity: separate earned scope from a lump-sum crew's metres and fold standby hours into the labour bill before computing the productivity factor.
scenarios.brief: A tide-gate flood corridor upgrade is pulling high-voltage cable through duct banks along an estuary levee. Two quantity streams and two hour streams land in the same weekly report, and only some of each belong to the crew being measured. The learner must build the productivity factor and the two variances from the correct subset, then judge the crew's real performance.
objectives: Compute planned and actual unit rates in metres pulled per labour hour
Derive the productivity factor as actual rate divided by planned rate
Exclude out-of-scope subcontract quantity from earned metres before rating the crew
Include standby and weather-hold hours in the actual hours denominator
Calculate hours variance and quantity variance against the labour bill
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic infrastructure productivity exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, organisation or crew.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Earned quantity for THIS labour bill: 18,400 m (main corridor) + 11,600 m (north spur) = 30,000 m. The 8,400 m pulled by the separate lump-sum specialist crew sits outside this bill and is excluded; counting it is the flattering error.

Step 2 - Actual hours: every hour charged to the crew counts, productive or not: 16,900 + 1,850 = 18,750 hours.

Step 3 - planned_productivity = 42,000 / 21,000 = 2.000 m per hour.

Step 4 - actual_productivity = 30,000 / 18,750 = 1.600 m per hour.

Step 5 - factor = 1.600 / 2.000 = 0.800, so the crew is 20 percent below the bill rate.

Step 6 - hours_variance = 18,750 - 21,000 = -2,250 hours.

Step 7 - qty_variance = 30,000 - 42,000 = -12,000 m.

Reading: the negative hours variance is not a saving. 71.4 percent of the metres were delivered for 89.3 percent of the hours, which is exactly the 0.800 factor. The careless route, (30,000 + 8,400) / 16,900 = 2.272 m per hour and a factor of 1.136, would report the crew as beating the plan.

scenarios.title: Decoy Launcher Integration — PERT Chain and Trials-Window Confidence
scenarios.project_type: Corvette mid-life decoy launcher integration refit
scenarios.summary: Run a three-point PERT analysis on a five-package shipboard decoy launcher integration, then estimate the probability of finishing inside a fixed 50-day trials window — after spotting a change request that only looks approved.
scenarios.brief: A navy's mid-life refit programme is fitting a new soft-kill decoy launcher to the lead ship of a corvette class. Five sequential work packages take the ship from harness fabrication through to harbour acceptance trials, and the dockyard has only a 50-day alongside window before the vessel must rejoin the fleet cycle. The integration contractor has lodged a change request to soften the software-integration estimates, and its status in the contractor tracker does not match the change board's decision — you must work from the true contractual baseline.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates for a serial activity chain.
Compute the standard deviation of a chain by summing activity variances, not standard deviations.
Interpret a z-score under the normal approximation to state the probability of meeting a fixed completion window.
Distinguish an approved change from a rejected one and apply the correct contractual baseline to the analysis.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, vessels, and organisations are synthetic and simplified for training purposes only.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Resolve the change status. CR-114 shows "approved — pending signature" in the contractor tracker, but the change board minutes record it as REJECTED. The contractual baseline for WP-D therefore remains 10 / 13 / 22 days; the proposed 8 / 10 / 14 figures must NOT be used.

Step 2 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A: (8 + 40 + 14)/6 = 10.33
B: (5 + 28 + 11)/6 = 7.33
C: (6 + 36 + 12)/6 = 9.00
D: (10 + 52 + 22)/6 = 14.00
E: (4 + 24 + 8)/6 = 6.00
Expected chain duration = 10.33 + 7.33 + 9.00 + 14.00 + 6.00 = 46.67 days.

Step 3 — Variance per activity, ((p − o)/6)^2:
A: (6/6)^2 = 1.00; B: (6/6)^2 = 1.00; C: (6/6)^2 = 1.00; D: (12/6)^2 = 4.00; E: (4/6)^2 = 0.44.
Chain variance = 7.44; standard deviation = sqrt(7.44) = 2.73 days. (Sum variances first — never sum standard deviations.)

Step 4 — Probability of meeting the 50-day window:
z = (deadline − expected) / std_dev = (50 − 46.67) / 2.73 = 1.22.
Φ(1.22) ≈ 0.889, so prob_on_time ≈ 88.91%.

Interpretation: roughly an 89% chance of clearing harbour trials inside the alongside window — reasonable confidence, but the software-integration package (WP-D) contributes over half the total variance and is where risk-reduction effort should focus.
