scenarios.title: MRI Suite Recommissioning: PERT Deadline Confidence
scenarios.summary: Use three-point estimates for a hospital MRI suite recommissioning chain to compute the expected duration, standard deviation, and the probability of reopening before a 21-week deadline.
scenarios.brief: A community hospital is decommissioning its ageing MRI scanner and installing a replacement 3-Tesla unit in the same shielded suite. Outpatient scans are being diverted to a costly external provider, and the diversion contract expires in 21 weeks — so the imaging manager needs a defensible estimate of whether the suite reopens in time. The four handover activities run strictly in sequence, and the magnet rigging step carries the widest uncertainty because crane access depends on third-party scheduling.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates
Compute the standard deviation of a serial activity chain by summing activity variances
Interpret a normal-approximation z-score as the probability of meeting a fixed deadline
Distinguish which activity contributes most schedule risk from its variance
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real hospital, vendor, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A Suite strip-out and shielding remediation: (4 + 4x5 + 6)/6 = 30/6 = 5.00 weeks
B Magnet delivery and rigging: (2 + 4x3 + 10)/6 = 24/6 = 4.00 weeks
C Ramp-up, shimming and calibration: (3 + 4x6 + 9)/6 = 36/6 = 6.00 weeks
D Clinical acceptance and physicist sign-off: (2 + 4x4 + 6)/6 = 24/6 = 4.00 weeks

Step 2 — Expected project duration (serial chain): 5 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 19.00 weeks.

Step 3 — Variance per activity, var = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A: (2/6)^2 = 0.1111
B: (8/6)^2 = 1.7778 (largest — rigging drives the risk)
C: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000
D: (4/6)^2 = 0.4444
Total variance = 3.3333 weeks^2.

Step 4 — Project standard deviation: sqrt(3.3333) = 1.83 weeks (2 dp).

Step 5 — Probability of meeting the 21-week deadline:
z = (21 - 19) / 1.8257 = 1.10 (2 dp: 1.10; unrounded 1.0954)
P(z <= 1.0954) from the standard normal distribution = approximately 0.8633.

Final answers: expected_duration = 19.00 weeks; std_dev = 1.83 weeks; prob_on_time = 86.33% (roughly an 86% chance of reopening before the diversion contract lapses — comfortable, but hinging on the rigging window).

3. The probability, as a percentage to 2 decimal places, that the suite reopens within the 21-week deadline.

scenarios.title: Drydock Countdown: Hybrid Ferry Refit PERT Analysis
scenarios.summary: Run a PERT three-point analysis on a five-activity drydock refit chain, filter out a rejected change request, and estimate the probability of handing the dock back on time.
scenarios.brief: A coastal yard has a 42-day drydock window to convert a double-ended ferry from diesel to hybrid-electric propulsion. The refit runs as a strict chain of five activities, and the dock master needs a defensible probability of on-time hand-back before committing to the next vessel's booking. A late change request complicates the plan: the superintendent's draft schedule still shows an extra alignment task that the change board formally rejected last week.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates
Compute the path standard deviation by combining activity variances
Interpret a z-score against a fixed deadline to estimate the probability of on-time completion
Distinguish approved scope from a rejected change request when assembling the analysis baseline
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real vessel, yard, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Baseline scope. Change request CR-17 (shaft-line laser re-alignment, 3/4/6 days) was REJECTED by the change board, so it is excluded. The chain is A-B-C-D-E only.

Step 2 — Expected durations, te = (o + 4m + p)/6:
A: (4+24+10)/6 = 6.3333
B: (8+40+16)/6 = 10.6667
C: (5+36+13)/6 = 9.0000
D: (6+32+12)/6 = 8.3333
E: (3+20+9)/6 = 5.3333
Expected project duration = 6.3333+10.6667+9.0000+8.3333+5.3333 = 39.67 days.

Step 3 — Variances, var = ((p-o)/6)^2:
A: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000
B: (8/6)^2 = 1.7778
C: (8/6)^2 = 1.7778
D: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000
E: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000
Sum of variances = 6.5556. Path standard deviation = sqrt(6.5556) = 2.56 days.

Step 4 — Probability of on-time hand-back at the 42-day deadline:
z = (42 - 39.6667) / 2.5604 = 0.91.
From the standard normal distribution, P(Z <= 0.91) is approximately 0.8189, so the probability of on-time completion is about 81.89%.

Interpretation: roughly a 4-in-5 chance of returning the dock on schedule; the largest variance contributors (B and C) are the best targets for risk response.

config.prompt:
The graving dock hosting a ferry's hybrid-electric propulsion refit must be handed back in 42 days. The refit is a strict finish-to-start chain (o/m/p, days):
A Hull survey and shaft withdrawal: 4, 6, 10
B Engine removal and foundation cut-out: 8, 10, 16
C Battery room steelwork and insulation: 5, 9, 13
D Electric motor and converter installation: 6, 8, 12
E Acceptance trials and class survey: 3, 5, 9
Caution: the draft schedule also shows CR-17 'shaft-line laser re-alignment' (3, 4, 6 days) after D, but the change board REJECTED it — exclude it.
Using PERT on the approved chain, compute: 1) Expected project duration (days), summing te=(o+4m+p)/6; 2) Path standard deviation (days), sqrt of the summed variances ((p-o)/6)^2; 3) Probability of on-time hand-back (%) within the 42-day window, via the normal approximation. Round answers to 2 decimals, probability as a percentage.

scenarios.title: Calder Verge Replenishment Loop: PERT Risk on the Injection Permit Window
scenarios.summary: Guided lab on three-point PERT for a serial water-treatment retrofit chain: derive expected duration, variance, standard deviation, and the probability of beating a regulatory injection-permit deadline.
scenarios.brief: The Calder Verge Groundwater Replenishment Loop is replacing its chloramine polishing barrier with UV advanced oxidation, and the aquifer injection permit variance that lets the plant keep recharging expires on a fixed date. Six commissioning activities run strictly end to end, so a slip anywhere is a slip everywhere. The sponsor board has stopped accepting "we should be fine" and wants schedule risk expressed as a single probability it can carry into the regulator meeting.
objectives: Compute activity expected durations from optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates using te = (o + 4m + p) / 6
Aggregate a serial chain into a total expected duration and a total variance by summing activity-level values
Derive the chain standard deviation from summed variance and explain why variances, not standard deviations, are additive
Convert a deadline into a z-score and translate it into a probability of on-time completion for a sponsor audience
Interpret the resulting probability as schedule risk against a fixed regulatory permit window
scenarios.provenance: Synthetic guided lab authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab using the standard three-point (beta-PERT) model with a normal approximation for chain totals.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real facility, permit, schedule or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (deadline 86 working days):

1) Activity expected duration, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A = (8 + 44 + 21)/6 = 73/6 = 12.1667
B = (14 + 68 + 27)/6 = 109/6 = 18.1667
C = (9 + 52 + 22)/6 = 83/6 = 13.8333
D = (6 + 36 + 17)/6 = 59/6 = 9.8333
E = (11 + 60 + 26)/6 = 97/6 = 16.1667
F = (7 + 40 + 18)/6 = 65/6 = 10.8333

2) The chain is serial, so expected_duration = sum of te = 486/6 = 81.00 days.

3) Activity variance, v = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A = (13/6)^2 = 4.6944; B = (13/6)^2 = 4.6944; C = (13/6)^2 = 4.6944;
D = (11/6)^2 = 3.3611; E = (15/6)^2 = 6.2500; F = (11/6)^2 = 3.3611
Variances add along the chain: variance = 974/36 = 27.0556 -> 27.06.

4) std_dev = sqrt(27.0556) = 5.2015 -> 5.20 days. Standard deviations do NOT add; summing them (12.67) is the classic error.

5) z = (deadline - expected_duration) / std_dev = (86 - 81) / 5.2015 = 0.9613.
prob_on_time = Phi(0.9613) = 0.8318.

Sponsor reading: roughly an 83 percent chance of commissioning inside the permit window, i.e. about one chance in six of losing recharge authorisation - enough tension to justify buying float on activities B and E, which carry the widest spreads.

config.prompt: The Calder Verge Groundwater Replenishment Loop must swap its final barrier from chloramine polishing to UV advanced oxidation before the aquifer injection permit variance lapses. Six commissioning activities run strictly end to end, and the sponsor board wants schedule risk stated in numbers rather than adjectives. Using the three-point estimates in the figures below (optimistic, most likely and pessimistic, all in working days), apply the standard PERT model to this serial chain. Report the expected chain duration, the chain variance and the chain standard deviation, each rounded to 2 decimals. Then, treating the chain total as normally distributed, report the probability of finishing on or before the permit deadline given in the figures, as a decimal between 0 and 1 rounded to 4 decimals.

ask.label: Probability of finishing on or before the permit deadline (decimal 0-1, 4 dp)

scenarios.title: Refuelling Outage Chain: PERT Risk of Blowing the Grid Window
scenarios.summary: Expert PERT lab on an eight-activity nuclear outage chain: derive expected duration, variance and standard deviation, then the probability of finishing inside the grid operator's allowed window.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic two-unit nuclear station has one dependent chain of eight outage activities standing between shutdown and criticality approach. The planning team has been quoting the sum of the most likely durations to the grid operator, which sits comfortably inside the allowed window. Your job is to rebuild the estimate properly with three-point PERT statistics and report the true probability of finishing on time.
objectives: Compute PERT expected duration te = (o + 4m + p) / 6 for each chain activity and aggregate the chain mean.
Calculate per-activity variance ((p - o)/6)^2 and sum it correctly across an eight-activity dependent chain.
Derive the chain standard deviation from summed variance rather than by summing individual standard deviations.
Convert a deadline into a z-score and report the probability of on-time completion under a normal approximation.
Explain why the sum of most likely durations understates the schedule when pessimistic tails are skewed.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic guided lab; all figures invented by the author.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, activities and figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they are not drawn from any real plant, outage or schedule.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (deadline = 94 days):

Step 1 - Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6.
A (4,6,14): 42/6 = 7.00
B (10,12,20): 78/6 = 13.00
C (6,9,12): 54/6 = 9.00
D (15,18,33): 120/6 = 20.00
E (5,8,11): 48/6 = 8.00
F (8,11,20): 72/6 = 12.00
G (3,4,11): 30/6 = 5.00
H (9,15,21): 90/6 = 15.00
Chain expected duration = 7 + 13 + 9 + 20 + 8 + 12 + 5 + 15 = 89.00 days.

Trap check: the sum of the most likely values is only 83 days, because A, D, F and G carry long pessimistic tails. Quoting 83 hides six days of expected work.

Step 2 - Variance per activity, ((p - o)/6)^2.
A: (10/6)^2 = 2.7778; B: (10/6)^2 = 2.7778; C: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; D: (18/6)^2 = 9.0000; E: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; F: (12/6)^2 = 4.0000; G: (8/6)^2 = 1.7778; H: (12/6)^2 = 4.0000.
Chain variance = 26.33 days squared. Note D alone supplies about a third of it.

Step 3 - Chain standard deviation = sqrt(26.3333) = 5.13 days. Do not sum the individual standard deviations (1.67 + 1.67 + 1.00 + 3.00 + 1.00 + 2.00 + 1.33 + 2.00 = 13.67 days), which overstates the spread by more than a factor of two - variances add, standard deviations do not.

Step 4 - z = (deadline - te) / sd = (94 - 89) / 5.1316 = 0.9744.
P(on time) = Phi(0.9744) = 0.8351.

Answers: expected_duration = 89.00, std_dev = 5.13, variance = 26.33, prob_on_time = 0.8351.

config.prompt: Outage planners at a synthetic two-unit nuclear station are scheduling a reactor-island refurbishment as one dependent chain of eight activities (A through H), running from nozzle dam installation and coolant drain-down through weld inspection, pump seal replacement, hydro-test, refill and vent, to criticality approach testing. Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations in days for each activity, plus the outage window the grid operator will allow, are given in the figures below. Treat the durations as independent and the chain total as approximately normal. Using PERT, compute the expected chain duration in days, the chain standard deviation in days, and the total chain variance in days squared (each to 2 decimal places), then the probability of completing within the allowed window, as a decimal between 0 and 1 to 4 decimal places.

ask.label: Probability of finishing within the allowed window (decimal 0-1, 4 dp)

scenarios.title: Mobile Dialysis Van Nurse Loading
scenarios.summary: A six-week mobile dialysis outreach schedule where nurse demand outruns the rostered crew. Read the demand-versus-capacity table and quantify the staffing shortfall.
scenarios.brief: A regional health network is launching a mobile dialysis van circuit that visits four rural clinic sites on a rotating six-week cycle. Nursing demand is forecast per week in crew-hours, and the rostered dialysis crew supplies a capacity that ramps up in two steps as a second van is phased in mid-cycle. The scheduler suspects the rise in treatment volume will outrun the roster before that extra capacity lands. Your job is to size that gap precisely before overtime is authorised.
objectives: Compare period-by-period resource demand against available capacity in a staffing histogram
Calculate the single-period peak overload (largest shortfall) from a demand-capacity table
Calculate the total over-demand as the sum of all period shortfalls
Count the number of periods in which demand exceeds capacity
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic resource-loading exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real health service, roster, or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Compute the shortfall for each period: shortfall = max(0, demand - capacity). Week 1: 12 - 20 = -8 -> 0. Week 2: 18 - 20 = -2 -> 0. Week 3: 26 - 20 = 6. Week 4: 30 - 22 = 8. Week 5: 22 - 24 = -2 -> 0. Week 6: 14 - 24 = -10 -> 0.
Step 2 - Peak overload = largest single-period shortfall = max(0, 0, 6, 8, 0, 0) = 8 crew-hours, in week 4.
Step 3 - Total over-demand = sum of all shortfalls = 6 + 8 = 14 crew-hours.
Step 4 - Overloaded periods = count of periods with shortfall > 0 = weeks 3 and 4 = 2.
Cross-check: peak demand = 30 crew-hours (week 4) and peak capacity = 24 crew-hours (weeks 5-6). Note that peak overload is NOT peak demand minus peak capacity (30 - 24 = 6), because those two peaks occur in different weeks; the shortfall must be evaluated period by period.
Final answers: peak_overload = 8.00, total_overdemand = 14.00, overloaded_periods = 2.

config.prompt: A regional health network runs a mobile dialysis van on a six-week rotation through four rural clinic sites. The table gives forecast nursing demand and rostered crew capacity for each week, both in crew-hours per week: Week 1 demand 12, capacity 20; Week 2 demand 18, capacity 20; Week 3 demand 26, capacity 20; Week 4 demand 30, capacity 22; Week 5 demand 22, capacity 24; Week 6 demand 14, capacity 24. Compare demand against capacity week by week and report the peak overload (the largest shortfall in any single week), the total over-demand (the sum of all weekly shortfalls), and the number of overloaded weeks. Give the crew-hour figures to two decimal places and the count as a whole number.

ask.label: Total over-demand (sum of weekly shortfalls, crew-hours)

scenarios.title: Hull Block Outfitting: Pipefitting Crew Overload Profile
scenarios.summary: Expert guided lab on resource loading for a shipyard pipefitting crew across 12 outfitting weeks, where total capacity covers total demand but several weeks are badly overloaded.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic shipyard is outfitting twelve hull blocks for a dual-fuel bulk carrier, and the pipefitting trade is the constraining resource. Weekly crew-hour demand is driven by the block erection sequence, while available capacity shifts as travelling teams are loaned in and out. The resource plan was signed off on the strength of a season-total comparison that showed capacity comfortably covering demand. Your job is to profile the week-by-week load and expose what the totals hide.
objectives: Extract peak single-period demand and peak single-period capacity from a resource histogram
Compute the largest single-period overload as demand minus capacity within that period only
Aggregate period shortfalls into a total over-demand figure without netting surplus periods
Count the number of periods in which demand exceeds available capacity
Explain why an aggregate capacity-versus-demand comparison can mask period overloads
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic resource-management exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real shipyard, vessel or workforce.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Peak demand: scan the demand column only. It rises to 7400 crew-hours in period 7, so peak_demand = 7400.
Step 2 - Peak capacity: scan the capacity column only. The highest is 7200 crew-hours, also period 7, so peak_capacity = 7200. Note the peak-demand period is NOT the worst period: its shortfall is only 7400 - 7200 = 200.
Step 3 - Period shortfalls, shortfall = max(0, demand - capacity): P1 0; P2 300; P3 800; P4 900; P5 300; P6 800; P7 200; P8 6900 - 5400 = 1500; P9 200; P10 0; P11 0; P12 0.
Step 4 - Peak overload: the largest shortfall is period 8, so peak_overload = 1500.
Step 5 - Total over-demand: sum positive shortfalls only, never netting surplus periods. 300 + 800 + 900 + 300 + 800 + 200 + 1500 + 200 = 5000.
Step 6 - Overloaded periods: P2 through P9 inclusive = 8 periods.
Trap check: total demand is 59900 and total capacity is 60000, so the programme nets to a 100 crew-hour surplus, and the late slack (period 12 alone spares 2900) flatters the plan. Netting is invalid for a capacity-limited trade: 5000 crew-hours still cannot be worked when needed.
Answers: peak_demand = 7400; peak_capacity = 7200; peak_overload = 1500; total_overdemand = 5000; overloaded_periods = 8.

config.prompt: A shipyard is outfitting twelve hull blocks for a dual-fuel bulk carrier. Pipefitting is the constraining trade. The table gives, for each of the twelve outfitting weeks, the pipefitting demand and the available pipefitting capacity, both in crew-hours. Capacity varies week to week as travelling teams are loaned in and released. Using the weekly figures only, report: the peak single-week demand, the peak single-week capacity, the largest single-week overload (demand less capacity within that week alone), the total over-demand across the programme (the sum of the weekly shortfalls), and the number of weeks in which demand exceeds capacity. Give every answer in whole crew-hours, except the week count, which is a whole number.

scenarios.title: Risk Register EMV: Timber Footbridge Over the Marsh Channel
scenarios.summary: Build an expected monetary value (EMV) view of a four-item risk register for a timber footbridge job, computing individual risk EMVs and the register total the sponsor wants for contingency sizing.
scenarios.brief: Your contractor is erecting a 60-metre glulam timber footbridge across a tidal marsh channel, and piling can only proceed during low-water windows. The project sponsor has capped contingency and wants it justified from the risk register rather than a flat percentage. As the project controls trainee, you have been handed the register with agreed probabilities and cost impacts, and asked to turn it into expected monetary values before Thursday's risk review.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value (EMV) of an individual threat or opportunity as probability times impact
Distinguish threats (negative impact) from opportunities (positive impact) in a risk register
Interpret the register total EMV as a starting point for contingency sizing
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
EMV for each risk = probability x impact. Threats carry negative impacts, opportunities positive impacts.

Step 1 — R1 Piling rig stranded by early tide (threat): EMV_R1 = 0.30 x (-20000) = -6000.

Step 2 — R2 Glulam beam delivery damage (threat): EMV_R2 = 0.20 x (-15000) = -3000.

Step 3 — R3 Early handrail package discount (opportunity): EMV_R3 = 0.50 x (+8000) = +4000.

Step 4 — R4 Protected-bird nesting stoppage (threat): EMV_R4 = 0.10 x (-40000) = -4000.

Step 5 — Register total EMV = sum of all four: -6000 + (-3000) + 4000 + (-4000) = -9000.

Interpretation: the register carries a net expected cost exposure of 9000, driven mainly by R1; the opportunity R3 offsets part of the threat exposure. This net figure is a rational starting point when arguing contingency with the sponsor, though contingency is often set on threats alone or at a chosen confidence level rather than the raw net EMV.

config.prompt: You are the project controls trainee on a 60-metre glulam timber footbridge across a tidal marsh channel; the sponsor wants contingency justified from the risk register. Negative impacts are threats; positive impacts are opportunities. Using EMV = probability x impact, compute: (1) the EMV of risk R1, (2) the EMV of risk R3, and (3) the register total EMV (the sum of all four risk EMVs). Report values to 2 decimal places, keeping the sign (negative for net cost, positive for net saving).

scenarios.title: Stormwater Diversion Tunnel — Risk Register EMV Review
scenarios.project_type: Urban stormwater diversion tunnel and pump station
scenarios.summary: Quantify a five-item risk register for a stormwater diversion tunnel, computing individual expected monetary values and the register total while correctly handling an embedded opportunity.
scenarios.brief: The Marlow Basin stormwater diversion programme is driving a 2.4 km bored tunnel and a mid-shaft pump station beneath a dense corridor of ageing utilities. The sponsor has asked for a quantified risk position before the next funding gate, because the contingency drawdown to date has been faster than planned. As the project controls analyst, you must convert the qualitative register into expected monetary values, remembering that one register entry is an opportunity, not a threat, and must carry a positive sign.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value (EMV) of individual threats and opportunities using EMV = probability x impact
Distinguish threats (negative impact) from opportunities (positive impact) when signing EMV results
Aggregate individual EMVs into a register-level total to inform a contingency recommendation
Interpret a negative register total as the probability-weighted contingency exposure
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, organisation, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Recall the formula: EMV = probability x impact. Threats carry negative impacts, opportunities positive impacts; keep the sign throughout.

Step 2 — Compute each risk's EMV:
- R1 Utility strike during shaft excavation: 0.35 x (-180000) = -63000
- R2 Early TBM breakthrough incentive (opportunity): 0.25 x (+120000) = +30000
- R3 Wet-weather standdown on open-cut sections: 0.60 x (-95000) = -57000
- R4 Segment-liner steel price escalation: 0.40 x (-150000) = -60000
- R5 Unrecorded heritage brickwork find at the outfall: 0.15 x (-220000) = -33000

Step 3 — Asked values:
- emv_R2 = +30000.00 (positive because R2 is an opportunity — the common error is signing it negative like the surrounding threats)
- emv_R4 = -60000.00

Step 4 — Register total EMV = sum of all five EMVs:
-63000 + 30000 - 57000 - 60000 - 33000 = -183000.00

Interpretation: the register's probability-weighted exposure is a net cost of 183000, which is the analytical basis for the contingency recommendation at the funding gate. Note the opportunity offsets 30000 of threat exposure; omitting it or mis-signing it shifts the total by 60000.

scenarios.title: Tie-In Window Risk Register: Expected Monetary Value
scenarios.project_type: Crude stabilization unit tie-in during plant turnaround
scenarios.summary: Price a four-line risk register for a stabilization-unit tie-in squeezed into a 21-day turnaround window, computing individual and total EMV to size the sponsor's contingency ask.
scenarios.brief: Your contractor has a 21-day plant turnaround window to cut in a new crude stabilization unit at a synthetic onshore processing facility. The sponsor is nervous: if hot-work permits slip or the legacy flange survey finds corrosion, the tie-in could overrun the window and force a second shutdown. The project engineer has tabled a four-line risk register — three threats and one opportunity from pre-fabricating a spool offsite — and the sponsor wants a single expected-value number to justify the contingency line before the steering meeting.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value of an individual threat and an individual opportunity using EMV = probability x impact
Aggregate signed EMVs across a risk register to produce a net contingency figure
Interpret a negative register total as the expected cost exposure the sponsor should provision
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not reflect any real facility, contractor, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — EMV of each risk uses EMV = probability x impact, keeping the sign (negative = threat cost, positive = opportunity saving).

R1 Hot-work permit delays: 0.3 x (-40000) = -12000
R2 Corroded legacy flanges found in survey: 0.2 x (-25000) = -5000
R3 Scaffold crew double-booked during peak turnaround: 0.5 x (-10000) = -5000
R4 Offsite pre-fabricated spool passes fit-up first time: 0.25 x (+20000) = +5000

Step 2 — Register total EMV is the sum of the signed values:
-12000 + (-5000) + (-5000) + 5000 = -17000

Answers: emv_R1 = -12000; emv_R4 = +5000; emv (register total) = -17000. The negative total means the register carries an expected net cost exposure of 17000, which is the figure the sponsor should compare against the contingency line.

scenarios.title: Hull 7 Pre-Erection Risk Register: Signed EMV at a Bunkering-Vessel Yard
scenarios.summary: Expert guided lab on expected monetary value across an eight-line shipbuilding risk register that mixes threats with two genuine opportunities. Learners compute both line-level and register-level EMV with correct signs.
scenarios.brief: Hull 7 of a synthetic Meridian-class LNG bunkering vessel programme has reached its pre-erection risk review at Berth 4. The yard's controls cell keeps a compact quantitative register in thousands of units, in which two lines are upside opportunities rather than threats. Two large-impact, low-probability threats sit alongside a high-probability nuisance item, so the register's shape invites eyeballing rather than arithmetic. The learner must produce the signed expected monetary value of the register and of five named lines.
objectives: Compute line-level expected monetary value as probability multiplied by signed impact
Aggregate line EMVs into a register-level EMV with correct sign handling
Distinguish opportunity lines from threat lines when forming an aggregated total
Explain why a low-probability, high-impact threat can contribute less EMV than a high-probability moderate threat
Report signed EMV results to a stated rounding precision
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; fictional shipbuilding programme constructed by the author.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, hull names and register entries are synthetic and simplified for training; they describe no real yard or vessel programme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: line EMV = probability x signed impact; register EMV = sum of all line EMVs. Opportunities carry positive impact and therefore add to the total.

R1: 0.35 x -2400 = -840.00
R2: 0.60 x -750 = -450.00
R3: 0.25 x -3200 = -800.00

scenarios.title: Tugboat Fit-Out Sequencing: Critical Path at Berth 3
scenarios.summary: Run a forward and backward pass on a six-activity tug fit-out network to find the project duration, the critical path, and the total float on the electrical branch.
scenarios.brief: A mid-size yard is fitting out a 28 m harbour tug at its outfitting berth, and the delivery date hinges on two work fronts that split after the hull modules are joined: a mechanical branch (piping, then engine room outfit) and an electrical branch (cable pulls, then wheelhouse console). Both branches must finish before commissioning trials can start. The berth planner has asked you to run the critical path calculation so the yard knows which branch drives the delivery date and how much slack the other branch really has.
objectives: Compute early and late dates for a small activity network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path and the overall project duration of a fit-out sequence
Compute total float for a non-critical activity and interpret it as schedule slack
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real yard, vessel, or schedule.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur). A: ES 0, EF 4. B (after A): ES 4, EF 10. C (after A): ES 4, EF 7. D (after B): ES 10, EF 15. E (after C): ES 7, EF 11. F (after D and E): ES = max(15, 11) = 15, EF 18. Project duration = 18 days.

Step 2 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF - dur). F: LF 18, LS 15. D: LF 15, LS 10. E: LF 15, LS 11. B: LF 10, LS 4. C: LF = LS of E = 11, LS 8. A: LF = min(LS B, LS C) = min(4, 8) = 4, LS 0.

Step 3 — Total float (TF = LS - ES). A: 0, B: 0, D: 0, F: 0 — these form the critical path A → B → D → F. C: TF = 8 - 4 = 4. E: TF = 11 - 7 = 4.

Answers: project_duration = 18; critical_path = {A, B, D, F}; float_C = 4 days. Interpretation: the electrical branch (C, E) can slip up to 4 days in total before it delays commissioning trials; the mechanical branch has no slack.

scenarios.title: Service Reservoir Relining Outage — CPM Schedule Analysis
scenarios.project_type: Potable water service reservoir relining outage
scenarios.summary: Build the CPM network for a reservoir relining outage, find the project duration and critical path, and compute total float on the non-critical branches — while spotting a rejected change hiding in the contractor's draft.
scenarios.brief: A regional water utility has taken one cell of a buried service reservoir out of supply for structural repair and spray-applied relining. The outage window is tight because the network is on single-cell resilience while the work runs. The contractor has issued a draft programme, but it quietly assumes a cure-time reduction that the utility's change board rejected last week. As the project controls analyst, you must run the forward and backward pass on the approved logic and durations to confirm the outage length and where the schedule risk really sits.
objectives: Compute early/late dates via forward and backward pass on an activity-on-node network
Determine the project duration and identify the critical path through a merge point
Compute total float for non-critical activities and interpret what it means for outage risk
Distinguish approved schedule data from a rejected change embedded in a contractor draft
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real utility, contractor, or asset.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Use the APPROVED durations. Change request CR-014 (cure period of activity E reduced from 9 to 6 days) was REJECTED by the change board, so E = 9 days stands, even though the contractor's draft shows 6.

Step 2 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur):
A: 0–3. B: 3–7. C: 3–8. F: 3–10. D: 7–13. E: ES = max(EF C, EF D) = max(8, 13) = 13, EF = 22. G: ES = max(EF E, EF F) = max(22, 10) = 22, EF = 26. H: 26–28.

Project duration = 28 days.

Step 3 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − dur):
H: 26–28. G: 22–26. E: 13–22. F: LF = LS of G = 22, LS = 15. D: 7–13. C: LF = LS of E = 13, LS = 8. B: 3–7. A: 0–3.

Step 4 — Total float (TF = LS − ES):
A = 0, B = 0, D = 0, E = 0, G = 0, H = 0 → critical path = A–B–D–E–G–H.
float_C = 8 − 3 = 5 days.
float_F = 15 − 3 = 12 days.

Interpretation: the outage is driven by the crack survey → concrete repair → liner cure chain, not by silt removal or the pipework replacement. Had the rejected cure reduction been used, the duration would have been understated by 3 days.

scenarios.title: Outage Window Check: Valve Replacement CPM
scenarios.summary: Run a critical path analysis on a six-activity feedwater valve replacement during a reactor maintenance outage: find the duration, the critical path, and the calibration crew's float.
scenarios.brief: A small modular reactor demonstration unit has entered a 3-week planned maintenance window, and the outage controls team must confirm that the feedwater isolation valve replacement fits inside it. Two work fronts run in parallel after mobilisation: the mechanical crew erects scaffold and shielding before swapping the valve, while the I&C crew calibrates loop instruments and inspects the pipe welds. Both fronts must finish before the reinstatement test can run. Your job is to time-analyse the six-activity network and tell the outage manager how long the job takes, which activities cannot slip, and how much slack the calibration crew really has.
objectives: Compute early and late start/finish dates for a small activity network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path through a network containing a merge point
Compute total float for a non-critical activity and interpret it as permissible slip
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real facility, outage, or vendor data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + duration, starting at day 0):
- A: ES 0, EF 2
- B: ES 2, EF 6
- C: ES 2, EF 5
- D: ES 6, EF 11
- E: ES 5, EF 7
- F (merge of D and E): ES = max(11, 7) = 11, EF 14

project_duration = 14 working days.

Step 2 - Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF - duration):
- F: LF 14, LS 11
- D: LF 11, LS 6
- E: LF 11, LS 9
- B: LF 6, LS 2
- C: LF 9, LS 6
- A: LF = min(2, 6) = 2, LS 0

Step 3 - Total float (TF = LS - ES):
- A: 0, B: 0, D: 0, F: 0 (critical)
- C: 6 - 2 = 4
- E: 9 - 5 = 4

critical_path = {A, B, D, F} (the mechanical chain: mobilise, scaffold/shield, valve replacement, reinstatement test).

float_C = 4 days. The calibration crew can slip up to 4 working days without delaying the reinstatement test or the outage window; note C and E share this float along their path, so consuming it on C leaves none for E.

scenarios.title: Storm-Surge Pumping Station: The Chain That Guards the Commissioning Window
scenarios.summary: Run a full forward and backward pass on a 10-activity cofferdam pumping-station network, then separate the true critical chain from two parallel branches sitting only one day behind it.
scenarios.brief: A storm-surge pumping station is being built inside a temporary cofferdam on a tidal inlet, and the marine contract reserves a single wet-commissioning window at the end of the build. The sponsor has been told the job is "on track" because no single trade is late. But three separate chains feed the final commissioning milestone, and two of them are almost as long as the driving one. Your job is to produce the network arithmetic that shows which activities actually hold the window and how thin the cushion really is elsewhere.
objectives: Perform a forward pass to compute early start and early finish across a multi-merge network
Perform a backward pass to compute late start, late finish and total float for every activity
Identify total project duration and the complete set of zero-float critical activities
Distinguish near-critical branches carrying 1 day of float from branches with genuine cushion
Explain why a low-float parallel chain is a sponsor-level risk rather than a comfort
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic CPM guided lab; network topology and durations constructed by the author.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, activities and the project are synthetic and simplified for training and represent no real project, organisation or works programme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur):
A 0->12; B 12->21; C 12->31; D 21->32.
E: ES = max(EF C 31, EF D 32) = 32 -> 45.
F 32->49; G 45->53.
H: ES = max(EF F 49, EF G 53) = 53 -> 59. J 53->58.
K: ES = max(EF H 59, EF J 58) = 59 -> 66.
Project duration = EF of K = 66 working days.

Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF - dur), setting LF(K) = 66:
K LS 59, LF 66. H LF 59, LS 53. J LF 59, LS 54.
G LF = min(LS H 53, LS J 54) = 53, LS 45. F LF 53, LS 36. E LF 45, LS 32.
D LF = min(LS E 32, LS F 36) = 32, LS 21. C LF 32, LS 13. B LF 21, LS 12. A LF 12, LS 0.

Total float = LS - ES:
A 0, B 0, C 13-12 = 1, D 0, E 0, F 36-32 = 4, G 0, H 0, J 54-53 = 1, K 0.

Answers: project_duration = 66; critical_path = {A, B, D, E, G, H, K}; float_C = 1; float_F = 4; float_J = 1.

Sponsor read: the driving chain is cofferdam -> pile caps -> base slab -> wall lifts -> fit-out -> gantry install -> commissioning. Rebar prefabrication and control cabinet integration each hold only 1 day of cushion, so one day of slip on either creates a second critical chain into the fixed commissioning window.

scenarios.title: Structuring the Millrace Canal Footbridge WBS
scenarios.summary: Roll up a work breakdown structure for a prefabricated timber footbridge and check that a declared branch value honours the 100% rule.
scenarios.brief: A district authority is replacing a closed canal crossing with a prefabricated timber footbridge assembled from factory-built deck modules. The planning lead has drafted a three-branch WBS, but the Substructure package owner has written a declared value onto their branch header, and the sponsor wants confirmation that the structure still adds up before baseline sign-off. All figures are in thousands.
objectives: Compute the project root total by rolling up leaf values through the WBS hierarchy.
Apply the 100% rule to verify that a parent's declared value equals the sum of its children.
Distinguish leaf work packages that carry estimates from summary nodes that only aggregate them.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaf work packages (nodes that carry a value): Piling = 300, Abutments = 200, Timber Deck Modules = 400, Handrails and Parapets = 100, Testing and Handover = 200.

Step 2 — Roll up each branch:
- Substructure (1.1) = 300 + 200 = 500
- Superstructure (1.2) = 400 + 100 = 500
- Testing and Handover (1.3) is itself a leaf = 200

Step 3 — Compute the root total: root_total = 500 + 500 + 200 = 1200.

Step 4 — Check the 100% rule. The only parent with an explicitly declared value is Substructure (1.1), declared at 500. Its children sum to 300 + 200 = 500, which matches exactly, so the declared value is consistent with the 100% rule.

Final answers: root_total = 1200; hundred_percent_valid = true.

scenarios.title: Estuary Flood Barrier Gate Refurbishment — WBS Roll-Up and 100% Rule Check
scenarios.summary: Roll up a refurbishment WBS for a tidal flood barrier gate and test whether a planner's hard-coded package value violates the 100% rule.
scenarios.brief: A regional water authority is refurbishing one of the two mitre gates on its estuary flood barrier during a scheduled navigation closure window. The planning engineer has drafted a three-branch WBS covering mechanical overhaul, control-system upgrades, and civil access works, with estimates loaded at the work-package level. Before baselining, the controls lead notices that the Gate Mechanical Overhaul branch carries an explicitly declared summary value entered by hand during an earlier estimate cycle, and asks you to verify the structure before it goes to the sponsor.
objectives: Compute a WBS root total by rolling up leaf work-package values through the hierarchy
Distinguish system-rolled parent totals from manually declared parent values
Interpret the 100% rule and determine whether a declared parent value makes the structure invalid
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation, asset, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up the leaves. Only leaf nodes carry scope values; the root total is the sum of all leaf work packages.

Branch 1.1 Gate Mechanical Overhaul (children): 1.1.1 Hydraulic ram replacement 620 + 1.1.2 Bearing and trunnion refurbishment 480 + 1.1.3 Seal and gasket renewal 310 = 1410.
Branch 1.2 Control Systems Upgrade: 1.2.1 SCADA migration 540 + 1.2.2 Sensor network installation 275 = 815.
Branch 1.3 Civil and Access Works: 1.3.1 Walkway and platform repairs 330 + 1.3.2 Corrosion protection recoating 415 = 745.

Root total = 1410 + 815 + 745 = 2970.

Step 2 — Test the 100% rule. The rule requires every parent that carries an explicitly declared value to equal the sum of its children exactly. Node 1.1 was hand-entered at 1450, but its children sum to 1410 (a 40 discrepancy left over from an earlier estimate cycle). Declared 1450 != rolled-up 1410, so the structure fails the check.

Answers: root_total = 2970; hundred_percent_valid = false.

Takeaway: the roll-up always uses leaf values — a stale manual entry at parent level does not change the true scope total, but it does invalidate the WBS until reconciled.

scenarios.summary: Roll up a five-branch work breakdown structure for a brownfield produced-water treatment skid retrofit and test it against the 100% rule before the control budget is baselined.
scenarios.brief: A mid-size onshore gas processing plant is retrofitting its produced-water treatment skid with a new hydrocyclone package to meet tighter discharge limits during a planned 21-day turnaround. The project controls lead has drafted a work breakdown structure with declared control-account values on two of the parent branches, and the sponsor wants confirmation that the structure rolls up cleanly before the control budget is locked. Your job is to verify the roll-up arithmetic that the baseline will stand on.
objectives: Compute the root total of a WBS by rolling up leaf-level values through parent branches
Interpret the 100% rule and verify that declared parent values equal the sum of their children
Distinguish leaf work packages that carry value from summary parent nodes in a scope hierarchy
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real facility, company, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaf work packages (nodes that carry a value): Process Design = 70, Piping and Layout Design = 50, Hydrocyclone Package Procurement = 260, Skid Fabrication = 110, Site Installation and Tie-ins = 70, Commissioning and Performance Test = 40.

Step 2 — Roll up each parent branch (parent value = sum of its children):
Engineering (1.1) = 70 + 50 = 120.
Fabrication and Installation (1.3) = 110 + 70 = 180.
Procurement (1.2) and Commissioning (1.4) are themselves leaves: 260 and 40.

Step 3 — Compute the root total:
root_total = 120 + 260 + 180 + 40 = 600.

Step 4 — Test the 100% rule. Two parents carry declared values: Engineering declares 120 and its children sum to 70 + 50 = 120 (match); Fabrication and Installation declares 180 and its children sum to 110 + 70 = 180 (match). Every declared parent value equals its children's sum, so the structure satisfies the 100% rule.

Final answers: root_total = 600; hundred_percent_valid = true.

scenarios.title: Tidal Barrier Gate Refurbishment: WBS Roll-Up and 100 Percent Rule Test
scenarios.summary: Roll up a 14-node tidal-barrier refurbishment work breakdown structure and test whether a sponsor-declared branch budget honours the 100 percent rule.
scenarios.brief: A tidal-surge barrier refurbishment must be delivered inside one 30-week marine window, so the control team decomposes the gate works into four branches and nine work packages before baselining. The sponsor has also written a control budget against the mechanical branch, carried over from an earlier order-of-magnitude estimate. The learner must roll the structure up from its work packages and decide whether the declared parent figures honour the 100 percent rule.
objectives: Roll a multi-level work breakdown structure up from its work packages to a root total.
Test each declared parent value against the sum of its children to apply the 100 percent rule.
Distinguish a sponsor-declared control budget from a validated bottom-up roll-up.
Explain the reporting consequence of a parent node that does not reconcile to its children.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; synthetic infrastructure decomposition exercise graded by the deterministic wbs engine.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real barrier, authority or contract.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Roll up each branch from its work packages. Gate Mechanical Overhaul: 4,200,000 + 2,750,000 + 1,480,000 = 8,430,000. Hydraulic and Power Systems: 3,150,000 + 2,565,000 = 5,715,000. Marine Civil Works: 6,480,000 + 2,310,000 = 8,790,000. Control and Instrumentation: 1,870,000 + 1,195,000 = 3,065,000.

Step 2 - Root total = sum of branch roll-ups = 8,430,000 + 5,715,000 + 8,790,000 + 3,065,000 = 26,000,000.

Step 3 - Apply the 100 percent rule: every declared parent value must equal the sum of its children. Only node 1.1 carries a declared value: 8,000,000 against children summing to 8,430,000, a shortfall of 430,000. The rule is broken, so hundred_percent_valid = false.

The trap: an analyst who accepts the sponsor's declared 8,000,000 for node 1.1 instead of rolling up its three work packages reports 25,570,000 and usually also calls the structure valid. Parent values are never additive evidence; they are assertions to be reconciled against the children beneath them.

Final answers: root_total = 26,000,000; hundred_percent_valid = false.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - extend every line (qty x rate): B1 486.5x312.75 = 152152.875; B2 34x468.90 = 15942.60; B3 512.25x154.40 = 79091.40; B4 62x1842.60 = 114241.20; B5 7340x12.85 = 94319.00; B6 148x226.35 = 33499.80; B7 18x3415.50 = 61479.00; B8 268.4x588.20 = 157872.88; B9 3x9275.00 = 27825.00; B10 214x143.65 = 30741.10; B11 96x512.80 = 49228.80; B12 11x2687.40 = 29561.40.

Step 2 - total = sum of extensions = 845955.055, reported as 845955.06.

Step 3 - line_count = number of priced lines = 12.

Step 4 - average_rate = (sum of the 12 unit rates) / 12. The rates sum to 19640.40, so 19640.40 / 12 = 1636.70.

Teaching point: the money-weighted rate is total / total quantity = 845955.055 / 9193.15 = 92.02 per unit. The unweighted mean of 1636.70 is about eighteen times higher because it gives the single 9275.00 plinth line and the 3415.50 airlock line the same voice as the 12.85 ductwork rate that carries 7340 units and 94319.00 of value. Quote 1636.70 to a sponsor as a cost-per-unit benchmark and the capital paper is indefensible; the plain mean describes the rate schedule, not the spend.

scenarios.project_type: Freight branch line re-signalling and slab-track renewal

scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: net cash for each period = inflow - outflow. Cumulative position after period n = sum of net cash for periods 1..n. Peak funding requirement = absolute value of the most negative cumulative position. Final position = cumulative after the last period.

Period nets:
P1: 480000 - 1265000 = -785000; cumulative -785000
P2: 615000 - 1487500 = -872500; cumulative -1657500
P3: 742000 - 1653000 = -911000; cumulative -2568500
P4: 1268000 - 1594500 = -326500; cumulative -2895000
P5: 2135000 - 1428000 = +707000; cumulative -2188000
P6: 2410000 - 1176500 = +1233500; cumulative -954500
P7: 1985000 - 892000 = +1093000; cumulative +138500
P8: 1642000 - 705500 = +936500; cumulative +1075000

Answers:
cumulative_4 = -2895000.00 (the trough; the period net is still negative but shrinking)
cumulative_6 = -954500.00
peak_funding = 2895000.00 (most negative cumulative, -2895000, reported positive)
final_position = 1075000.00

Sponsor reading: the branch ends 1075000 to the good, but it must be financed through a 2895000 trough at end of period 4, and it does not cross back above zero until period 7. Size the facility on the trough, not the closing balance.

scenarios.project_type: die-casting cell retrofit for electric drive housings
scenarios.summary: Track twelve monthly cash periods on a manufacturing retrofit where a mid-project rebound hides a deeper later trough and a strong final month masks the true funding requirement.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic contract manufacturer is retrofitting an aging die-casting cell into a high-pressure line for electric drive housings. Tooling, furnace rebuild and cell commissioning consume cash long before qualified parts ship. A customer prepayment in the middle months briefly flatters the curve before rework and second-shift ramp costs push the balance lower still. The controls team must size the credit facility from the cumulative position, not from the closing balance.
objectives: Build a period-by-period cumulative net cash position from inflow and outflow data
Compute the final cash position at the end of the twelve-period horizon
Identify peak funding requirement as the deepest cumulative deficit rather than the first trough
Distinguish a temporary mid-project rebound from a genuine recovery in the funding curve
Report cumulative positions at named checkpoint periods with correct signs

scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, periods and the project itself are synthetic and simplified for training; they reflect no real company or engagement.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: net_p = inflow_p - outflow_p; cumulative_p = cumulative_(p-1) + net_p; final_position = cumulative_12; peak_funding = absolute value of the most negative cumulative balance.

Nets: P1 -820; P2 -830; P3 -880; P4 +270; P5 +360; P6 -860; P7 -1080; P8 -510; P9 +540; P10 +840; P11 +1270; P12 +2030.

Cumulative curve: P1 -820; P2 -1650; P3 -2530; P4 -2260; P5 -1900; P6 -2760; P7 -3840; P8 -4350; P9 -3810; P10 -2970; P11 -1700; P12 +330.

The trap: the prepayment in periods 4 and 5 lifts the curve from -2530 to -1900, which reads like recovery, and period 7 at -3840 looks like the trough. Rework and the second-shift ramp drive the curve deeper, so the true minimum is -4350 at period 8. The strong closing month (+2030) also makes the programme look self-funding, but the facility must cover 4350.

Answers: cumulative_3 = -2530.00; cumulative_5 = -1900.00; cumulative_7 = -3840.00; cumulative_8 = -4350.00; cumulative_11 = -1700.00; final_position = 330.00; peak_funding = 4350.00.

Check: total inflow 15430 - total outflow 15100 = 330, matching cumulative_12.

scenarios.title: Aseptic Filling Suite Retrofit — Rolling Up the Cost Breakdown Structure
scenarios.summary: Roll up a four-leaf cost breakdown structure for a sterile filling suite retrofit and quantify the total variance the sponsor is asking about.
scenarios.brief: A contract manufacturer is retrofitting an aseptic filling suite to add isolator-based filling capacity for a new injectable product. Month-end actuals have just landed and the sponsor has heard rumours of an overspend on the HVAC package and the filling isolator. As the project cost controller, you must roll the leaf-level figures up the cost breakdown structure and report the position at the root before the steering meeting.
objectives: Compute the root budget of a cost breakdown structure by summing leaf-level budgets.
Compute the root actual cost by rolling up leaf-level actuals.
Compute and interpret cost variance (budget minus actual) at the root, distinguishing overspend from underspend.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, facility, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaves. Only leaf nodes carry budget and actual: 1.1.1 HVAC and HEPA Filter Upgrade (budget 120, actual 132), 1.1.2 Cleanroom Wall and Ceiling Panels (budget 80, actual 76), 1.2.1 Isolator Filling Machine (budget 300, actual 315), 1.2.2 Qualification and Validation (budget 100, actual 92).

Step 2 — Roll up the root budget. Root budget = sum of all leaf budgets = 120 + 80 + 300 + 100 = 600.

Step 3 — Roll up the root actual. Root actual = sum of all leaf actuals = 132 + 76 + 315 + 92 = 615.

Step 4 — Compute the root variance. Variance = budget − actual = 600 − 615 = −15. The negative sign means the project has spent 15 more than budgeted to date — an overspend, driven mainly by the HVAC upgrade (−12) and the isolator machine (−15), partly offset by savings on panels (+4) and qualification (+8).

Final answers: root_budget = 600, root_actual = 615, root_variance = −15.

scenarios.title: Rollup Under Pressure: Dispatch Platform Replatform CBS
scenarios.summary: Roll up a cost breakdown structure for a troubled SaaS replatforming programme, separate a genuine underspend opportunity from the overruns, and refuse to book a rejected change request that a stale dashboard shows as approved.
scenarios.brief: Your firm is eleven sprints into replatforming its legacy dispatch monolith into microservices, and the steering group suspects the programme is bleeding money. The cost breakdown structure has three branches: Core Services Rebuild, Data Migration, and Cutover and Hardening. A portfolio dashboard has not refreshed since the last change board, so one rejected change request still displays as approved, and one work package has quietly come in under budget thanks to an automated validation tool. You must produce the defensible rollup the sponsor will see.
objectives: Compute parent and root budgets and actuals by rolling up leaf-level CBS values
Compute cost variance as budget minus actual at node and root level
Distinguish approved control budget from rejected change requests when stale reporting conflicts
Interpret a favourable work-package variance (opportunity) inside an overrunning programme
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, organisations, and events are synthetic and simplified for training purposes only.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Handle the twist. Change request CR-31 (12,000 uplift to Schema Conversion & ETL) was REJECTED at the change board; the dashboard entry showing it as approved is stale. The control budget for node 1.2.1 therefore remains 38,000. Do not add 12,000 anywhere.

Step 2 — Roll up budgets from the leaves.
Node 1.1 budget = 84,000 + 62,000 + 45,500 = 191,500.
Node 1.2 budget = 38,000 + 21,000 = 59,000.
Node 1.3 budget = 29,500.
Root budget = 191,500 + 59,000 + 29,500 = 280,000.00.

Step 3 — Roll up actuals from the leaves.
Node 1.1 actual = 91,300 + 70,450 + 44,120 = 205,870.
Node 1.2 actual = 47,600 + 16,800 = 64,400.
Node 1.3 actual = 33,900.
Root actual = 205,870 + 64,400 + 33,900 = 304,170.00.

Step 4 — Variances (variance = budget - actual; negative = overrun).

scenarios.project_type: Rural fibre backhaul upgrade to hilltop base stations
scenarios.summary: Roll up a four-element cost breakdown structure for a rural fibre backhaul upgrade and quantify the total variance the sponsor is worried about.
scenarios.brief: A regional carrier is upgrading the fibre backhaul that links three hilltop base stations to its core network, replacing an ageing microwave hop. Midway through construction, the trenching crew hit rockier ground than surveyed and the sponsor has asked for a quick roll-up of the cost breakdown structure to see whether the project as a whole is still inside budget. You are the project controls analyst preparing that one-page answer.
objectives: Compute the root-level budget of a cost breakdown structure by summing its leaf elements
Compute the root-level actual cost from leaf-level actuals
Interpret total cost variance (budget minus actual) and its sign as under- or overspend
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Root budget. Sum the budgets of the four leaf elements: root_budget = 40000 (Trenching and Ducting) + 25000 (Fibre Cable and Splicing) + 30000 (Tower Site Equipment) + 5000 (Testing and Commissioning) = 100000.

Step 2 — Root actual. Sum the actuals of the same leaves: root_actual = 43500 + 24000 + 32500 + 4500 = 104500.

Step 3 — Root variance. Variance = budget - actual, so root_variance = 100000 - 104500 = -4500. The negative sign means the project is overspent by 4500 overall: the trenching overrun (40000 - 43500 = -3500) and the tower equipment overrun (30000 - 32500 = -2500) outweigh the savings on cable/splicing (+1000) and commissioning (+500). This confirms the sponsor's concern — the whole programme is 4.5% over budget, driven mainly by ground conditions on the trenching element.

scenarios.title: Kestrel Vale Bypass: Change Register Discipline
scenarios.summary: Restate the baseline on a 14 km bypass road where a rejected noise-barrier package looks approved, a big junction realignment is still pending, and a value-engineering saving sits among the threats.
scenarios.brief: The Kestrel Vale Bypass is a 14 km dual-carriageway relief road being delivered under an NEC-style target contract, and the change register has become the sponsor's biggest worry after a wet winter. Five change requests are on the register this period, ranging from an emergency retaining-wall drainage redesign to a value-engineering opportunity on recycled pavement. The community liaison panel has loudly "endorsed" a noise-barrier upgrade, but the change board formally rejected it — and a large junction realignment is still awaiting decision. As the project controls lead, you must restate the performance measurement baseline using only the changes that have actually been approved.
objectives: Distinguish approved changes from pending and rejected requests when restating a baseline
Compute the net approved cost delta, including a negative value-engineering opportunity
Compute the net approved schedule delta from a mixed change register
Derive the revised budget at completion and revised duration from the approved deltas only
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, contract, or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures:

Step 1 — Filter the register to formally approved changes only. Approved: C1 (+265000 cost, +3 weeks), C4 (-140000 cost, 0 weeks), C5 (+95000 cost, +2 weeks). Excluded: C2 is pending (sponsor support is not approval) and C3 is rejected (a liaison panel endorsement is not change-board approval). Approved count = 3.

Step 2 — Approved cost delta = sum of approved cost deltas = 265000 + (-140000) + 95000 = 220000.00. Note the value-engineering opportunity C4 reduces the net delta.

Step 3 — Approved schedule delta = 3 + 0 + 2 = 5 weeks.

Step 4 — Revised BAC = baseline BAC + approved cost delta = 8400000 + 220000 = 8620000.00.

Step 5 — Revised duration = baseline duration + approved schedule delta = 46 + 5 = 51 weeks.

Common traps: adding C2 (910000 / 6 weeks) because the sponsor "supports" it, or C3 (180000 / 1 week) because the panel "endorsed" it — only formal change-board approval moves the performance measurement baseline.

scenarios.title: Meridian Bowl Canopy Retrofit: Change Register Reconciliation
scenarios.project_type: Stadium canopy retrofit and pitch-systems replacement
scenarios.summary: Reconcile an eight-item change register on a 42,000-seat venue retrofit, isolating approved changes from pending and rejected ones to restate the budget at completion and the project duration.
scenarios.brief: Meridian Bowl is a 42,000-seat multipurpose venue undergoing a canopy retrofit and a full pitch-systems replacement between two event seasons. The change register has grown to eight items spanning structural redesign, descopes, procurement rebates and a large retractable-tray upgrade that the sponsor has not yet signed. Several deltas are negative, and one approved item adds cost while pulling days out of the schedule. Your job is to restate the baseline using only what has actually been approved.
objectives: Classify change-register items by approval status and exclude pending and rejected items from baseline restatement
Aggregate signed cost deltas, including descopes and procurement credits, into a single approved cost impact
Aggregate signed schedule deltas, including a duration-saving item, into a single approved schedule impact
Restate budget at completion and project duration from an approved baseline plus approved deltas
Report the count of approved changes as an auditable control total
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; fully invented venue, register and figures.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, projects and figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real venue, contract or change register.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: baseline_bac = 96,400,000 and baseline_duration = 610 days.

Step 1 - Filter by status. Approved items are C1, C3, C5, C7, C8. Pending items C2 and C6 and rejected item C4 are excluded entirely, no matter how large their deltas. approved_count = 5.

Step 2 - Approved cost delta = sum of cost_delta over approved items, keeping signs:
2,450,000 + (-1,180,000) + 4,120,000 + 640,000 + (-930,000)
= 1,270,000 + 4,120,000 = 5,390,000
= 5,390,000 + 640,000 = 6,030,000
= 6,030,000 - 930,000 = 5,100,000.
approved_cost_delta = 5,100,000.00

Step 3 - Approved schedule delta = sum of schedule_delta over approved items:
18 + (-9) + 26 + (-14) + 0 = 21.
approved_schedule_delta = 21.00 days. Note C7 adds 640,000 of cost yet returns 14 days; cost and schedule signs are independent.

Step 4 - revised_bac = baseline_bac + approved_cost_delta
= 96,400,000 + 5,100,000 = 101,500,000.00

Step 5 - revised_duration = baseline_duration + approved_schedule_delta
= 610 + 21 = 631.00 days

Common traps: sweeping the 6,900,000 / 45-day pending tray upgrade into the revised baseline because it is expected to be signed; taking absolute values and losing the two descopes and the rebate; and including the rejected gantry relocation because it was already priced.

scenarios.title: Fill-Finish Capacity Decision for a Lyophilized Biologic Launch
scenarios.summary: Score five capacity options for a lyophilized biologic launch using weighted cost, schedule and risk penalties, then identify the winning penalty score.
scenarios.brief: A mid-size biologics developer has an approvable lyophilized monoclonal product with a launch window its single legacy fill line cannot supply. The capacity board has scored five expansion routes on capital outlay, time to qualified supply and an integrated technical/regulatory risk index. A late launch erodes exclusivity revenue, while an unqualified line risks a regulatory hold, so the sponsor has set explicit weights on each dimension. Your job is to turn those weights into comparable penalty scores so the board debates one number per option instead of three.
objectives: Apply a weighted additive penalty model to capital options with mixed units
Compute individual option scores from cost, schedule and risk inputs using sponsor-set weights
Determine the minimum (winning) penalty score across a full option set
Interpret a narrow score separation as a signal of decision sensitivity for a sponsor briefing
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic decision-analysis exercise; no external source data.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, options and organisations are synthetic and simplified for training; they are not benchmarks or real project data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: Score = w_cost x |cost| + w_sched x |schedule| + w_risk x risk, with w_cost = 1.25, w_sched = 0.80, w_risk = 1.60. Lowest score wins (penalty model).

Step 1 - O1 (retrofit legacy lyo suite): 1.25 x 18.4 = 23.00; 0.80 x 14.5 = 11.60; 1.60 x 6.8 = 10.88. Score_O1 = 45.48.

Step 2 - O2 (modular cleanroom pods): 1.25 x 26.8 = 33.50; 0.80 x 9.5 = 7.60; 1.60 x 4.2 = 6.72. Score_O2 = 47.82.

Step 3 - O3 (contract site tech transfer): 1.25 x 31.6 = 39.50; 0.80 x 7.0 = 5.60; 1.60 x 5.6 = 8.96. Score_O3 = 54.06.

Step 4 - O4 (greenfield fill line): 1.25 x 44.4 = 55.50; 0.80 x 22.0 = 17.60; 1.60 x 3.1 = 4.96. Score_O4 = 78.06.

Step 5 - O5 (split sourcing): 1.25 x 29.6 = 37.00; 0.80 x 11.5 = 9.20; 1.60 x 5.9 = 9.44. Score_O5 = 55.64.

Step 6 - Best score = min(45.48, 47.82, 54.06, 78.06, 55.64) = 45.48.

Answers: score_O1 = 45.48; score_O2 = 47.82; score_O5 = 55.64; best_score = 45.48. Sponsor note: the leader is only 2.34 penalty points clear of the modular option, so a modest shift in the risk weighting or the retrofit risk index could flip the recommendation.

scenarios.title: Data Residency Route Selection Under Weighted Cost, Schedule and Risk
scenarios.summary: Score five in-region data-residency delivery routes for a SaaS analytics platform using a weighted cost-schedule-risk penalty model, then identify the best achievable score.
scenarios.brief: A multi-tenant SaaS analytics platform has committed to in-region data residency ahead of its enterprise renewal window, and five delivery routes have cleared feasibility. Each route carries a different capital cost, delivery duration and residual-risk exposure, and the sponsor board has agreed explicit weights rather than arguing preferences option by option. Your job is to turn the weighted trade-off into a defensible penalty score per option so the board can see which route actually wins on the agreed criteria.
objectives: Apply a weighted additive penalty model to normalised cost, schedule and risk attributes
Compute per-option weighted scores for a multi-option software delivery decision
Identify the winning option by lowest penalty score and state the score to 2 decimals
Explain why the cheapest or fastest option is not automatically the weighted winner
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic advanced decision-analysis exercise; no external source data.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they model no real product, vendor or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Formula: score = w_cost*cost + w_sched*schedule + w_risk*risk, with w_cost = 1.4, w_sched = 0.85, w_risk = 0.6. Lower score wins (penalty scale). Attributes are already normalised: cost in millions, schedule in months, risk on 0-10. Carry full precision through the sum and round half-up at the final step only.

O1: 1.4*4.65 = 6.51; 0.85*11.5 = 9.775; 0.6*6.2 = 3.72 -> 20.005 = 20.01 (2 dp).
O2: 1.4*6.28 = 8.792; 0.85*14.25 = 12.1125; 0.6*4.4 = 2.64 -> 23.5445 = 23.54.
O3: 1.4*3.92 = 5.488; 0.85*8.75 = 7.4375; 0.6*7.8 = 4.68 -> 17.6055 = 17.61.
O4: 1.4*5.41 = 7.574; 0.85*12.0 = 10.20; 0.6*5.1 = 3.06 -> 20.834 = 20.83.
O5: 1.4*7.15 = 10.01; 0.85*7.5 = 6.375; 0.6*3.6 = 2.16 -> 18.545 = 18.55.

Ranking (best first): O3 17.61, O5 18.55, O1 20.01, O4 20.83, O2 23.54.

Answers: score_O3 = 17.61; score_O5 = 18.55; score_O1 = 20.01; best_score = 17.61 (O3).

Sponsor reading: O3 wins despite carrying the highest residual risk (7.8) because risk is the lightest weight (0.6) while cost carries 1.4. O5, the lowest-risk and fastest route, loses by only 0.94, so the decision is weight-sensitive. Holding cost and schedule weights fixed, O5 overtakes O3 when 12.925 + 7.8w exceeds 16.385 + 3.6w, i.e. when the risk weight w rises above roughly 0.82 - well inside the range a board might defend. That sensitivity, not the raw ranking, is the message for the board.

scenarios.title: Duct Quantity Assurance on a Coastal Ridge Fibre Densification Programme
scenarios.summary: Audit contractor-reported duct-laying quantities against surveyed quantities, then report record count, completeness, mean absolute error and anomaly count before certifying an interim payment.
scenarios.brief: A regional operator is trenching fibre backhaul duct along a coastal ridge to feed newly densified radio sites. Each week the trenching contractor's field app submits metres of duct laid per section, and an independent survey crew re-measures the same sections. This period some sections came back with no field-app reading at all, and several others diverge from survey. The interim payment certificate is due, and the sponsor will not release it until the data-quality picture is quantified.
objectives: Compute record count and completeness percentage for a partially populated field-reporting dataset
Calculate mean absolute error between reported and surveyed quantities using present readings only
Identify and count anomalous records that breach a stated deviation threshold
Explain to a sponsor why completeness and error magnitude are separate quality signals in a payment certification
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic data-quality exercise; no external source data.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, identifiers and organisations are synthetic and simplified for training purposes only.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - record_count: count every section row in the register, whether or not a field reading exists. There are 15 rows, so record_count = 15.

Step 2 - completeness_pct: count rows carrying a reported value. Sections DX-104 and DX-109 have no reading, so present = 13. completeness_pct = 100 x 13 / 15 = 86.6667 -> 86.67.

Step 3 - mean_abs_error: over PRESENT rows only, |value - expected|: DX-101 13, DX-102 45, DX-103 4, DX-105 22, DX-106 3, DX-107 71, DX-108 24, DX-110 19, DX-111 58, DX-112 8, DX-113 11, DX-114 36, DX-115 12. Sum = 326. mean_abs_error = 326 / 13 = 25.0769 -> 25.08. Rows with no reading are excluded from numerator and denominator; they are a completeness problem, not an accuracy problem.

Step 4 - anomaly_count: count present rows whose absolute deviation exceeds the threshold of 42. Breaches are DX-102 (45), DX-107 (71) and DX-111 (58); deviations at or below 42 do not count. anomaly_count = 3.

Sponsor read-out: 86.67 completeness, 25.08 average metres of deviation and 3 threshold breaches - certify the clean sections and hold the three breaching plus two unreported sections pending re-survey.

scenarios.summary: Audit a 14-feed PDU telemetry extract taken during load-bank commissioning of a liquid-cooled AI training hall, then report record count, completeness, mean absolute error and anomaly count.
