Two feeds returned no reading at all. The sponsor wants to know whether the gaps and the spread are a metering problem or a real electrical one before signing the certificate.
objectives: Compute record count and completeness percentage from a telemetry extract containing omitted readings
Calculate mean absolute error between measured and expected values using present readings only
Apply a deviation threshold to count anomalous readings without distorting the error statistic
Interpret completeness and error metrics as an evidence gate for a commissioning handover decision
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic advanced data-quality exercise set in data centre commissioning telemetry.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, feed identifiers and events are synthetic and simplified for training and do not represent any real facility or equipment.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - record_count: count every row in the extract regardless of whether a reading was returned. 14 feeds are listed, so record_count = 14.

Step 2 - completeness_pct = 100 x present / all. 12 rows carry a reading; PDU-A4 and PDU-C1 have no value key. 100 x 12 / 14 = 85.7142... = 85.71.

Step 3 - mean_abs_error: take |value - expected| for the 12 PRESENT rows only; missing rows are excluded entirely, not treated as zero error. Deviations: A1 1.30, A2 6.30, A3 1.35, B1 0.90, B2 7.25, B3 0.85, B4 1.45, C2 1.65, C3 5.25, C4 2.15, D1 1.25, D2 1.55. Sum = 31.25, so mean_abs_error = 31.25 / 12 = 2.6041... = 2.60.

Step 4 - anomaly_count: count present rows whose absolute deviation exceeds the threshold of 4.5. Breaches are PDU-A2 (6.30), PDU-B2 (7.25) and PDU-C3 (5.25), so anomaly_count = 3.

Sponsor reading: completeness of 85.71 sits below a typical 90 percent evidence bar, so the two dead feeds must be recovered before the 2.60 mean absolute error can be defended, and the three breaching feeds (two over-drawing, one under-drawing) point to an electrical investigation rather than a metering recalibration alone.

config.prompt: You are the controls lead on the commissioning of Hall 3, a liquid-cooled hall built for dense AI training racks at a colocation campus. During the final load-bank step, the branch-circuit monitoring platform logged the measured draw on each power distribution unit feed against the modelled design draw for that step. The extract below lists one row per feed with its expected draw and, where the platform returned one, the measured value; two feeds reported nothing. A deviation counts as an anomaly when the absolute gap between measured and expected exceeds the stated threshold. From this extract compute the record count, the completeness percentage, the mean absolute error across present readings only, and the anomaly count. Round the percentage and the mean absolute error to 2 decimal places and report counts as whole numbers.

ask.label: Completeness percentage of the telemetry extract
Mean absolute error across present readings
Anomaly count (present readings breaching the threshold)

scenarios.title: Kestrel Vale Bypass: Earned Schedule After a Rejected Variation
scenarios.summary: A bypass programme's dashboard flatters progress with a rejected drainage variation. Strip it out, interpolate earned schedule at month 6, and forecast the true completion date with SPI(t).
scenarios.brief: The Kestrel Vale Bypass is a 9.5 km single-carriageway highway realignment with three roundabouts and a wildlife green bridge, planned over a 10-month earthworks-to-surfacing programme. At the end of month 6 the delivery partner's dashboard claims cumulative earned value of 3000, but the project controls office has flagged that 250 of that claim relates to a drainage realignment variation whose change request was formally REJECTED at the last change board — it only looks approved on the dashboard. The sponsor wants a time-based (earned schedule) view of progress before the surfacing subcontract is locked in.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by linear interpolation between cumulative planned-value periods
Distinguish approved baseline scope from rejected change work when establishing earned value
Compute time-based schedule metrics SV(t) and SPI(t) at a status date
Forecast total project duration using EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) and interpret the slippage
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, organisation, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Correct the earned value. The dashboard claims EV = 3000, but 250 of that belongs to a drainage realignment variation whose change request was rejected; it is not baseline scope. Corrected EV = 3000 - 250 = 2750.

Step 2 — Locate EV on the cumulative PV curve. PV(4) = 2300 and PV(5) = 3200, so 2300 < 2750 < 3200: ES lies between months 4 and 5.

Step 3 — Interpolate ES. ES = 4 + (EV - PV(4)) / (PV(5) - PV(4)) = 4 + (2750 - 2300) / (3200 - 2300) = 4 + 450/900 = 4.50 months.

Step 4 — Time-based schedule variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 4.50 - 6 = -1.50 months. The project has earned only 4.5 months of planned progress in 6 elapsed months: 1.5 months behind.

Step 5 — Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 4.50 / 6 = 0.75.

Step 6 — Time forecast at completion. EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) = 10 / 0.75 = 13.33 months, i.e. roughly 3.3 months of forecast slippage against the 10-month baseline if current schedule performance persists.

Final answers: es = 4.50; sv_time = -1.50; spi_time = 0.75; eac_time = 13.33.

ask.label: Schedule variance in time SV(t) = ES - AT (months, 2 decimal places)
Schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT (2 decimal places)
Estimate at completion for time EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) (months, 2 decimal places)

scenarios.title: Grandstand on the Clock: Earned Schedule at the Harbour Arena
scenarios.summary: Convert cost-based progress data into time-based measures for a six-week demountable grandstand build: interpolate earned schedule, then derive SV(t) and SPI(t) at the week-4 status point.
scenarios.brief: Coastline Events has erected a six-week demountable grandstand programme for a pop-up beach volleyball arena on a reclaimed harbour lot: scaffold towers, seating decks, camera gantries and egress stairs, all planned against a cumulative weekly planned-value curve. At the end of week 4 the site team reports earned value of 360 against a total planned value of 600, and the venue director wants a time-based read on progress because the broadcast rights holder has a fixed rehearsal date. Your job is to convert the cost-denominated data into earned schedule measures.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by interpolating earned value against a cumulative planned-value curve
Compute the time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT and state its sign convention
Compute and interpret the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real venue, contractor, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Locate EV on the cumulative PV curve. EV = 360. The plan shows PV(3) = 300 and PV(4) = 420, so 300 < 360 <= 420 and ES lies between week 3 and week 4.

Step 2 - Interpolate ES. ES = C + (EV - PV(C)) / (PV(C+1) - PV(C)), where C = 3 is the last whole period with PV <= EV.
ES = 3 + (360 - 300) / (420 - 300) = 3 + 60/120 = 3 + 0.50 = 3.50 weeks.

Step 3 - Time-based schedule variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 3.50 - 4 = -0.50 weeks. The negative sign means the work earned by the end of week 4 was planned to be complete half a week earlier than has actually elapsed - the build is running about half a week behind plan.

Step 4 - Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 3.50 / 4 = 0.875, which rounds to 0.88 to 2 decimal places. An SPI(t) below 1.00 confirms the programme is progressing slower than planned in time terms.

Final answers: ES = 3.50 weeks; SV(t) = -0.50 weeks; SPI(t) = 0.88 (0.875 unrounded).

config.prompt: You are the project controls analyst for a six-week demountable grandstand build at a pop-up beach volleyball arena on a reclaimed harbour lot. The cumulative planned-value curve for the programme is: week 1 = 80, week 2 = 180, week 3 = 300, week 4 = 420, week 5 = 520, week 6 = 600 (planned duration 6 weeks). At the end of week 4 (AT = 4), cumulative earned value is 360. Using earned schedule with linear interpolation between plan periods, compute: (1) Earned Schedule ES in weeks, (2) the time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT in weeks, and (3) the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT. Report ES and SV(t) to 2 decimal places and SPI(t) to 2 decimal places. Units are plain value units; no currency symbols are used.

ask.label: Schedule Performance Index SPI(t) = ES / AT

scenarios.title: Back-Loaded Release Train: Earned Schedule at Sprint 9
scenarios.summary: Expert earned-schedule drill on a 12-sprint software release train with a deliberately back-loaded baseline curve. Learners derive ES, SV(t), SPI(t) and EAC(t) by linear interpolation.
scenarios.brief: A platform team is rewriting a telemetry ingestion service and has baselined the work as a 12-sprint release train with a steep, back-loaded S-curve: light discovery sprints, a heavy mid-train build, then a tapering hardening tail. Time now is the end of sprint 9, and cumulative earned value sits well below the cumulative plan. Because the remaining plan flattens out, cost-style ratios and eyeballed "about one sprint late" judgements both mislead here; only interpolated earned schedule places the achieved work correctly on the baseline timeline.
objectives: Locate earned schedule by finding the baseline period whose cumulative PV brackets the reported EV
Interpolate ES linearly within the bracketing period rather than rounding to whole sprints
Compute SV(t) = ES - AT and SPI(t) = ES / AT and state them in time units
Forecast EAC(t) = planned duration / SPI(t) and distinguish it from a PV-ratio schedule index
Explain why a back-loaded baseline curve distorts the naive EV/PV schedule read
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic expert-level earned schedule scenario; no external source data.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real organisation, product or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (AT = 9, EV = 600, planned duration = 12):

Step 1 - Bracket the EV on the baseline curve. Cumulative PV at sprint 7 = 570 and at sprint 8 = 675. Since 570 <= 600 < 675, the completed whole periods N = 7.

Step 2 - Interpolate. ES = N + (EV - PV_N) / (PV_(N+1) - PV_N) = 7 + (600 - 570) / (675 - 570) = 7 + 30/105 = 7.2857 -> ES = 7.29 sprints.

Step 3 - Time variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 7.2857 - 9 = -1.7143 -> SV(t) = -1.71 sprints (behind schedule).

Step 4 - Time index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 7.2857 / 9 = 0.8095 -> SPI(t) = 0.81.

Step 5 - Forecast. EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) = 12 / 0.8095 = 14.8235 -> EAC(t) = 14.82 sprints, about 2.82 sprints of overrun.

Trap: the careless read is EV / PV_at = 600 / 765 = 0.784, implying 12 / 0.784 = 15.31 sprints. That ratio is distorted by the back-loaded curve and is a value index, not a time index. Rounding the bracketed ES down to 7.00 whole sprints is the second trap and overstates the slip.

config.prompt: A platform team is rewriting a telemetry ingestion service as a 12-sprint release train. The baselined cumulative planned value per sprint, the current sprint (time now), and the cumulative earned value achieved to date are all given in the figures below; the planned duration equals the final baseline sprint. The baseline curve is deliberately back-loaded, and a proposed scope change has not been baselined, so no adjustment for it is required. Using earned schedule mechanics, compute: the earned schedule ES in sprints, the time-based schedule variance SV(t) in sprints, the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t), and the time-based estimate at completion EAC(t) in sprints. Interpolate linearly between baseline sprints where the earned value falls between two of them. Report every answer rounded to 2 decimals.

scenarios.title: Level-Crossing Barrier Renewal: First EVM Health Check
scenarios.project_type: Regional rail level-crossing barrier renewal programme
scenarios.summary: A regional rail corridor is renewing 40 level-crossing barrier units. Four months in, the sponsor wants a first earned-value health check: cost variance, SPI, and CPI from a single snapshot.
scenarios.brief: The Marshvale Corridor programme is replacing 40 ageing level-crossing barrier units with modern obstacle-detecting barriers along a regional rail line. Installation runs in overnight possessions, and several crossings have taken longer than planned because buried cable troughs were found in worse condition than surveyed. The programme sponsor has asked the controls team for a first earned-value snapshot to see whether the overspend rumoured by the site team is real, and how far behind the possession schedule the works actually are.
objectives: Compute cost variance (CV) from earned value and actual cost at a single reporting snapshot
Compute the schedule performance index (SPI) and cost performance index (CPI) from PV, EV, and AC
Interpret whether an SPI and CPI below 1.0 signal schedule slippage and overspend to a project sponsor
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real railway, supplier, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 800, EV = 720, AC = 900, BAC = 2000.

Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 720 - 900 = -180. A negative CV means the work performed so far has cost 180 more than the value earned — the site team's overspend concern is real.

Step 2 — Schedule performance index: SPI = EV / PV = 720 / 800 = 0.90. The programme is delivering 90% of the work it planned to have finished by this snapshot, so the possession schedule is slipping.

Step 3 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 720 / 900 = 0.80. Every 1.00 spent is earning only 0.80 of budgeted work — the degraded cable troughs are eroding cost efficiency.

Final answers: CV = -180; SPI = 0.90; CPI = 0.80 (indices to 2 decimal places).

config.prompt: You are the project controls analyst on a regional rail programme replacing 40 level-crossing barrier units along the Marshvale Corridor. Installation happens in overnight possessions, and degraded cable troughs at several crossings have slowed the crews. Cost performance index (CPI), to 2 decimal places

scenarios.title: Weld-Cell Retrofit Line: Cost Forecast Under a Rejected Change
scenarios.project_type: Robotic weld-cell retrofit of a tractor-cab assembly line
scenarios.summary: Month-5 EVM snapshot of a robotic weld-cell retrofit that is overspending; compute CPI, EAC, VAC and TCPI while ignoring a change request the vendor treats as approved but the board rejected.
scenarios.brief: Mervale Agri-Systems is retrofitting the tractor-cab assembly line at its Plant 4 with six robotic weld cells. Five months in, integration rework on the fixture tooling has pushed spending ahead of earned progress, and the sponsor wants a defensible completion forecast before the next steering meeting. Complicating matters, the integration vendor's latest invoice cover letter references change request CR-014 (an extra 150000 for a seventh cell) as if it were approved — the change board rejected it last week, so the original budget at completion still governs.
objectives: Compute CPI from a single earned value snapshot
Forecast completion cost using EAC = BAC / CPI and derive the variance at completion
Compute TCPI against BAC and interpret the required cost efficiency to recover
Distinguish the approved BAC from a rejected change request when selecting inputs
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, project, or costs.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 736,000; EV = 662,400; AC = 745,200; BAC = 1,840,000.

Step 0 — Select the right budget. CR-014 (150,000) was REJECTED by the change board, so BAC remains 1,840,000. Do not inflate BAC.

Step 1 — CPI = EV / AC = 662,400 / 745,200 = 0.8888... ≈ 0.89. Each unit spent is earning about 0.89 of value: a cost overrun.

Step 2 — EAC = BAC / CPI = 1,840,000 x 745,200 / 662,400 = 2,070,000. This assumes current cost efficiency persists to completion.

Step 3 — VAC = BAC - EAC = 1,840,000 - 2,070,000 = -230,000. Negative VAC means a projected overrun of 230,000 against the approved budget.

Step 4 — TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 1,177,600 / 1,094,800 = 1.0756... ≈ 1.08. Remaining work must run about 8% more cost-efficiently than planned to finish on BAC — demanding, given the current CPI of 0.89.

Rounding: indices (CPI, TCPI) to 2 decimal places; money values (EAC, VAC) to the nearest whole number.

config.prompt: Mervale Agri-Systems is retrofitting its Plant 4 tractor-cab assembly line with six robotic weld cells. At the end of month 5, the controls system reports the planned value (PV), earned value (EV), actual cost (AC), and approved budget at completion (BAC) shown below. The integration vendor's invoice cover letter cites change request CR-014 — an extra 150000 for a seventh weld cell — as if it were approved, but the change control board REJECTED CR-014 last week, so base every calculation on the approved figures shown below only. Compute: 1) Cost Performance Index (CPI); 2) Estimate at Completion assuming current cost efficiency continues (EAC = BAC / CPI); 3) Variance at Completion (VAC = BAC - EAC); 4) To-Complete Performance Index against the approved BAC (TCPI). Round indices to 2 decimal places and money values to the nearest whole number. Do not use currency symbols.

ask.label: To-Complete Performance Index against the approved BAC (TCPI)

scenarios.title: Cold-Chain Vaccine Packaging Line: Mid-Qualification EVM Check
scenarios.summary: A foundation earned-value drill: compute cost variance, CPI, and SPI for a vaccine cold-chain packaging line at a single reporting snapshot to diagnose a suspected overspend.
scenarios.brief: A pharmaceutical manufacturer is qualifying a new cold-chain packaging line for a temperature-sensitive vaccine, and the sponsor has flagged concern that costs are running ahead of progress. At the latest reporting snapshot the controls team has planned value, earned value, actual cost, and the budget at completion in hand. Your job is to turn those four raw figures into the standard earned-value variance and indices that reveal whether the worry is justified.
objectives: Compute the cost variance (CV) from earned value and actual cost at a reporting snapshot.
Compute the cost performance index (CPI) and schedule performance index (SPI) to two decimal places.
Interpret index and variance signs to judge whether a project is over budget and behind schedule.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project, product, or organization.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (PV=200, EV=180, AC=200, BAC=400):

Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 180 - 200 = -20. The negative sign means more was spent than the value earned, so the line is over budget.

Step 2 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 180 / 200 = 0.90. Below 1.0 confirms the overspend — only 0.90 of value is earned per unit of cost.

Step 3 — Schedule performance index: SPI = EV / PV = 180 / 200 = 0.90. Below 1.0 shows the work is also behind the planned schedule.

Result: CV = -20, CPI = 0.90, SPI = 0.90. The sponsor's concern is justified: the qualification is both over budget and behind schedule at this snapshot.

config.prompt: A pharmaceutical manufacturer is qualifying a new cold-chain packaging line for a temperature-sensitive vaccine. scenarios.title: Billing Engine Rewrite: Month-5 Performance Snapshot
scenarios.summary: A subscription-billing platform rewrite is burning cash faster than it earns value, and a stale status deck wrongly shows a rejected scope change as approved. Compute the indices and forecast the damage.
scenarios.brief: Your product company is midway through a ten-month rewrite of its monolithic subscription-billing engine into event-driven microservices. Month 5 telemetry shows the team completing fewer story-point bundles than planned while contractor invoices run hot. The sponsor wants a clean forecast before Thursday's steering review — but a circulating status deck still shows a scope addition as approved when the change control board in fact rejected it, so the baseline must not be inflated.
objectives: Compute CPI and SPI from a single earned value snapshot
Compute a CPI-based estimate at completion and the variance at completion
Distinguish the approved performance measurement baseline from a rejected change that appears approved in stale reporting
Interpret cost and schedule indices to explain overspend to a sponsor
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, project, or costs.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 240000, EV = 200000, AC = 250000, BAC = 480000.

Step 0 — Fix the baseline. The 60000 partner-portal scope addition was REJECTED by the change control board, so the stale deck showing it as approved is wrong. BAC stays at 480000; do not add the 60000.

Step 1 — Cost Performance Index: CPI = EV / AC = 200000 / 250000 = 0.80. Every unit spent is earning only 0.80 of value.

Step 2 — Schedule Performance Index: SPI = EV / PV = 200000 / 240000 = 0.83 (0.8333 rounded to 2 decimal places). Work is progressing at about 83% of the planned rate.

Step 3 — Estimate at Completion (CPI method, assuming current cost efficiency continues): EAC = BAC / CPI = 480000 / 0.80 = 600000.

Step 4 — Variance at Completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 480000 - 600000 = -120000. The project is forecast to overrun its budget by 120000 if cost efficiency does not improve.

Interpretation: both indices below 1.0 mean the rewrite is simultaneously behind schedule and over cost; the sponsor should expect roughly a 25% cost overrun at completion unless the burn rate changes.

config.prompt:
You are the project controls analyst on a ten-month rewrite of a monolithic subscription-billing engine into event-driven microservices. At the end of month 5 you pull the earned value snapshot: planned value (PV), earned value (EV), actual cost (AC), and budget at completion (BAC) are shown below.

Caution: a proposed 60000 scope addition for a partner-portal entitlement module appears as 'Approved' in last week's status deck, but the change control board formally REJECTED it. The performance measurement baseline is unchanged — use only the BAC shown below and do not add the rejected 60000.

Compute for the sponsor's steering review: (1) the Cost Performance Index (CPI) and (2) the Schedule Performance Index (SPI), each rounded to 2 decimal places; (3) the Estimate at Completion (EAC) using the CPI method (EAC = BAC / CPI); and (4) the Variance at Completion (VAC = BAC - EAC). Report monetary results to 2 decimal places. Plain numbers only, no currency symbols.

scenarios.title: Floodplain Viaduct Bypass: Forecasting the Funding Tranche
scenarios.summary: A segmental-viaduct bypass slips after two casting moulds crack. Derive CPI, SPI, two competing estimates at completion, TCPI and VAC to give the sponsor board a defensible forecast.
scenarios.brief: A 14 km bypass is being built to pull freight off a congested valley route, and its critical path runs through a 41-span segmental viaduct crossing a braided floodplain. Two casting-yard moulds cracked in week 9, forcing added night shifts and premium-rate labour while span erection fell behind the plan. The sponsor board must release the next funding tranche and is asking whether the remaining work can still be delivered inside the approved budget. Your job is to convert the raw performance data into indices, forecasts and a recovery target the board can act on.
objectives: Compute CPI and SPI from PV, EV and AC and state the direction of each variance
Produce a CPI-based estimate at completion and a composite CPI x SPI estimate at completion from the same data set
Calculate the to-complete performance index against the approved budget at completion
Quantify variance at completion and interpret the funding implication for the sponsor board
Distinguish when an optimistic versus pessimistic forecast basis is appropriate for a schedule-driven overrun
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as scenario SC-EVM-203; all figures invented by the author for training use.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, figures and events are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project or cost data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 48600, EV = 43740, AC = 47850, BAC = 128400.

1. CPI = EV / AC = 43740 / 47850 = 0.914 (0.9141066). Every unit spent has returned about 0.914 units of value.
2. SPI = EV / PV = 43740 / 48600 = 0.900. Work is being earned at 90 percent of the planned rate.
3. Supporting variances: CV = EV - AC = 43740 - 47850 = -4110; SV = EV - PV = 43740 - 48600 = -4860. Both unfavourable.
4. EAC (CPI-based) = BAC / CPI = BAC x AC / EV = 128400 x 47850 / 43740 = 140465.02. This assumes the current cost efficiency persists to completion.
5. EAC (composite) = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI). Remaining work = 128400 - 43740 = 84660. CPI x SPI = 0.9141066 x 0.900 = 0.8226959. 84660 / 0.8226959 = 102905.58. EAC = 47850 + 102905.58 = 150755.58. This pessimistic basis assumes the schedule slip keeps dragging cost.
6. TCPI (to BAC) = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 84660 / (128400 - 47850) = 84660 / 80550 = 1.051. Remaining work must be performed 15 percent more efficiently than performance to date to land on budget.
7. VAC = BAC - EAC(CPI) = 128400 - 140465.02 = -12065.02, an overrun of roughly 9.4 percent of BAC.

Cross-checks: ETC = EAC - AC = 92615.02; percent complete = EV / BAC = 34.06 percent; percent spent = AC / BAC = 37.27 percent — value earned trails cash burned, consistent with CPI below 1.

config.prompt: You control costs on a 14 km dual-carriageway bypass whose critical path runs through a 41-span segmental viaduct across a braided floodplain. Two casting-yard moulds cracked in week 9, night-shift crews were added, and the sponsor board wants a defensible forecast before the next tranche of funding is released. Using the planned value, earned value, actual cost and budget at completion in the figures below, compute: the cost performance index, the schedule performance index, the CPI-based estimate at completion, the composite (CPI x SPI) estimate at completion, the to-complete performance index against the original budget, and the variance at completion. Report indices to three decimals and all money measures to two decimals. Show negative variances as negative numbers.

ask.label: Estimate at completion, composite CPI x SPI (EAC)

scenarios.title: Dispatch Console Rewrite: Forecasting the Final Bill
scenarios.summary: Forecast the final cost of a six-month warehouse dispatch software rewrite: compute the final CPI, a CPI-based EAC, and the VAC from cumulative earned value data.
scenarios.brief: A six-month rewrite of an ageing warehouse dispatch console is wrapping up its final month, and the sponsor is nervous: mid-project reports showed schedule slippage in month 3 and a spending spike in month 4. As the project controls analyst, you must use the cumulative earned value data to state where cost performance stands now and forecast the final bill.
objectives: Compute the final cumulative CPI from earned value and actual cost data.
Compute a CPI-based estimate at completion (EAC = BAC / CPI).
Interpret the variance at completion (VAC) as the forecast overrun or underrun against budget.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Read the final cumulative figures (Month 6): EV = 1080, AC = 1200, PV = 1200, BAC = 1200.

Step 2 — Final CPI = EV / AC = 1080 / 1200 = 0.90. Each unit spent has earned only 0.90 of value, so the project is running over cost.

Step 3 — Final EAC = BAC / final CPI = 1200 / 0.90 = 1333.33. If the current cost efficiency continues to the end, the total cost is forecast at 1333.33.

Step 4 — VAC = BAC - EAC = 1200 - 1333.33 = -133.33. The negative sign confirms a forecast overrun of about 133 against the 1200 budget.

Context checks (per-month cumulative indices): SPI by month = 0.90, 0.80, 0.70, 0.80, 0.84, 0.90 — worst schedule performance was Month 3 (SPI 0.70). CPI by month = 0.90, 0.91, 0.90, 0.80, 0.84, 0.90 — worst cost performance was Month 4 (CPI 0.80), when spending caught up with the plan while earned value lagged.

objectives: Compute the final cumulative CPI from EV and AC figures

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Final CPI. Use the last period's cumulative figures: EV = 1100, AC = 1300. CPI = EV / AC = 1100 / 1300 = 0.8462, which rounds to 0.85. Every unit of spend is earning about 0.85 units of budgeted work — the coolant-loop rework is dragging cost efficiency down.

Step 2 — EAC. EAC = BAC / CPI. Use the unrounded CPI: EAC = 1200 / (1100 / 1300) = 1200 x 1300 / 1100 = 1418.18. If current cost efficiency continues, the fit-out will finish at about 1418 against a 1200 budget.

Step 3 — VAC. VAC = BAC - EAC = 1200 - 1418.18 = -218.18. The negative sign means a forecast overrun of roughly 218, about 18% over budget — this is the figure the sponsor needs before committing the next tenant.

Final answers: final_cpi = 0.85, final_eac = 1418.18, vac = -218.18.

scenarios.worked_solution:

scenarios.brief: The Northreach Regional Rail Authority is assembling its renewal and enhancement portfolio ahead of a five-year control-period submission. Six candidate schemes compete for one funding envelope: resignalling, tunnel drainage, a freight loop, a battery shunter conversion, a sensor fleet and a level-crossing grade separation. objectives: Normalise each candidate's NPV against the largest absolute NPV in the candidate set
Apply a weighted portfolio score combining normalised NPV, strategic fit and delivery risk

Step 2 - Score each scheme with score = 0.5 x (npv / 214300) + 0.2 x fit - 0.3 x risk. RL1: 0.5 x (182400/214300) + 0.2 x 0.88 - 0.3 x 0.42 = 0.425572 + 0.176 - 0.126 = 0.4756. RL2: 0.5 x (96750/214300) + 0.2 x 0.61 - 0.3 x 0.28 = 0.225735 + 0.122 - 0.084 = 0.2637. RL3: 0.5 x 1 + 0.2 x 0.74 - 0.3 x 0.71 = 0.5 + 0.148 - 0.213 = 0.4350. RL6: 0.5 x (129850/214300) + 0.2 x 0.92 - 0.3 x 0.63 = 0.302963 + 0.184 - 0.189 = 0.2980. Step 3 - top_score is the maximum of those values, 0.4756 (RL1). Step 4 - total_npv = 182400 + 96750 + 214300 - 38900 + 57200 + 129850 = 641600. RL4 is value-destroying and drags the portfolio total down while still scoring worst.

Step 1 — Total weight. Sum the package weights: 40 + 25 + 20 + 10 + 5 = 100. So total_weight = 100.

Leadership has been circulating a headline completion figure taken straight off the status board. Your job is to produce the properly weighted roll-up before the month-end report is issued.
objectives: Compute the total weight of a multi-package control account from package weights
Calculate weighted overall percent complete as sum(weight x percent) divided by total weight
Distinguish a weighted roll-up from an unweighted average of package readings
Apply stated rounding conventions when reporting progress measures
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic progress-measurement exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, packages and organisations are synthetic and simplified for training purposes only.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Total weight: add every package weight. 8 + 46 + 52 + 39 + 31 + 12 + 15 + 9 + 6 + 29 = 247. total_weight = 247.

Step 2 - Earned weight per package = weight x percent: 1.1: 800; 1.2: 1472; 1.3: 936; 1.4: 975; 1.5: 372; 1.6: 1200; 1.7: 1320; 1.8: 900; 1.9: 570; 1.10: 145. Sum = 8690.

Step 3 - Weighted overall percent complete = 8690 / 247 = 35.18218..., so overall_percent = 35.18.

Trap check: the unweighted mean of the ten readings is (100+32+18+25+12+100+88+100+95+5)/10 = 575/10 = 57.50 percent. That figure is meaningless here: the four heaviest packages (46, 52, 39, 31 - together 168 of 247 weight, about 68 percent of the account) all sit below 33 percent complete, while the 100 percent readings come from packages carrying only 8, 12 and 9 weight. Reporting 57.50 would overstate progress by more than 22 percentage points.

Report the total weight as a plain number and the overall percent complete as a percentage rounded to two decimal places.

ask.label: Total weight of the control account

scenarios.title: Viaduct Bearing Delivery Slip on the Coastal Bypass Deck Package
scenarios.summary: Objectives rewritten to remove disclosed formulas; all other fields, figures and the worked method verified correct.
scenarios.brief: Section C4 of a coastal bypass upgrade replaces the deck of a 1.9 km viaduct while single-lane running is maintained beneath. The deck package drives the programme end date, and only a thin band of float survived the re-sequenced winter possession. The specialist bearing fabricator has now served a formal delay notice on its assembly deliveries. The sponsor wants the schedule consequence quantified before the next contract board.
objectives: Distinguish float absorption from critical delay when a supplier slip hits a driving package
Determine how much of a notified supplier delay reaches the contractual completion date
Restate the programme duration once delay breaks through the remaining float
Quantify the float eroded by the slip for procurement and contract board reporting
Explain to a sponsor why part of a supplier delay is invisible to the end date and part is not
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic highways procurement exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, supplier or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: project_duration = 418 working days, remaining_float = 27 working days, supplier_delay_days = 63 working days.

Step 1 - Critical delay. Float absorbs delay first; only the excess reaches the completion date.
critical_delay = max(0, supplier_delay_days - remaining_float) = max(0, 63 - 27) = 36.00 working days.

Step 2 - New project duration. The critical delay adds to the baseline because the deck package sits on the driving path.
new_project_duration = project_duration + critical_delay = 418 + 36 = 454.00 working days.

Step 3 - Float consumed. Float erodes only up to the float that exists, and only up to the size of the delay.
float_consumed = min(remaining_float, supplier_delay_days) = min(27, 63) = 27.00 working days.

Sponsor reading: 27 days of the 63-day slip vanish into float that no longer protects anything, and 36 days land directly on the section opening date. The deck package is now zero-float, so every later supplier interface becomes critical.

For a varied supplier delay, repeat Steps 1-3 with the figure shown; since the notified delay always exceeds 27 days here, float_consumed stays 27.00 and critical_delay moves one-for-one with the delay.

scenarios.title: Kinetic Pitch Tray Delay: Single-Source Fabricator Slippage at a Coastal Arena
scenarios.project_type: retractable pitch-tray and roof fit-out for a coastal arena
scenarios.summary: A sole-source fabricator slips delivery of the drive rails for an arena's kinetic pitch tray. Convert supplier slippage into critical-path delay, a revised programme duration, and float consumed.
scenarios.brief: Harbour Point Arena is a 61,400-seat coastal venue whose signature feature is a kinetic pitch tray that rolls out of the bowl on twin drive rails so the turf can cure outdoors between events. The rails are sole-sourced from a specialist fabricator, and the procurement package carries a modest protected float window before roof-closure and turf-lay activities go hard-logic. The fabricator has now notified a slip on the rail delivery date. The sponsor board wants the programme consequence quantified before the next commercial review.
objectives: Separate supplier slippage absorbed by float from slippage that lands on the critical path
Compute critical delay as the excess of supplier delay over remaining float
Revise total programme duration by adding only the critical portion of the delay
Quantify float consumed as a residual-buffer indicator for a sole-source package
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab from standard critical-path and procurement float-consumption relationships.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, entities and events are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real venue, supplier or programme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: project_duration = 418 days, remaining_float = 9 days, supplier_delay_days = 23 days.

Step 1 - Critical delay. Float absorbs slippage first, so only the excess reaches the critical path.
critical_delay = max(0, supplier_delay_days - remaining_float) = max(0, 23 - 9) = 14 days.

Step 2 - Revised programme duration. Only the critical portion extends the end date.
new_project_duration = project_duration + critical_delay = 418 + 14 = 432 days.

Step 3 - Float consumed. Slippage cannot burn more buffer than exists.
float_consumed = min(remaining_float, supplier_delay_days) = min(9, 23) = 9 days.

Sponsor read-out: the rail package has consumed its entire 9-day protected buffer and still pushes handover out by 14 days to a 432-day programme. The activity is now zero-float, so any further fabricator slippage transfers day-for-day to the opening date and should trigger expediting or a parallel-supply decision. Report all three answers as whole days.

scenarios.title: Night Possession Weld Output: Productivity Factor on a Re-Railing Programme
scenarios.project_type: Freight-corridor re-railing and flash-butt welding programme
scenarios.summary: Advanced rail productivity drill: convert planned and earned flash-butt weld quantities and labour hours into planned productivity, actual productivity, a productivity factor, and hours and quantity variances.
scenarios.brief: A freight-corridor re-railing programme is running flash-butt welding from a mobile welding train inside short night possessions. Weld output is visibly behind the tender curve, and the welding labour hours booked have already overrun the allowance. The sponsor needs to know whether the crews are genuinely less productive per hour or whether the story is simply lost possession time. You will convert the raw quantity and hours data into a defensible productivity picture.
objectives: Calculate planned and actual labour productivity in welds per labour hour from quantity and hours data.
Derive the productivity factor as actual productivity divided by planned productivity.
Compute hours variance and quantity variance and state their sign convention correctly.
Interpret a sub-unity productivity factor alongside a quantity shortfall for a sponsor briefing.
Apply the specified rounding to productivity, factor and variance measures.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as scenario SC-PROD-203; all data invented for instruction.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real rail programme, contractor or workforce.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: planned_qty = 2340 welds, planned_hours = 7410 labour hours, earned_qty = 1896 welds, actual_hours = 7896 labour hours.

Step 1 - Planned productivity = planned_qty / planned_hours = 2340 / 7410 = 0.3158 welds per labour hour (0.315789...).

Step 2 - Actual productivity = earned_qty / actual_hours = 1896 / 7896 = 0.2401 welds per labour hour (0.240122...).

Step 3 - Productivity factor = actual productivity / planned productivity = 0.240122 / 0.315789 = 0.7604. A factor below 1.0 means each labour hour is buying less weld output than the tender assumed; here roughly 24 percent less.

Step 4 - Hours variance = actual_hours - planned_hours = 7896 - 7410 = 486 labour hours. Positive, so the welding allowance is overspent in hours.

Step 5 - Quantity variance = earned_qty - planned_qty = 1896 - 2340 = -444 welds. Negative, so physical output is short of plan.

Interpretation for the sponsor: the crews burned 486 more hours than allowed and still finished 444 welds short. Because the factor is 0.7604 rather than close to 1.0, the shortfall is not explained by lost possession time alone - the hourly rate of welding itself has degraded, so adding possessions without addressing crew productivity will not recover the programme.

Final values: planned_productivity 0.3158, actual_productivity 0.2401, factor 0.7604, hours_variance 486, qty_variance -444.

Report the two productivity values and the factor to 4 decimal places, and report both variances as whole numbers.

scenarios.title: Seam-Weld Cell Ramp-Up: Labour Productivity Diagnosis
scenarios.summary: Advanced productivity drill on a stainless heat-exchanger weld cell: turn planned and earned weld counts into productivity rates, a performance factor, and hour and quantity variances.
scenarios.brief: A contract fabricator has stood up a new robotic seam-welding cell to produce stainless heat-exchanger shells. The ramp-up plan assumed a steady weld rate once fixtures were proven, but changeover trials and weld rework have pushed the second shift into unplanned overtime while the finished weld count lags the curve. The sponsor wants shift performance stated as a rate and a factor, not as anecdotes from the shop floor.
objectives: Compute planned productivity as planned quantity divided by planned labour hours
Compute actual productivity from earned quantity and actual labour hours
Derive the productivity factor as actual productivity divided by planned productivity
Quantify hours variance and quantity variance against the ramp-up baseline
Interpret whether the cell is under- or over-performing its ramp-up assumption
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic advanced productivity-analysis exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real facility, product line or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (planned_qty 17940 welds, planned_hours 3120, earned_qty 15873 welds, actual_hours 3468):

Step 1 - Planned productivity = planned_qty / planned_hours = 17940 / 3120 = 5.750 welds per labour hour.

Step 2 - Actual productivity = earned_qty / actual_hours = 15873 / 3468 = 4.577 welds per labour hour (4.576990 unrounded).

Step 3 - Productivity factor = actual / planned = 4.576990 / 5.750 = 0.796. Below 1.0, so each labour hour delivers about 20 percent fewer welds than the ramp-up plan assumed.

Step 4 - Hours variance = actual_hours - planned_hours = 3468 - 3120 = +348 labour hours above plan.

Step 5 - Quantity variance = earned_qty - planned_qty = 15873 - 17940 = -2067 welds short of planned scope.

Sponsor reading: the cell burned 348 extra hours and still finished 2067 welds short, so this is a rate problem (factor 0.796), not a manning problem. At the observed rate, the remaining 2067 welds would absorb roughly 2067 / 4.577 = 452 further labour hours unless changeover and rework losses are removed.

scenarios.title: Lyophilizer Requalification PERT Timeline
scenarios.summary: Apply three-point PERT estimating to a five-activity lyophilizer requalification chain: compute expected duration, standard deviation, and on-time probability against a fixed deadline.
scenarios.brief: A pharmaceutical site has pulled a freeze-drying (lyophilizer) unit offline for a mandatory requalification campaign before it can return to sterile production. The validation lead has gathered optimistic, most-likely, and pessimistic durations for each sequential activity and must brief the sponsor on how long the campaign will take and how likely it is to finish within the release window. Use PERT three-point estimating to quantify the schedule and its risk.
objectives: Compute the PERT expected duration of a sequential activity chain from three-point estimates.
Compute the standard deviation of the chain by combining individual activity variances.
Interpret the probability of completing the campaign on or before a fixed deadline using the normal approximation.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real facility, product, or qualification programme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Use PERT three-point estimating on each activity, then combine.

Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A: (4 + 4*6 + 14)/6 = 42/6 = 7
B: (3 + 4*5 + 7)/6 = 30/6 = 5
C: (2 + 4*3 + 10)/6 = 24/6 = 4
D: (6 + 4*8 + 16)/6 = 54/6 = 9
E: (1 + 4*3 + 5)/6 = 18/6 = 3

Step 2 — Expected duration of chain (sum): 7 + 5 + 4 + 9 + 3 = 28 days.

Step 3 — Activity standard deviations, (p - o)/6, and variances:
A: (14-4)/6 = 10/6 = 1.6667, var = 2.7778
B: (7-3)/6 = 4/6 = 0.6667, var = 0.4444
C: (10-2)/6 = 8/6 = 1.3333, var = 1.7778
D: (16-6)/6 = 10/6 = 1.6667, var = 2.7778
E: (5-1)/6 = 4/6 = 0.6667, var = 0.4444

Step 4 — Project variance (sum) = 2.7778 + 0.4444 + 1.7778 + 2.7778 + 0.4444 = 8.2222.
Project standard deviation = sqrt(8.2222) = 2.87 days.

Step 5 — Probability of finishing on or before the deadline of 32 days.
Z = (deadline - expected) / std_dev = (32 - 28) / 2.8674 = 4 / 2.8674 = 1.395.
Normal CDF at Z = 1.395 gives approximately 0.9185, i.e. about 91.84%.

Final answers: expected_duration = 28 days; std_dev = 2.87 days; prob_on_time = 91.84%.

scenarios.title: Feature Store Cutover: PERT Chain Under a Partner Deadline
scenarios.summary: Estimate the completion probability of a five-step feature-store migration chain using PERT three-point estimates — while spotting a compression change that was never actually approved.
scenarios.brief: A streaming-media platform is replacing the feature store behind its recommendation engine before a partner integration window opens. The migration runs as a strict five-activity chain: schema mapping, historical data backfill, a dual-write shim, shadow-traffic validation, and a cutover rehearsal. A contractor proposed crashing the backfill step, but the change board deferred that request without approval — the baseline three-point estimates still govern the plan.
objectives: Compute the PERT expected duration of a serial activity chain from three-point estimates.
Compute the path standard deviation by summing activity variances, not standard deviations.
Interpret a z-score against a fixed deadline to state the probability of on-time completion.
Distinguish approved baseline estimates from a proposed but rejected change request.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organization or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected durations, te = (o + 4m + p)/6 for each activity:
A Schema mapping (4,6,9): te = 37/6 = 6.1667
B Historical backfill (8,12,20): te = 76/6 = 12.6667 (use the BASELINE figures — the crash proposal o=5, m=8, p=12 was deferred by the change board, never approved)
C Dual-write shim (5,7,12): te = 45/6 = 7.5000
D Shadow-traffic validation (6,9,15): te = 57/6 = 9.5000
E Cutover rehearsal (3,5,8): te = 31/6 = 5.1667

Expected chain duration = 6.1667 + 12.6667 + 7.5 + 9.5 + 5.1667 = 41.00 days.

Step 2 — Activity variances, var = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A: (5/6)^2 = 0.6944; B: (12/6)^2 = 4.0000; C: (7/6)^2 = 1.3611; D: (9/6)^2 = 2.2500; E: (5/6)^2 = 0.6944.
Sum of variances = 9.0000. Path standard deviation = sqrt(9.0000) = 3.00 days. (Never add standard deviations directly.)

Step 3 — Probability of finishing by the 45-day deadline:
z = (deadline - expected) / sd = (45 - 41) / 3 = 1.3333.
From the standard normal distribution, Phi(1.3333) = 0.9088, so the probability of on-time completion is approximately 90.88%.

Final answers: expected_duration = 41.00 days; std_dev = 3.00 days; prob_on_time = 90.88%.

scenarios.title: Valley Fibre Cutover: Beating the Road-Closure Clock
scenarios.summary: Estimate whether a three-activity fibre backhaul build will finish inside a 23-day road-closure concession using PERT three-point estimates and the normal approximation.

The road authority has granted a single 23-working-day lane-closure concession, and the delivery lead wants to know how likely the three-activity build chain is to finish inside it. You will apply the PERT three-point method to the crew's optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from three-point estimates using (o + 4m + p) / 6.
Compute the standard deviation of an activity chain by summing variances ((p - o) / 6)^2.
Interpret a z-score against a fixed deadline to estimate the probability of on-time completion.
Explain why chain uncertainty combines through variances rather than standard deviations.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or authority.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A: (3 + 24 + 9) / 6 = 6.00 days
B: (5 + 32 + 11) / 6 = 8.00 days
C: (4 + 28 + 10) / 6 = 7.00 days
Chain expected duration = 6 + 8 + 7 = 21.00 days.

Step 2 - Variance per activity, var = ((p - o) / 6)^2:
A: ((9 - 3) / 6)^2 = 1.00
B: ((11 - 5) / 6)^2 = 1.00
C: ((10 - 4) / 6)^2 = 1.00
Chain variance = 3.00, so chain standard deviation = sqrt(3.00) = 1.73 days.

Step 3 - Probability of meeting the 23-day concession:
z = (deadline - expected) / std dev = (23 - 21) / 1.7321 = 1.15.
From the standard normal distribution, Phi(1.1547) = 0.8759.
Probability of on-time completion = 87.59% (approximately 87.6%).

Interpretation: the build is expected to finish with 2 days of buffer inside the concession, and there is roughly an 88% chance of completing before the lane closure expires — a healthy but not certain margin, so the residual ~12% risk should be flagged to the sponsor.

scenarios.title: Hall C Liquid-Cooling Retrofit: PERT Analysis Under a Contested Deadline
scenarios.summary: Run a PERT analysis on a five-activity liquid-cooling retrofit chain in a live data hall and estimate the probability of hitting a contractual re-energisation deadline that a rejected change request tried to move.
scenarios.brief: A colocation operator is converting Hall C from air cooling to direct liquid cooling so a hyperscale tenant can deploy high-density compute racks. The retrofit runs as a strict five-activity chain because the hall's chilled-water loop must stay isolated until commissioning completes. The tenant's hosting agreement sets a re-energisation deadline of 52 working days; a subcontractor's change request to relax it to 56 days is stamped "logged" in the weekly report but was formally REJECTED by the change board, so the 52-day date stands. The delivery director wants a defensible probability of finishing on time before the next tenant review.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from three-point (o, m, p) estimates and aggregate them along an activity chain.
Compute the chain standard deviation by summing activity variances, not standard deviations.
Interpret a z-score against the normal distribution to estimate the probability of meeting a deadline.
Distinguish the governing contractual deadline from a rejected change request that appears in project reporting.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation, facility, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p)/6:
A Drain and isolate chilled-water loop: (4 + 24 + 10)/6 = 6.33
B Install CDU skids: (8 + 40 + 14)/6 = 10.33
C Pipework and manifold tie-ins: (10 + 52 + 22)/6 = 14.00
D Leak test and fluid charge: (5 + 28 + 12)/6 = 7.50
E Integrated systems commissioning: (6 + 36 + 15)/6 = 9.50

Step 2 — Chain expected duration: E = 6.33 + 10.33 + 14.00 + 7.50 + 9.50 = 47.67 days.

Step 3 — Variance per activity, v = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; B: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; C: (12/6)^2 = 4.0000; D: (7/6)^2 = 1.3611; E: (9/6)^2 = 2.2500.
Sum of variances = 9.6111. Chain standard deviation = sqrt(9.6111) = 3.10 days. (Never add standard deviations directly.)

Step 4 — Governing deadline. The change request for 56 days was REJECTED by the change board, so the contractual 52-day deadline applies.

Step 5 — Probability of on-time completion:
z = (52 - 47.67)/3.10 = 1.40.
From the standard normal distribution, P(Z <= 1.40) is approximately 0.919, so the probability of re-energising Hall C on time is about 91.9%.

Interpretation: the chain carries a healthy margin against the 52-day deadline, but activity C (tie-ins) contributes the largest variance and remains the best target for risk response if the estimates deteriorate.

scenarios.title: Marrowfield Ridge Bypass: PERT Risk on a Single-Diversion Closure Corridor
scenarios.summary: Advanced three-point PERT drill on a six-activity highway closure chain: derive expected path duration, standard deviation, variance and the probability of reopening by the contractual deadline.
scenarios.brief: The Marrowfield Ridge bypass is served by a single diversion route, so its six closure activities cannot overlap - verge stripping, embankment fill, culvert diversion, viaduct deck jointing, surfacing, and gantry commissioning run strictly end to end. The delivery team has replaced single-point durations with optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates after two earlier closures overran. The sponsor holds a contractual reopening date and wants to know, in probability terms, how exposed the scheme is. Your job is to turn the three-point estimates into a defensible confidence statement.
objectives: Compute beta PERT expected durations te=(o+4m+p)/6 for every activity on a sequential chain
Aggregate activity variances correctly, recognising that variances add along a path while standard deviations do not
Derive the path standard deviation and the z-score for a stated contractual deadline
Convert the z-score into a probability of on-time reopening and interpret it as schedule confidence for a sponsor
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab using standard beta-PERT and normal-approximation schedule risk technique; all figures invented for training.
scenarios.disclaimers: All activities, durations and deadlines are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real highway scheme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (deadline 148 days). Per activity, te=(o+4m+p)/6, sigma=(p-o)/6, variance=sigma^2.
A 14/18/32: te = 118/6 = 19.67, sigma = 3.00, var = 9.00
B 21/27/45: te = 174/6 = 29.00, sigma = 4.00, var = 16.00
C 9/13/23: te = 84/6 = 14.00, sigma = 2.33, var = 5.44
D 26/34/54: te = 216/6 = 36.00, sigma = 4.67, var = 21.78
E 11/16/27: te = 102/6 = 17.00, sigma = 2.67, var = 7.11
F 18/23/40: te = 150/6 = 25.00, sigma = 3.67, var = 13.44
Step 1 - Expected path duration = sum of te = 19.67+29.00+14.00+36.00+17.00+25.00 = 140.67 days.
Step 2 - Path variance = sum of activity variances (they add on a chain) = 9.00+16.00+5.44+21.78+7.11+13.44 = 72.78 days squared. Never sum the standard deviations.
Step 3 - Path standard deviation = sqrt(72.78) = 8.53 days.
Step 4 - z = (deadline - expected duration)/sigma = (148 - 140.67)/8.531 = 7.33/8.531 = 0.8596.
Step 5 - P(T <= 148) = Phi(0.8596) = 0.8050.
Answers: expected_duration 140.67, std_dev 8.53, variance 72.78, prob_on_time 0.8050.
Sponsor reading: the deadline sits only about 7.3 days above the mean, roughly 0.86 sigma, giving about 80.5% confidence and close to a 1-in-5 chance of a late reopening. Activity D alone contributes 21.78 of the 72.78 total variance, so tightening the viaduct deck jointing estimate is the highest-leverage risk response.

config.prompt:
You are controls lead on the Marrowfield Ridge bypass. A single diversion route serves the whole section, so the six closure activities - verge stripping, embankment fill, culvert diversion, viaduct deck jointing, binder and surface course, and gantry commissioning - must run strictly in sequence with no overlap. Optimistic, most likely and pessimistic day estimates for each activity, together with the sponsor's contractual reopening deadline, are given in the figures below.

Using three-point (beta) PERT, treating the activity durations as independent and the path total as approximately normal, report the expected path duration in days, the path standard deviation in days, the path variance in days squared, and the probability of reopening on or before the deadline. Round the expected duration, standard deviation and variance to 2 decimal places, and give the probability as a decimal between 0 and 1 rounded to 4 decimal places.

ask.label: Probability of reopening on or before the deadline (decimal 0-1)

scenarios.title: Small-Cell Densification: Integration Crew Overload Profile
scenarios.summary: Read a nine-window resource histogram for an RF integration crew pool and quantify peak demand, peak capacity, the worst single-period shortfall, cumulative over-demand and how many windows are overloaded.
scenarios.brief: A fixed-wireless operator is bolting small cells onto street furniture across a dense urban cluster, and the accredited RF integration pool ramps up in three capacity steps as new crews finish certification. The demand curve, however, is driven by site-access permits that land in bursts, so it does not ramp in the same shape. The sponsor has been asked to fund contractor top-up but wants the size and shape of the gap on one page first. Your job is to turn the raw demand-versus-capacity table into the five numbers that decision rests on.
objectives: Extract peak single-period demand and peak single-period capacity from a multi-period resource histogram
Compute period-by-period shortfall as demand minus capacity, treating non-negative slack periods as zero overload
Identify the peak overload period as the largest single-period shortfall
Aggregate total over-demand across all periods and count the number of overloaded periods
Express the resulting gap in crew-hours terms a sponsor can act on when sizing contractor top-up
scenarios.provenance: Synthetic scenario authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; standard resource-levelling demand-versus-capacity method.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real operator, crew pool, or rollout programme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Shortfall per period = max(0, demand - capacity), in crew-hours.
P1: 1240 - 1380 = -140 -> 0 (slack)
P2: 1585 - 1380 = 205
P3: 1742 - 1470 = 272
P4: 2108 - 1470 = 638
P5: 2364 - 1655 = 709
P6: 2051 - 1655 = 396
P7: 1896 - 1940 = -44 -> 0 (slack)
P8: 2275 - 1940 = 335
P9: 1610 - 1940 = -330 -> 0 (slack)

Step 2 - peak_demand = max(demand) = 2364.00 (period 5).

Step 3 - peak_capacity = max(capacity) = 1940.00 (periods 7, 8 and 9, after the third certification step).

Step 4 - peak_overload = max(shortfall) = 709.00 crew-hours, in period 5. This sizes the single worst crew-hour hole and therefore the minimum surge the contractor frame must be able to absorb in one two-week window.

Step 5 - total_overdemand = 205 + 272 + 638 + 709 + 396 + 335 = 2555.00 crew-hours. This is the cumulative unmet effort that must be bought in, deferred, or absorbed by re-sequencing permit-driven site releases.

Step 6 - overloaded_periods = count of periods with shortfall > 0 = periods 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 = 6.

Sponsor reading: the pool is short in six of nine windows, and although capacity eventually overtakes demand in periods 7 and 9, that late slack (44 + 330 = 374 crew-hours) cannot be moved backwards to cover a 2555 crew-hour gap concentrated in the middle of the programme.

Final answers: peak_demand = 2364.00; peak_capacity = 1940.00; peak_overload = 709.00; total_overdemand = 2555.00; overloaded_periods = 6.

config.prompt: A regional fixed-wireless operator is densifying its network with small cells mounted on street furniture, tracked across nine consecutive two-week windows. Each window lists the RF integration and commissioning demand in crew-hours alongside the crew-hours the accredited integration pool can actually supply. The sponsor will not approve a contractor top-up until the staffing pinch is quantified. From the periods table, compute: peak demand, peak capacity, peak overload (the largest single-period shortfall where demand exceeds capacity), total over-demand (the sum of every period shortfall), and the number of overloaded periods. Ignore any window where capacity meets or exceeds demand. Work in crew-hours per period and round each answer to 2 decimal places.

ask.label: Peak demand (crew-hours in a single period)
Peak capacity (crew-hours in a single period)
Total over-demand (sum of all period shortfalls, crew-hours)

scenarios.title: Hall D Liquid-Cooling Retrofit: Commissioning Crew Overload
scenarios.summary: An eight-week liquid-cooling retrofit inside a live colocation hall outruns its commissioning crew. Read the demand-versus-capacity profile and quantify the peak, the worst week and the total shortfall.
scenarios.brief: A colocation campus is converting Hall D from rear-door air cooling to direct-to-chip liquid cooling without taking the hall offline. Every manifold pressure test, leak check and rack energisation must be signed off by one pooled certified commissioning crew, whose roster is capped by badge-and-escort limits inside a live white space. The schedule has been levelled once already, yet the profile still shows weeks where planned crew-hours exceed anything the roster can supply. The sponsor wants the size and shape of that gap before approving a second commissioning shift.
objectives: Read a period-by-period resource demand and capacity profile accurately
Identify peak demand and peak capacity across an eight-period horizon
Compute the largest single-period shortfall (peak overload) from a levelled profile
Sum period shortfalls to size total over-demand in crew-hours
Count overloaded periods to scope the mitigation window for a sponsor
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab from a synthetic data centre retrofit resource profile.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real facility, crew or programme.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Peak demand = max(demand) over weeks 1-8: 1840, 2260, 2680, 3145, 3410, 2955, 2115, 1730. Peak demand = 3410 crew-hours (week 5).

Step 2 - Peak capacity = max(capacity): 2120, 2120, 2260, 2260, 2680, 2680, 2405, 2405. Peak capacity = 2680 crew-hours (weeks 5 and 6).

Step 3 - Period shortfall = max(0, demand - capacity):
W1: 1840-2120 = -280 -> 0
W2: 2260-2120 = 140
W3: 2680-2260 = 420
W4: 3145-2260 = 885
W5: 3410-2680 = 730
W6: 2955-2680 = 275
W7: 2115-2405 = -290 -> 0
W8: 1730-2405 = -675 -> 0

Step 4 - Peak overload = max(shortfall) = 885 crew-hours in week 4. This is not the peak-demand week: week 5 demands more but also has higher capacity, so week 4 is the binding constraint.

Step 5 - Total over-demand = 140 + 420 + 885 + 730 + 275 = 2450 crew-hours.

Step 6 - Overloaded periods = weeks with shortfall > 0 = weeks 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 = 5.

Final values: peak_demand 3410; peak_capacity 2680; peak_overload 885; total_overdemand 2450; overloaded_periods 5.

config.prompt: A colocation campus is converting Hall D from rear-door air cooling to direct-to-chip liquid cooling while the hall stays live, so every manifold pressure test, leak check and rack energisation must be signed off by one pooled certified commissioning crew. From these figures, determine: the peak demand in any single week; the peak capacity in any single week; the largest single-week shortfall (peak overload); the total over-demand across all eight weeks; and the number of weeks in which demand exceeds capacity. Report the first four measures in crew-hours and the last as a whole count, rounding every answer to two decimals.

ask.label: Peak demand (crew-hours in any single week)

scenarios.title: Contingency Check on the Marlow Vale Branch Signalling Renewal
scenarios.summary: Quantify a four-item risk register for a rural branch-line signalling renewal, computing expected monetary value for individual threats, one opportunity, and the register as a whole.
scenarios.brief: The fictional Marlow Vale branch is a 12 km rural rail line getting a full signalling renewal: new colour-light signals, cable troughing, and two relocated gantries. The sponsor has challenged the contingency figure ahead of the quarterly gate review, and the project controls lead has asked you to put numbers on the live risk register. Three threats and one cost-saving opportunity are on the table, and the contingency conversation hinges on the register's expected monetary value.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value (EMV) of an individual threat as probability times impact
Compute the EMV of an opportunity and recognise its positive sign
Aggregate individual risk EMVs into a register-level total to inform a contingency discussion
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real railway, supplier, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
EMV of a single risk = probability x impact (threats carry negative impacts, opportunities positive).

Step 1 — R1 Cable strike during troughing: 0.40 x (-50,000) = -20,000.
Step 2 — R2 Late gantry steel delivery: 0.25 x (-80,000) = -20,000.
Step 3 — R3 Cutting-face stabilisation works: 0.10 x (-120,000) = -12,000.
Step 4 — R4 Recovered copper cable resale (opportunity): 0.50 x (+30,000) = +15,000.
Step 5 — Register total EMV = sum of all four = -20,000 + (-20,000) + (-12,000) + 15,000 = -37,000.

Answers: emv_R2 = -20,000; emv_R4 = +15,000; emv (register total) = -37,000. The negative total indicates the register is net-adverse by 37,000, which is the risk-based figure to weigh against the held contingency.

config.prompt: You are the project controls analyst on the Marlow Vale branch signalling renewal, a 12 km rural line receiving new colour-light signals, cable troughing, and two relocated gantries. Report values to 2 decimal places, keeping the sign convention (threats negative, opportunities positive).

risks.name: Cable strike during troughing excavation

scenarios.title: Powder-Coating Line Retrofit: Risk Register EMV
scenarios.summary: Quantify a five-entry risk register for a powder-coating line retrofit at an appliance plant, computing expected monetary value for individual risks and the register total while netting threats against opportunities.
scenarios.brief: Valtara Appliance Works is retrofitting its ageing manual paint shop with an automated powder-coating line during a planned three-week summer shutdown. The steering group is nervous: the shutdown window is fixed, the robot integrator has slipped on past jobs, and the sponsor wants a single number that tells her whether the register is net threat or net opportunity before she sizes the contingency reserve. As the project controls analyst, you must quantify each register entry and the register as a whole using expected monetary value.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value (EMV) of an individual threat and an individual opportunity from probability and impact
Compute the register-total EMV by summing signed EMVs across all entries
Distinguish threats (negative impact) from opportunities (positive impact) and interpret the sign of the net result for contingency sizing
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, project, or market data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
EMV of a single risk = probability x impact (impact keeps its sign: negative = threat, positive = opportunity).

Step 1 — EMV per entry:
- R1 Refractory panel rework: 0.30 x (-48000) = -14400.00
- R2 Integrator schedule slip penalty: 0.25 x (-60000) = -15000.00
- R3 Bulk resin discount (opportunity): 0.60 x (+25000) = +15000.00
- R4 Grid interruption during commissioning: 0.10 x (-90000) = -9000.00
- R5 Early pilot-batch acceptance (opportunity): 0.35 x (+20000) = +7000.00

Step 2 — Register total EMV = sum of all signed EMVs:
-14400 - 15000 + 15000 - 9000 + 7000 = -16400.00

Answers:
- emv_R2 = -15000.00
- emv_R3 = +15000.00
- emv (register total) = -16400.00

Interpretation: even after netting the two opportunities, the register carries a net expected exposure of 16400, so the sponsor should size the contingency reserve around this net threat position rather than treating the resin discount as already banked.

scenarios.title: Coastal Fixed-Wireless Densification: Risk Register EMV
scenarios.summary: Convert a six-line telecoms risk register - four threats and two opportunities - into line-item and total expected monetary value to defend a contingency figure to the sponsor board.
scenarios.brief: The Halvern Coast corridor programme is densifying fixed-wireless access across 640 nodes, backed by a microwave ring feeding four aggregation hubs. Two threats sit on the regulatory critical path and one sits on the radio design, while a transit co-location deal and a vendor volume rebate could claw money back. The sponsor board has rejected a flat percentage contingency and asked the controls lead to defend a number line by line. Your job is to convert the quantified register into expected monetary value.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value of an individual quantified risk as probability multiplied by signed impact
Apply correct sign conventions so threats reduce and opportunities increase register value
Aggregate line-item EMVs into a single register-level EMV for contingency argument
Interpret a negative register EMV as the expected net exposure a sponsor must fund
Report EMV results to a stated rounding precision without dropping signs
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab using standard quantitative risk analysis practice (EMV = probability x impact).
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, organisations and locations are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: EMV(risk) = probability x impact, keeping the sign of the impact (negative = threat, positive = opportunity). Register EMV = sum of all line EMVs.

Line by line:
R1: 0.42 x (-1,860,000) = -781,200.00
R2: 0.28 x (-2,450,000) = -686,000.00
R3: 0.55 x (-940,000) = -517,000.00
R4: 0.17 x (-3,200,000) = -544,000.00
R5: 0.33 x 2,750,000 = +907,500.00
R6: 0.62 x 610,000 = +378,200.00

Aggregate:
Threat subtotal = -781,200 - 686,000 - 517,000 - 544,000 = -2,528,200.00
Opportunity subtotal = 907,500 + 378,200 = +1,285,700.00
Total EMV = -2,528,200.00 + 1,285,700.00 = -1,242,500.00

Answers:
emv_R1 = -781200.00
emv_R4 = -544000.00
emv_R5 = 907500.00
emv_R6 = 378200.00
emv = -1242500.00

Sponsor reading: the register carries an expected net exposure of 1,242,500. The two opportunities offset just over half the threat exposure, but only R6 is more likely than not, so a contingency set purely on the net figure leans on an anchor-tenancy deal (R5) that fails two times in three. A defensible reserve is argued from the -2,528,200 threat exposure, with the opportunity EMV tracked separately as upside rather than pre-spent.

scenarios.title: Phase 2 Contingency Gate: EMV of a Hyperscale Campus Risk Register
scenarios.project_type: Hyperscale data centre campus phase 2 build
scenarios.summary: Expert EMV drill on an eight-item hyperscale data centre risk register mixing long-lead plant threats with two genuine opportunities. Learners compute the register EMV and five named line-item EMVs.
scenarios.brief: A 96 MW hyperscale campus is entering its second build phase, and the controls team must re-baseline the contingency draw before the next stage gate. The register mixes long-lead plant threats with two upside items tied to a heat-reuse offtake and pre-fabricated cooling skids. Leadership wants the expected monetary value of the register and of several named line items, not a gut feel.
objectives: Compute expected monetary value for individual threats and opportunities using EMV = probability x impact
Preserve impact sign so opportunities offset rather than inflate threat exposure
Aggregate line-item EMVs into a single register-level expected value
Distinguish high-probability low-impact items from low-probability catastrophic items when ranking exposure
Report EMV results to a stated rounding convention with the correct sign
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic expert-level quantitative risk analysis exercise.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real campus, supplier or register.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Apply EMV = probability x impact to each register line, keeping the sign (negative = threat, positive = opportunity).

R1: 0.35 x -480000 = -168000.00
R2: 0.20 x -1250000 = -250000.00
R3: 0.45 x -260000 = -117000.00
R4: 0.30 x 900000 = +270000.00
R5: 0.15 x 420000 = +63000.00
R6: 0.55 x -140000 = -77000.00
R7: 0.08 x -1600000 = -128000.00
R8: 0.62 x -95000 = -58900.00

Total EMV = sum of all eight line EMVs.
Threat subtotal = -(168000 + 250000 + 117000 + 77000 + 128000 + 58900) = -798900.00
Opportunity subtotal = 270000 + 63000 = +333000.00
Total EMV = -798900.00 + 333000.00 = -465900.00

Traps: R7 carries the largest raw impact but only the fourth-largest EMV (-128000.00) because its probability is 0.08, while R2 at a smaller impact yields -250000.00; R8 is the most likely item at 0.62 yet contributes just -58900.00. Taking absolute values of R4 and R5 would overstate exposure by 666000.

Answers: emv = -465900.00; emv_R2 = -250000.00; emv_R4 = 270000.00; emv_R5 = 63000.00; emv_R7 = -128000.00; emv_R8 = -58900.00.

R5 pre-fab cooling skids enable early hall handover, probability 0.15, impact 420000. R6 slab pour rework, probability 0.55, impact -140000.
