scenarios.title: Valley Cluster Backhaul Upgrade — CPM Schedule Analysis
scenarios.project_type: Rural fixed-wireless backhaul and small-cell cluster upgrade
scenarios.summary: Run a full critical path analysis on an eight-activity fixed-wireless upgrade schedule, resolve a rejected change request that muddies the durations, and quantify float on the parallel fibre branch.
scenarios.brief: A regional operator is upgrading a remote valley cluster: a microwave backhaul link must be redesigned and its mast strengthened before new radio units can go live, while a parallel crew stages small-cell hardware and splices fibre tails. The delivery manager needs the critical path confirmed before committing a cutover date to the wholesale customer, and a recently rejected change request has caused confusion about which mast-works duration is contractual.
objectives: Compute early/late dates for a CPM network with two merge points using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path and the overall project duration of a multi-branch telecoms rollout schedule
Compute total float on non-critical activities and interpret what it means for crew re-sequencing
Distinguish approved baseline durations from rejected change-request durations when building the network
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real operator, network, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Fix the durations. Change request CR-014 (mast strengthening D reduced from 8 to 5 days) was REJECTED at the change board, so the baseline duration of 8 days stands. Use D = 8.

Step 2 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur):
A: 0–4. B: 4–10. C: 4–9. D: 10–18. E: ES = max(EF_C, EF_D) = max(9, 18) = 18, EF = 24 (merge point). F: 9–16. G: ES = max(EF_E, EF_F) = max(24, 16) = 24, EF = 29 (merge point). H: 29–31.

Step 3 — Project duration = EF of H = 31 days.

Step 4 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − dur):
H: 29–31. G: 24–29. E: 18–24. F: LF = LS_G = 24, LS = 17. D: LF = LS_E = 18, LS = 10. C: LF = min(LS_E, LS_F) = min(18, 17) = 17, LS = 12. B: LF = LS_D = 10, LS = 4. A: LF = min(LS_B, LS_C) = min(4, 12) = 4, LS = 0.

Step 5 — Total float (TF = LS − ES):
A = 0, B = 0, D = 0, E = 0, G = 0, H = 0 → critical path = A, B, D, E, G, H.
C: 12 − 4 = 8 days. F: 17 − 9 = 8 days.

Final answers: project_duration = 31; critical_path = {A, B, D, E, G, H}; float_C = 8; float_F = 8.

config.prompt:
Auroria Telecom (fictional) is upgrading its Valley Cluster fixed-wireless site. The change board REJECTED CR-014 (mast strengthening D cut from 8 days to 5); use only the approved durations below.

Network (working days):
- A Site survey and access permits — 4 — no predecessors
- B Microwave link redesign — 6 — after A
- C Small-cell hardware staging — 5 — after A
- D Mast strengthening works — 8 — after B
- E Radio unit installation — 6 — after C and D
- F Fibre tail splicing — 7 — after C
- G Integration and drive test — 5 — after E and F
- H Wholesale service cutover — 2 — after G

Using CPM forward and backward passes, compute: (1) project_duration — total duration in working days; (2) critical_path — set of critical activity IDs; (3) float_C — total float of activity C in days; (4) float_F — total float of activity F in days. Report whole days; no rounding required.

scenarios.title: Modular Data Hall Fit-Out: Critical Path Under Pressure
scenarios.project_type: Modular data hall fit-out (Hall 2, 1.2 MW IT load)
scenarios.summary: Build the CPM network for a six-activity data hall fit-out, find the project duration and critical path, and compute total float on a parallel rack-installation branch.
scenarios.brief: A colocation operator is fitting out Hall 2 of an existing campus building to add 1.2 MW of IT capacity, and the sales team has already promised the anchor tenant a firm ready-for-service date. The fit-out plan splits after mobilisation into a mechanical branch (cooling pipework, then CRAH commissioning) and an IT-fabric branch (rack positioning, then cable trays and fibre), which reconverge at the integrated load test. The delivery lead needs to know which branch actually drives the date and how much slack the other one carries.
objectives: Compute early/late dates through a small activity network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path at a merge point where two branches reconverge
Compute total float for a non-critical activity and interpret it as schedule slack
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or facility.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur, using day-0 convention):
A: ES 0, EF 2. B (after A): ES 2, EF 7. C (after A): ES 2, EF 5. D (after B): ES 7, EF 11. E (after C): ES 5, EF 9. F (after D and E): ES = max(11, 9) = 11, EF 14.

Project duration = EF of F = 14 days.

Step 2 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − dur):
F: LF 14, LS 11. D: LF 11, LS 7. E: LF 11, LS 7. B: LF 7, LS 2. C: LF 7, LS 4. A: LF = min(2, 4) = 2, LS 0.

Step 3 — Total float (TF = LS − ES):
A: 0. B: 0. D: 0. F: 0 → critical path is A → B → D → F (mobilisation, cooling pipework, CRAH commissioning, integrated load test — the mechanical branch drives the date).
C: 4 − 2 = 2. E: 7 − 5 = 2.

Answers: project_duration = 14; critical_path = {A, B, D, F}; float_C = 2. Interpretation: rack positioning can slip up to 2 days without moving the ready-for-service date, but the cooling branch has zero slack.

scenarios.title: Bypass Overbridge: Critical Path Under a Contested Change
scenarios.summary: Run a full CPM forward and backward pass on a seven-activity highway overbridge network, resist a rejected acceleration change that looks approved, and identify the critical path and float.
scenarios.brief: You are the planning engineer on a grade-separation scheme converting a signalised junction on a rural bypass into an overbridge with slip roads. The works are sequenced around a single traffic-management switch, with drainage diversion and bulk earthworks running in parallel before the bridge deck can go in. The site agent insists a double-shift acceleration on the drainage diversion was approved by email, but the change register tells a different story, and the client wants a defensible completion date this week.
objectives: Compute early and late dates for a CPM network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path through a merge point and state the project duration
Compute total float for non-critical activities
Distinguish approved changes from rejected ones when selecting durations for analysis
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real highway scheme, organisation, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Fix the durations. Change request CR-042 (cut activity B from 7 to 5 days by double-shifting) appears "agreed" in an email chain, but the change register records it as REJECTED. A rejected change has no contractual effect, so B stays at 7 days.

Step 2 — Forward pass (ES/EF, day units):
A: ES 0, EF 4.
B (after A): ES 4, EF 11. C (after A): ES 4, EF 12.
D (after B): ES 11, EF 18. E (after C): ES 12, EF 16.
F (merge of D, E): ES = max(18, 16) = 18, EF 24.
G (after F): ES 24, EF 27.

Project duration = 27 days.

Step 3 — Backward pass (LF/LS):
G: LF 27, LS 24. F: LF 24, LS 18.
D: LF 18, LS 11. E: LF 18, LS 14.
B: LF 11, LS 4. C: LF 14, LS 6.
A: LF = min(4, 6) = 4, LS 0.

Step 4 — Total float = LS − ES:
A 0, B 0, C 2, D 0, E 2, F 0, G 0.

Critical path (zero-float chain) = A, B, D, F, G.
float_E = 14 − 12 = 2 days (shared with C along the earthworks branch).

Check: had the rejected CR been applied (B = 5), both branches would tie at 25 days — the register entry is what keeps the drainage branch critical.

scenarios.title: Pop-Up Beach Arena: Grandstand Build Critical Path
scenarios.summary: Run a forward and backward pass on a five-activity network for a temporary beach-sports arena build-out to find the project duration, the critical path, and the float on the cabling work.
scenarios.brief: A promoter has hired your contracting team to erect a temporary 4,000-seat beach-sports arena on a reclaimed harbour lot for a two-week championship. The venue is entirely modular: ground plates go down first, then grandstand frames, decking and seats, while power and broadcast cabling runs in parallel. Nothing opens until the safety inspection signs off, and the promoter wants to know exactly how many working days the build needs and where the schedule has slack.
objectives: Compute early and late dates for a small activity-on-node network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path through a network with one merge point
Compute total float for a non-critical activity and interpret what it means for the build sequence
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real venue, project, or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + duration, day-unit convention ES of start = 0):
A: ES 0, EF 0+3 = 3.
B (after A): ES 3, EF 3+6 = 9.
C (after B): ES 9, EF 9+4 = 13.
D (after A): ES 3, EF 3+7 = 10.
E (after C and D): ES = max(13, 10) = 13, EF 13+2 = 15.

Step 2 — Project duration = EF of the final activity E = 15 working days.

Step 3 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − duration):
E: LF 15, LS 13.
C: LF 13, LS 9.
D: LF 13, LS 13−7 = 6.
B: LF 9, LS 3.
A: LF = min(LS of B, LS of D) = min(3, 6) = 3, LS 0.

Step 4 — Total float = LS − ES (or LF − EF):
A: 0, B: 0, C: 0, E: 0 — all critical.
D: 6 − 3 = 3 days of float.

Answers: project_duration = 15; critical_path = {A, B, C, E}; float_D = 3. The cabling crew can start up to 3 working days late without delaying the safety inspection.

scenarios.title: Dome Turnaround: Roof Drive and Pitch Replacement in One Window
scenarios.project_type: Stadium roof-drive and pitch replacement turnaround
scenarios.summary: Expert CPM drill on an eleven-activity stadium shutdown where the roof stream and the pitch stream merge twice. Derive project duration, the critical set, and four total floats.
scenarios.brief: A 42,000-seat multi-use dome has one shutdown window between the closing concert of one season and the opening fixture of the next. In that window the retractable roof drive system and the entire playing surface are replaced concurrently, sharing a single handover milestone at the front and a single integrated rehearsal at the back. The roof stream and the pitch stream look independent on the wall chart, but they merge twice, and the wall chart alone will not tell you which merge governs the finish date.
objectives: Execute a CPM forward pass across two merge points to derive early start and early finish for every activity.
Execute a backward pass from the project finish to derive late start, late finish and total float.
Identify the complete set of critical activities and separate it from parallel chains that only appear to carry comfortable slack.
Quantify total float in whole days for four named non-critical activities from the completed passes.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; synthetic network built to CPM conventions with deterministic forward/backward-pass grading.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real venue, contractor or schedule.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Forward pass (ES/EF, zero-based): A 0/4. B 4/10. C 4/12. D 10/20. F 10/15. E 12/21. G merges D and F: ES = max(20,15) = 20, EF 24. H 21/28. J merges E and G: ES = max(21,24) = 24, EF 27. K 24/29. L merges H, J and K: ES = max(28,27,29) = 29, EF 33. Project duration = 33 days.

Backward pass (LS/LF), setting LF(L) = 33: L 29/33. H LF 29, LS 22. J LF 29, LS 26. K LF 29, LS 24. G LF = min(LS of J, K) = min(26,24) = 24, LS 20. D LF 20, LS 10. F LF 20, LS 15. E LF = min(LS of H, J) = min(22,26) = 22, LS 13. C LF 13, LS 5. B LF = min(LS of D, F) = min(10,15) = 10, LS 4. A LF = min(LS of B, C) = min(4,5) = 4, LS 0.

Total float = LS - ES: A 0, B 0, D 0, G 0, K 0, L 0 - critical. Critical path = A-B-D-G-K-L, length 4+6+10+4+5+4 = 33, confirming the duration.

Requested floats: float_E = 13-12 = 1; float_F = 15-10 = 5; float_H = 22-21 = 1; float_J = 26-24 = 2.

The trap: chain A-C-E-H-L totals 4+8+9+7+4 = 32 days and looks like a comfortable secondary path, but it carries only 1 day of float, so a single day lost on C, E or H makes it co-critical. J appears constrained by E, yet G (EF 24) is the binding predecessor, which is why its float is 2 rather than 3.

scenarios.title: Crossing 14 Signalling Renewal: WBS Roll-Up Check
scenarios.summary: Roll up a nine-node WBS for a level crossing signalling renewal, totalling the programme from leaf work packages and checking the 100% rule on a declared branch value before baseline sign-off.
scenarios.brief: A regional rail operator is renewing the life-expired signalling at an automatic level crossing known internally as Crossing 14. The planning engineer has drafted a work breakdown structure with estimated costs (in thousands) at the work-package level, and the sponsor will not sign the baseline until the structure is shown to roll up cleanly. You must total the programme from the leaf packages and confirm the 100% rule holds wherever a summary value has been declared.
objectives: Compute a WBS root total by rolling up leaf work-package values through parent levels.
Verify the 100% rule by comparing a declared parent value against the sum of its children.
Distinguish leaf work packages that carry estimates from summary nodes that only aggregate.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real railway, supplier, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Identify the leaf work packages (nodes with values and no children): Site Survey 40, Signalling Design 80, Cable Route and Troughing 150, Barrier Machines and Road Signals 210, Control Kiosk and Power Supply 90, Testing and Commissioning 130.

Step 2 - Roll up each branch:
- Design and Survey (1.1) = 40 + 80 = 120
- Installation (1.2) = 150 + 210 + 90 = 450
- Testing and Commissioning (1.3) = 130 (leaf reporting directly to root)

Step 3 - Compute the root total:
root_total = 120 + 450 + 130 = 700.00

Step 4 - Check the 100% rule. Only one parent declares an explicit value: Design and Survey at 120. Its children sum to 40 + 80 = 120, which matches exactly. Installation and the root declare no value, so they cannot violate the rule.
hundred_percent_valid = true

Final answers: root_total = 700.00 (thousands); hundred_percent_valid = true.

scenarios.title: SC-WBS-106 — Gearbox Assembly Cell Retrofit: WBS Roll-Up and 100% Rule Check
scenarios.summary: Roll up the control-account values for a gearbox assembly cell retrofit WBS and test whether a stale parent-level engineering estimate still satisfies the 100% rule.
scenarios.brief: A powertrain components plant is retrofitting a manual gearbox assembly line into an automated cell with two robot stations, new conveyors, and torque test rigs. The cost engineer has decomposed the work into a three-branch WBS, but the Engineering & Design branch still carries a parent-level figure keyed in during an earlier estimate revision, before the controls design package was re-scoped. The plant controller wants the project total confirmed from the leaf work packages and the structure checked for 100%-rule integrity before baselining.
objectives: Compute a WBS root total by rolling up leaf work-package values through the hierarchy.
Apply the 100% rule to detect a parent-level value that no longer equals the sum of its children.
Distinguish leaf-derived roll-up totals from stale, manually keyed parent values when validating a baseline.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, plant, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaf work packages (nodes that carry values and have no children): 1.1.1 Process Layout = 34000; 1.1.2 Controls Design = 48000; 1.2.1 Robot Stations = 210000; 1.2.2 Conveyor System = 96000; 1.2.3 Torque Test Rigs = 74000; 1.3.1 Mechanical Installation = 58000; 1.3.2 Commissioning and Acceptance Testing = 41000.

Step 2 — Roll up the root total from the leaves only:
root_total = 34000 + 48000 + 210000 + 96000 + 74000 + 58000 + 41000 = 561000.

Step 3 — Apply the 100% rule to every parent that carries an explicit value. Only node 1.1 (Engineering & Design) declares a value: 86000. Its children sum to 34000 + 48000 = 82000. Since 86000 does not equal 82000, the declared parent value violates the 100% rule — it is a stale figure from the earlier estimate revision, keyed in before Controls Design was re-scoped.

Step 4 — Conclude: hundred_percent_valid = false. The structure cannot be baselined until node 1.1 is corrected to 82000 (or its children re-estimated to match).

Final answers: root_total = 561000; hundred_percent_valid = false.

scenarios.title: Halberd Junction Corridor Uplift: Rolling Up a 13-Node Rail WBS
scenarios.summary: Roll a 13-node rail work breakdown structure up from its leaf packages to a defensible root total, then test the hierarchy against the 100% rule where one package manager's declared figure does not reconcile.
scenarios.brief: The Halberd Junction corridor is a 41 km single-track branch being uplifted with new trackform, two passing loops, a replacement interlocking and a battery-charging island. The sponsor will not take four separate package numbers to the board; she wants one root total and an assurance that the breakdown is structurally sound. The estimating team has loaded values at the leaf packages, but the passing-loop civils manager has also declared a headline figure for his own package. Your job is to roll the structure up honestly and say plainly whether the breakdown obeys the 100% rule.
objectives: Aggregate leaf-level package values up a multi-level WBS to a single root total
Distinguish estimator-loaded leaf values from a declared parent value when rolling up
Test a WBS against the 100% rule that each parent equals the sum of its children
Report a structural validity judgement a sponsor can act on before board approval
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic advanced scope-structuring exercise; no external source data.
scenarios.disclaimers: All names, packages and figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real rail project or estimate.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Identify the leaves (nodes with no children) and ignore any declared parent value for aggregation; under the 100% rule a parent is defined by its children.

Step 2 - Roll up each second-level package:
1.1 Trackform Renewal = 8420 + 6135 + 3290 = 17845
1.2 Passing Loop Civils = 4870 + 3615 + 2980 = 11465
1.3 Signalling and Interlocking = 9240 + 5075 = 14315
1.4 Traction Charging Island = 7360 (leaf, taken as-is)

Step 3 - Root total = 17845 + 11465 + 14315 + 7360 = 50985.00

Step 4 - Apply the 100% rule: every parent must equal the sum of its children. Node 1.2 carries a declared value of 11000 while its three children sum to 11465, a shortfall of 465. The declared figure understates the package, so the structure fails the 100% rule.

Final answers: root_total = 50985.00; hundred_percent_valid = false.

Sponsor read-across: the board number is 50985, and the 465 discrepancy in passing-loop civils must be reconciled before the breakdown is baselined, otherwise loop scope is under-funded from day one.

scenarios.worked_solution:

Step 3 - line_count = number of bill lines = 8

scenarios.title: Cash Curve Under Pressure: Edge Analytics Rollout
scenarios.project_type: retail in-store edge analytics platform rollout
scenarios.summary: Track the cumulative cash position of an eight-period edge-computing rollout, spot the deepest funding trough, and exclude a milestone billing tied to a change request that was rejected despite looking approved.
scenarios.brief: Your firm is delivering an in-store edge analytics platform for a mid-market grocery chain: camera-based shelf sensors, on-premise inference nodes in 40 stores, and a central telemetry dashboard. Hardware purchases and integration labour front-load the outflows, while milestone billings only ramp up once store clusters go live, so the project runs cash-negative for months. The finance sponsor wants to size the working-capital facility and is nervous about a disputed change request that the commercial tracker shows as "endorsed" — the change board minutes tell a different story.
objectives: Compute period net cash flow and the cumulative cash position across a multi-period project.
Determine peak funding requirement as the deepest cumulative deficit, expressed as a positive number.
Distinguish an approved change from a rejected-but-resubmittable change and exclude unearned billings from cash inflows.
Interpret the closing cumulative position as the project's final cash outcome.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, project, or financial data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Correct the inputs. The period 5 inflow of 240 includes a 60 milestone billing tied to change request CR-7. The change board decision log records CR-7 as "Rejected — resubmit with revised scope"; the commercial tracker's "endorsed" flag is not an approval. Exclude the 60, so period 5 inflow = 240 - 60 = 180.

Step 2 — Net cash flow per period: net_t = inflow_t - outflow_t.
P1: 0 - 120 = -120
P2: 40 - 150 = -110
P3: 90 - 140 = -50
P4: 150 - 130 = +20
P5: 180 - 145 = +35
P6: 210 - 120 = +90
P7: 230 - 105 = +125
P8: 240 - 95 = +145

Step 3 — Cumulative position: cum_t = cum_(t-1) + net_t.
P1: -120.00
P2: -230.00
P3: -280.00
P4: -260.00
P5: -225.00
P6: -135.00
P7: -10.00
P8: +135.00

Step 4 — Peak funding = the deepest cumulative deficit, reported as a positive number. The minimum cumulative value is -280.00 at period 3, so peak_funding = 280.00.

Step 5 — Answers:
cumulative_4 = -260.00
peak_funding = 280.00
final_position = 135.00

Note: if the rejected CR-7 billing were wrongly included, the final position would be overstated by 60 and periods 5-8 cumulatives would all be 60 too favourable — understating how long the project stays in deficit.

scenarios.title: Cash Flow Basics: CubeSat Reaction-Wheel Retrofit Line
scenarios.summary: Track period-by-period cash on a small satellite retrofit line, find the deepest funding hole created by up-front tooling spend, and confirm the closing cash position.
scenarios.brief: Orbita Dynamics (fictional) has won a six-month contract to retrofit upgraded reaction wheels into a batch of customer CubeSats. The contract pays on delivery milestones, but the team must buy precision balancing rigs and cleanroom tooling before the first payment lands, so the project runs cash-negative early. The sponsor wants to know exactly how much working capital to set aside and where the project ends up at contract close.
objectives: Compute cumulative net cash position period by period from inflows and outflows
Identify peak funding as the deepest cumulative deficit, expressed as a positive requirement
Interpret the final cumulative position as the project's closing cash result
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, contract, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Net cash each period: net = inflow − outflow.
P1: 0 − 40 = −40; P2: 20 − 50 = −30; P3: 30 − 45 = −15; P4: 80 − 30 = +50; P5: 90 − 25 = +65; P6: 60 − 20 = +40.

Step 2 — Cumulative position: running total of the period nets.
After P1: −40
After P2: −40 + (−30) = −70
After P3: −70 + (−15) = −85
After P4: −85 + 50 = −35
After P5: −35 + 65 = +30
After P6: +30 + 40 = +70

Step 3 — Answers:
• cumulative_3 = −85 (the position after period 3).
• peak_funding = the deepest cumulative deficit reported as a positive number. The lowest point is −85 (end of period 3), so peak funding = 85. This is the working-capital facility the sponsor must arrange.
• final_position = the cumulative position after the last period = +70. The project closes 70 cash-positive once all milestone payments are collected.

scenarios.title: Rolling Up the Meter Fleet: CBS Totals for a Water Utility AMI Rollout
scenarios.summary: Roll up a five-leaf cost breakdown structure for a regional water utility's smart meter replacement programme and quantify the overspend worrying the sponsor.
scenarios.brief: A regional water utility is midway through swapping 12,000 aging mechanical meters for radio-read smart meters across its northern service district. The programme controller has posted actuals against the five leaf accounts of the cost breakdown structure, and the sponsor has asked for a one-line rollup before Thursday's steering meeting: total budget, total actuals, and the programme-level variance. Early field reports suggest residential meter unit costs and crew hours are running hot.
objectives: Compute a root-level budget by rolling up leaf nodes of a cost breakdown structure.
Compute a root-level actual cost from posted leaf actuals.
Compute and interpret cost variance (budget minus actual) at the programme level, recognising a negative result as an overspend.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real utility, programme, or vendor.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up the budget. Only leaf nodes carry values; parents are sums of their children. Leaf budgets: 1.1.1 Residential meters 40000, 1.1.2 Commercial meters 25000, 1.2.1 Field installation labour 30000, 1.2.2 Traffic management 5000, 1.3.1 Radio read network 15000. Root budget = 40000 + 25000 + 30000 + 5000 + 15000 = 115000.

Step 2 — Roll up the actuals the same way. Leaf actuals: 43500 + 24000 + 32500 + 4800 + 15700. Root actual = 120500.

Step 3 — Compute the root variance with the convention Variance = Budget − Actual. Root variance = 115000 − 120500 = −5500. The negative sign means the programme is overspent by 5500, driven mainly by residential meter hardware (−3500) and field labour (−2500), partly offset by savings on commercial meters (+1000) and traffic management (+200).

Final answers: root_budget = 115000; root_actual = 120500; root_variance = −5500.

scenarios.title: Deep Decline Ore Handling Upgrade — CBS Roll-Up and Variance Drill
scenarios.project_type: underground mine ore handling system upgrade
scenarios.summary: Roll up a cost breakdown structure for an underground ore handling upgrade, compute total budget, actuals and variance, and spot the one branch delivering a saving amid overruns.
scenarios.brief: A mid-life underground base-metals operation is upgrading its ore handling chain: retrofitting the primary crusher, rebuilding the decline conveyor, and modernising electrical and controls. Month-end cost data has landed and the sponsor is alarmed by the overall overrun on the crusher works. The conveyor package, however, appears to be tracking under budget — you must confirm whether it is a genuine opportunity by rolling up the parent branch before reporting the project position.
objectives: Compute parent- and root-level budget and actual totals by rolling up leaf nodes of a cost breakdown structure.
Compute cost variance as budget minus actual and interpret its sign convention.
Distinguish a favourable (opportunity) branch variance from unfavourable variances within the same CBS.
Interpret a branch-level roll-up to support a sponsor-facing cost position statement.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real mine, company, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up each branch (leaves only carry costs). Crusher Retrofit (1.1): budget = 1,840,000 + 960,000 = 2,800,000; actual = 2,065,000 + 1,112,500 = 3,177,500. Decline Conveyor Rebuild (1.2): budget = 1,275,000 + 890,000 = 2,165,000; actual = 1,236,400 + 812,700 = 2,049,100.

Step 2 — Root budget = sum of all leaf budgets = 1,840,000 + 960,000 + 1,275,000 + 890,000 + 705,000 + 530,000 = 6,200,000.

Step 3 — Root actual = sum of all leaf actuals = 2,065,000 + 1,112,500 + 1,236,400 + 812,700 + 748,900 + 551,000 = 6,526,500.

Step 4 — Variance = budget − actual. Root variance = 6,200,000 − 6,526,500 = −326,500 (unfavourable: the project is overspent overall).

Step 5 — Branch variance for node 1.2 = 2,165,000 − 2,049,100 = +115,900 (favourable). This is the twist: despite the overall overrun driven by the crusher branch (−377,500) and smaller overruns on electrical (−43,900) and indirects (−21,000), the conveyor branch is a genuine saving. It partially offsets the crusher overrun but does not reverse the unfavourable root position.

Final answers: root_budget = 6,200,000.00; root_actual = 6,526,500.00; root_variance = −326,500.00; variance_1.2 = +115,900.00.

scenarios.title: Karsk Field Apron Floodlighting: Re-baselining After Change Board
scenarios.project_type: Regional airfield apron LED floodlighting retrofit
scenarios.summary: Re-baseline an airfield apron floodlighting retrofit from a four-entry change log, applying only approved changes while resisting a tempting pending scope extension.
scenarios.brief: Karsk Field, a fictional regional airfield, is midway through replacing its apron floodlighting with high-mast LED units so night turnarounds can resume year-round. The works are baselined at a budget at completion of 800000 and a duration of 40 weeks. Four weeks into delivery, the change log already holds four entries, and the operations director is pressing the project controls team to confirm what the approved baseline actually is before the next steering meeting — not what it might become if every pending request sails through.
objectives: Distinguish approved changes from pending and rejected changes when re-baselining
Compute the total approved cost delta from a multi-entry change log
Compute the revised budget at completion and revised duration from approved changes only
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real airport, contractor, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Filter the change log by status. Only approved changes move the baseline. Approved: C1 (+30000 cost, +2 weeks) and C3 (-10000 cost, +0 weeks). Excluded: C2 is pending (not yet decided, however likely) and C4 was rejected, so neither touches the baseline.

Step 2 — Total approved cost delta.
Approved cost delta = 30000 + (-10000) = 20000.

Step 3 — Revised BAC.
Revised BAC = baseline BAC + approved cost delta = 800000 + 20000 = 820000.

Step 4 — Revised duration.
Approved schedule delta = 2 + 0 = 2 weeks.
Revised duration = 40 + 2 = 42 weeks.

Final answers: approved cost delta = 20000; revised BAC = 820000; revised duration = 42 weeks. Note that including the pending C2 would have wrongly produced 910000 and 46 weeks — the classic error this drill targets.

scenarios.brief: Your firm is retrofitting a regional parcel cross-dock facility with a new tilt-tray sorter loop and dock-door conveyor spurs while the building stays partially operational at night. Midway through execution, the change control board has just closed its monthly cycle and five change requests are on your desk in various states. The site operations manager is pressuring the team to book every request into the forecast immediately, but the baseline may only move for changes the board actually approved.
objectives: Distinguish approved change requests from pending and rejected ones when re-baselining
Compute the net approved cost delta, correctly netting an approved cost-saving opportunity against approved additions
Compute the revised budget at completion and revised project duration from the approved changes only
Interpret why an operations sign-off memo does not substitute for change control board approval
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real facility, company, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: baseline BAC = 4,850,000 and baseline duration = 42 weeks.

Step 1 — Filter by status. Only APPROVED changes move the baseline. Approved: C1, C3, C5. Excluded: C2 (REJECTED — the operations manager's sign-off memo is not change control board approval) and C4 (PENDING — it may be tempting, but it stays out of the baseline until the board rules).

Step 2 — Approved cost delta = sum of cost deltas of approved changes only:
262,500 + (-84,000) + 45,500 = 224,000.
Note C3 is an opportunity (a saving), so it reduces the net delta rather than being ignored.

Step 3 — Revised BAC = baseline BAC + approved cost delta:
4,850,000 + 224,000 = 5,074,000.

Step 4 — Approved schedule delta = sum of schedule deltas of approved changes only:
3 + 0 + 1 = 4 weeks.

Step 5 — Revised duration = baseline duration + approved schedule delta:
42 + 4 = 46 weeks.

Final answers (canonical): approved_cost_delta = 224,000; revised_bac = 5,074,000; approved_schedule_delta = 4; revised_duration = 46. Had C2 or C4 been included, the BAC would have been overstated by up to 674,000 — exactly the error the sponsor's auditors look for.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Filter the change log by status. Only APPROVED changes move the baseline. Approved: C1 (+25000 cost, +2 duration) and C4 (-5000 cost, 0 duration). C2 (pending, +60000/+4) and C3 (rejected, +15000/+1) are excluded — pending means not yet authorized, rejected means never authorized.

Step 3 — Approved schedule delta = 2 + 0 = 2 weeks (C4 trims cost but not time).

scenarios.worked_solution:

scenarios.title: Boost Stage Trade Study for a Hypersonic Test Vehicle
scenarios.summary: Score five boost-stage candidates for a hypersonic test vehicle using a weighted additive penalty model where cost, schedule and risk are normalised and the lowest total wins.
scenarios.brief: A national-scale hypersonic flight-test program must pick the boost stage that will loft its reusable test vehicle to separation conditions. Five candidate stages have cleared technical screening, and the technical review board has scored each one for cost deviation, schedule deviation and residual technical risk against the approved baseline. The program office uses an additive penalty model in which the lowest total score wins, so the cheapest candidate is not automatically the recommendation.
objectives: Interpret pre-normalised cost, schedule and risk inputs as comparable penalty terms
Apply a weighted additive penalty model of the form w_cost x |cost| + w_sched x |schedule| + w_risk x risk
Treat a schedule pull-in as a deviation of equal magnitude to a slip of the same size
Compute the individual penalty score for a named alternative to 2 decimals
Identify the lowest total penalty score and explain why the cheapest option is not automatically preferred
scenarios.provenance: Synthetic aerospace trade-study scenario authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; figures constructed to exercise weighted additive decision scoring.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, options and figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real programme or supplier.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: score each option with score = w_cost x |cost| + w_sched x |schedule| + w_risk x risk, using all weights = 1. Schedule deviation is taken as an absolute magnitude, so an early pull-in is penalised the same as a slip of equal size. The lowest score is the preferred alternative.

O1: |12.5| + |4.0| + 6.4 = 22.90
O2: |4.2| + |-1.5| + 8.1 = 4.2 + 1.5 + 8.1 = 13.80
O3: |7.8| + |2.5| + 3.6 = 13.90
O4: |2.4| + |6.5| + 5.2 = 14.10
O5: |9.6| + |-3.2| + 2.1 = 9.6 + 3.2 + 2.1 = 14.90

Ranking (lowest penalty first): O2 13.80, O3 13.90, O4 14.10, O5 14.90, O1 22.90.

Answers: best_score = 13.80; score_O1 = 22.90; score_O4 = 14.10.

Interpretation: O4 has by far the smallest cost deviation (2.4) yet finishes third because its 6.5-month schedule deviation and mid-range risk outweigh the saving. O5 looks attractive on schedule, but the absolute-value rule means its 3.2-month pull-in adds penalty rather than credit. O2 wins by only 0.10 over O3, so the recommendation is not robust: a small shift in weights or in the risk index would flip the order, and the team should present the top two as a near-tie.

Compute per-option weighted scores using non-uniform criterion weights

Explain why the lowest-cost option is not automatically preferred under weighted scoring
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic decision-analysis drill.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: penalty score = w_cost x cost + w_sched x schedule + w_risk x risk, with w_cost = 1.0, w_sched = 0.8, w_risk = 2.0. Lower is better.

O1 (overhead reconductor): 1.0 x 12.4 = 12.40; 0.8 x 9 = 7.20; 2.0 x 9.4 = 18.80; total = 38.40.
O2 (underground duct bank): 1.0 x 28.6 = 28.60; 0.8 x 22 = 17.60; 2.0 x 2.0 = 4.00; total = 50.20.
O3 (battery storage plus new feeder tie): 1.0 x 17.9 = 17.90; 0.8 x 14 = 11.20; 2.0 x 4.2 = 8.40; total = 37.50.
O4 (mobile generation with phased rebuild): 1.0 x 15.8 = 15.80; 0.8 x 11 = 8.80; 2.0 x 7.8 = 15.60; total = 40.20.

Best (lowest) score = min(38.40, 50.20, 37.50, 40.20) = 37.50, achieved by O3.

Answers: score_O1 = 38.40; score_O3 = 37.50; best_score = 37.50.

Interpretation: O1 is cheapest and fastest but carries the highest residual risk; at a risk weight of 2.0 that exposure outweighs its 5.5 capital advantage over O3. The heavily weighted risk term is what moves the decision away from the low-cost option.

scenarios.title: Ridge 7 Weightometer Reconciliation: Shift Data Quality Screen
scenarios.summary: Screen 12 night-shift belt weightometer records against surveyed drawpoint tonnages, quantifying completeness, mean absolute error and tolerance breaches before the reconciliation is signed off.
scenarios.brief: The Ridge 7 magnetite operation reconciles belt weightometer tonnages against surveyed drawpoint expectations every fortnight. Over the last 12 night shifts the scale was pulled out mid-campaign for a calibration swap, so some shifts carry no measured tonnage at all. Metallurgical accounting will not accept the reconciliation until the controls team reports how complete the dataset is, how far measured tonnages drift from survey on average, and how many shifts breach the agreed tolerance. Run that screen.
objectives: Compute record_count as the total number of shift records, including shifts with no measured reading.
Compute completeness_pct as 100 x present readings divided by total records, rounded to 2 decimals.
Compute mean_abs_error as the mean of |measured - expected| tonnes across present readings only.
Compute anomaly_count as the number of present readings whose absolute deviation exceeds the stated threshold.
Distinguish a missing reading from an in-tolerance reading when judging dataset fitness for reconciliation.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic skill drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, site names and readings are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real operation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - record_count: count every shift record whether or not a measured tonnage exists. W-01 through W-12 gives record_count = 12.

Step 2 - completeness_pct = 100 x present / total. Measured tonnages are absent for W-06 and W-10, so present = 10. completeness_pct = 100 x 10 / 12 = 83.3333... = 83.33.

Step 3 - mean_abs_error = sum|value - expected| / present, over present readings only. Deviations in tonnes: W-01 |1195-1180| = 15; W-02 |1218-1240| = 22; W-03 |1252-1160| = 92; W-04 |1199-1205| = 6; W-05 |1276-1290| = 14; W-07 |1263-1225| = 38; W-08 |1215-1310| = 95; W-09 |1181-1175| = 6; W-11 |1236-1195| = 41; W-12 |1224-1230| = 6. Sum = 335. mean_abs_error = 335 / 10 = 33.50.

Step 4 - anomaly_count: present readings deviating by more than the 40 t threshold. Breaches are W-03 (92), W-08 (95) and W-11 (41). W-07 at 38 t sits inside tolerance and is not an anomaly; the two missing shifts cannot be anomalies.

Final: record_count = 12; completeness_pct = 83.33; mean_abs_error = 33.50; anomaly_count = 3.

scenarios.title: Floating Solar Telemetry Audit: String Yield Data Quality
scenarios.project_type: Floating solar array with hydrogen electrolyser offtake
scenarios.summary: Audit one day of string-level yield telemetry from a quarry-lake floating solar array, scoring record count, completeness, mean absolute error and anomaly count against a deviation threshold.
scenarios.brief: A 12-string floating solar array sits on a flooded quarry lake and feeds a small electrolyser skid that only starts when forecast yield is trusted. The overnight telemetry export arrived with gaps: a couple of string meters returned no reading at all, and several strings drifted from the modelled day-ahead yield. Before the operations lead signs off the electrolyser dispatch plan, the data set has to be scored for completeness and accuracy. You run that audit.
objectives: Compute record count and completeness percentage when readings are missing from a telemetry export
Calculate mean absolute error using only present readings, excluding gaps from the denominator
Apply a strict absolute deviation threshold to count anomalous present readings
Distinguish completeness defects from accuracy defects when reporting data quality
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; synthetic renewables telemetry constructed for this drill.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real asset, meter or performance model.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - record_count = every row in the export, present or not = 12.

Step 2 - completeness_pct = 100 x present / all. Rows STR-03 and STR-09 carry no value key, so present = 10. 100 x 10 / 12 = 83.3333 -> 83.33.

Step 3 - mean_abs_error = mean of |value - expected| over PRESENT rows only. Deviations: STR-01 0.6, STR-02 1.2, STR-04 1.1, STR-05 3.6, STR-06 1.0, STR-07 0.5, STR-08 1.8, STR-10 0.3, STR-11 2.4, STR-12 0.4. Sum = 12.9. 12.9 / 10 = 1.29.

Step 4 - anomaly_count = present rows whose deviation exceeds the threshold of 1.5: STR-05 (3.6), STR-08 (1.8) and STR-11 (2.4) = 3. STR-02 (1.2) and STR-04 (1.1) sit under the threshold; missing rows are never anomalies because there is no reading to test.

Final: record_count 12, completeness_pct 83.33, mean_abs_error 1.29, anomaly_count 3.

scenarios.title: Earned Schedule Check: Baggage Screening Line Retrofit
scenarios.summary: A six-week baggage screening retrofit is mid-installation and the terminal manager suspects the crew is behind. Use earned schedule interpolation to measure exactly how late the work is running.
scenarios.brief: A mid-size airport operator is replacing a legacy baggage screening line in one terminal pier with an inline automated screening conveyor. The work was planned as a six-week programme with progress measured weekly against a cumulative planned-value curve. At the end of week 4 the terminal duty manager reports that night-shift installation windows have been repeatedly cut short by airfield operations, and asks the project controls analyst to quantify the schedule position in time units rather than cost units.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by interpolating earned value against the cumulative planned-value curve
Compute the time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT and state whether the project is ahead or behind
Compute and interpret the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT to 2 decimal places
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real airport, project, or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: the cumulative planned-value curve is week 1 = 100, week 2 = 250, week 3 = 450, week 4 = 700, week 5 = 900, week 6 = 1000, with AT = 4 and EV = 550.

Step 1 — Locate EV on the plan curve. Find the last week whose cumulative PV does not exceed EV: PV(3) = 450 <= 550 < PV(4) = 700, so ES lies between weeks 3 and 4.

Step 2 — Interpolate: ES = 3 + (EV - PV(3)) / (PV(4) - PV(3)) = 3 + (550 - 450) / (700 - 450) = 3 + 100/250 = 3 + 0.40 = 3.40 weeks.

Step 3 — Time-based schedule variance: SV(t) = ES - AT = 3.40 - 4 = -0.60 weeks. The negative sign means the project has earned only 3.40 weeks of planned work in 4 weeks of elapsed time — it is 0.60 weeks behind.

Step 4 — Time-based schedule performance index: SPI(t) = ES / AT = 3.40 / 4 = 0.85. The crew is delivering schedule progress at 85% of the planned rate.

Final answers: ES = 3.40 weeks; SV(t) = -0.60 weeks; SPI(t) = 0.85.

scenarios.summary: A 10-week robotic sortation retrofit at a busy cross-dock terminal is drifting behind its planned-value curve. Convert earned value into earned schedule and forecast the true finish, ignoring a misleading parent-programme figure.
scenarios.brief: A regional parcel operator is retrofitting one bay of its cross-dock terminal with a robotic sortation loop while nightly freight keeps moving. The 10-week workstream sits inside a much larger 16-period terminal modernisation programme, and the programme dashboard keeps tempting people to quote parent-level numbers. At the end of week 6 the workstream owner wants a time-based read on progress: not how much value was earned, but how many weeks of the plan have actually been achieved and when the retrofit will really finish.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by interpolating earned value against the cumulative planned-value curve.
Compute the time-based variance SV(t) and index SPI(t) from ES and actual time.
Forecast completion with EAC(t) = planned duration / SPI(t).
Distinguish the workstream's own planned duration from a parent-programme duration when forecasting.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: Planned duration PD = 10 weeks, actual time AT = 6, EV = 385, cumulative PV curve: 40, 95, 165, 250, 345, 450, 560, 660, 740, 800.

Step 1 — Locate EV on the PV curve. Find the last period whose cumulative PV does not exceed EV: PV(5) = 345 <= 385 < PV(6) = 450, so ES lies between weeks 5 and 6.

Step 2 — Interpolate. ES = 5 + (EV - PV(5)) / (PV(6) - PV(5)) = 5 + (385 - 345) / (450 - 345) = 5 + 40/105 = 5.3810 -> ES = 5.38 weeks.

Step 3 — Time variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 5.3810 - 6 = -0.6190 -> -0.62 weeks (about 0.62 weeks behind schedule).

Step 4 — Time index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 5.3810 / 6 = 0.8968 -> 0.90.

Step 5 — Forecast duration. Use the workstream's own PD of 10 weeks, NOT the 16-period parent-programme figure. EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) = 10 / 0.8968 = 11.1504 -> 11.15 weeks, i.e. roughly 1.15 weeks later than planned if current schedule efficiency persists.

config.prompt: You control schedule performance for a 10-week robotic sortation retrofit in Bay 3 of a cross-dock parcel terminal. Caution: this retrofit sits inside a 16-period terminal modernisation programme whose parent-level duration appears on the dashboard; do not forecast against it — base every calculation on this workstream's own 10-week planned duration. Using the figures shown below, compute: (1) es — the earned schedule in weeks, interpolating linearly between the two planned-value points that bracket EV; (2) sv_time — the schedule variance in time, ES minus AT, in weeks; (3) spi_time — the time-based schedule performance index, ES divided by AT; (4) eac_time — the forecast total duration in weeks, planned duration divided by SPI(t). Report all values to 2 decimal places; negative sv_time means behind schedule.

Time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) (2 dp)

scenarios.title: Zone 7 Meter Replacement: Earned Schedule Under Outage-Window Pressure
scenarios.summary: An advanced earned schedule drill on a 12-period water-metering rollout: interpolate ES between the bracketing plan periods and convert it into time variance, a time-based index and a duration forecast.
scenarios.brief: A regional water utility is replacing legacy meters across a large pressure zone and recalibrating its district metered areas on a 12-period baseline. Shutdown windows, not money, are the binding constraint, so the sponsor board has asked for a time-based performance read rather than the usual cost-based indices. At the end of period 8 the planning team publishes the cumulative planned value curve alongside cumulative earned value. Your job is to convert that curve into earned schedule figures the board can act on.
objectives: Locate earned schedule on a cumulative planned value curve by linear interpolation between the two bracketing plan periods
Compute schedule variance (time) and interpret its sign against actual time
Compute the time-based schedule performance index from earned schedule and actual time
Forecast estimate at completion (time) from planned duration and SPI(t), rounded to two decimals
Explain why a time-based index reads differently from a value-based schedule index late in a schedule
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic earned schedule drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, quantities and figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real utility or program.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (at = 8, EV = 3625, planned duration = 12):

Step 1 - Bracket the earned value on the cumulative PV curve. PV(7) = 3325 and PV(8) = 4117, so 3325 < 3625 < 4117 and ES falls between periods 7 and 8.

Step 2 - Earned schedule by linear interpolation.
ES = n + (EV - PV(n)) / (PV(n+1) - PV(n))
ES = 7 + (3625 - 3325) / (4117 - 3325) = 7 + 300/792 = 7 + 0.378788 = 7.3788 -> es = 7.38

Step 3 - Schedule variance (time).
SV(t) = ES - AT = 7.3788 - 8 = -0.6212 -> sv_time = -0.62
Interpretation: the program has earned only what the baseline planned to have earned about 0.62 periods ago.

Step 4 - Schedule performance index (time).
SPI(t) = ES / AT = 7.3788 / 8 = 0.922348 -> spi_time = 0.92

Step 5 - Estimate at completion (time).
EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) = 12 / 0.922348 = 13.0102 -> eac_time = 13.01
Equivalently EAC(t) = PD x AT / ES = 12 x 8 / 7.3788 = 13.0102.

Sponsor read-out: at the current time-based rate the 12-period baseline lands near 13.01 periods, roughly one extra period of outage windows to negotiate with the network operations team.

scenarios.title: Back-Loaded Ventilation Decline: Earned Schedule Under a Late-Plan Ramp
scenarios.project_type: Underground ventilation shaft and access decline development
scenarios.summary: Expert earned schedule drill on a 12-period mining decline with a heavily back-loaded baseline. Compute ES, SV(t), SPI(t) and EAC(t) by linear interpolation between plan periods.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic underground polymetallic operation is driving a raise-bored ventilation shaft together with its access decline on a twelve-period baseline. The planned value curve is deliberately back-loaded: the early access rounds carry modest value while the mid- and late-plan bench rounds and raise-bore sections carry far more. Nine periods in, the crew reports a strong recent advance and the superintendent wants a time-based read rather than a cost-based one. Your job is to translate cumulative earned value into calendar position using the earned schedule method.
objectives: Locate earned schedule by linear interpolation between two cumulative plan periods
Compute time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT in periods
Compute time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT
Forecast EAC(t) = planned duration / SPI(t) from time-based performance
Distinguish time-based schedule indices from cost-based EV/PV schedule measures
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic earned schedule drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, the operation and the baseline are entirely synthetic and simplified for training purposes only.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (at = 9, EV = 7500, planned duration = 12):

Step 1 - Bracket EV on the cumulative plan curve. PV(7) = 6660 and PV(8) = 8300. Since 6660 < 7500 <= 8300, ES lies between periods 7 and 8. PV at the current period, PV(9) = 10060, is NOT used to locate ES.

Step 2 - Interpolate: ES = 7 + (EV - PV(7)) / (PV(8) - PV(7)) = 7 + 840 / 1640 = 7.5122 -> 7.51 periods.

Step 3 - SV(t) = ES - AT = 7.5122 - 9 = -1.4878 -> -1.49 periods.

Step 4 - SPI(t) = ES / AT = 7.5122 / 9 = 0.8347 -> 0.83.

Step 5 - EAC(t) = planned duration / SPI(t) = 12 / 0.834688 = 14.3766 -> 14.38 periods, about 2.38 periods beyond the baseline.

Trap check: the cost-based ratio EV / PV(at) = 7500 / 10060 = 0.746 looks far worse than SPI(t) = 0.83 because the back-loaded plan inflates PV in the current period; it is not SPI(t). Equally, rounding ES up to a whole period 8 merely because EV exceeds PV(7) discards the interpolation the method requires.

scenarios.title: Geothermal Tie-In Under Pressure: Reading the Cost Signal
scenarios.summary: A geothermal gathering-pipeline tie-in is burning cash faster than it earns value, and a rejected change order is muddying the baseline. Compute CPI, SPI, EAC, and VAC from a single status snapshot.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls analyst on a wellfield tie-in that connects six production wells to a 28 MW binary-cycle power plant. Rocky trenching conditions have slowed pipe laying and driven up drilling-support costs, and the sponsor wants a forecast before the next steering meeting. Complicating matters, a site memo circulating this week claims a budget uplift was approved — but the change board actually rejected it, so the original baseline still governs.
objectives: Compute the schedule and cost performance indices (SPI, CPI) from a single EVM status snapshot
Forecast the estimate at completion (EAC) using the CPI method and derive the variance at completion (VAC)
Distinguish the approved performance measurement baseline from a rejected change request when selecting BAC
Interpret index values below 1.0 as combined schedule and cost pressure for sponsor reporting
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 18900, EV = 16800, AC = 19600, BAC = 42000.

Step 0 — Confirm the baseline. Change request CR-014 (adding 3600) was REJECTED by the change board, so the approved BAC remains 42000. Ignore the site memo.

Step 1 — Cost Performance Index: CPI = EV / AC = 16800 / 19600 = 0.857... ≈ 0.86. Each unit spent is earning about 0.86 units of budgeted work — a cost overrun.

Step 2 — Schedule Performance Index: SPI = EV / PV = 16800 / 18900 = 0.888... ≈ 0.89. The project is progressing at about 89% of the planned rate.

Step 3 — Estimate at Completion (CPI method): EAC = BAC / CPI = 42000 / (16800/19600) = 42000 × 19600 / 16800 = 49000. If current cost efficiency persists, the job finishes at 49000.

Step 4 — Variance at Completion: VAC = BAC − EAC = 42000 − 49000 = −7000. The forecast overrun at completion is 7000 against the approved baseline — the number the sponsor needs at the steering meeting.

Check: TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC) = 25200 / 22400 = 1.125, confirming the remaining work would need markedly better-than-current efficiency to finish on budget.

config.prompt: You are the project controls analyst on a wellfield tie-in connecting six geothermal production wells to a 28 MW binary-cycle power plant. scenarios.title: Overspend on the Kiosk Fleet: Cost Variance and CPI
scenarios.summary: A regional transit operator's kiosk software rollout is burning cash faster than it earns value. Compute cost variance, CPI, and percent spent from a single status snapshot to size the overspend.
scenarios.brief: Velatra Transit Systems is rolling out new self-service ticketing kiosk software across its station network in staged waves. At the month-six checkpoint, the delivery lead reports that invoiced integration and field-testing costs are running ahead of the value of work actually completed, and the sponsor wants a plain-numbers read on cost health. You are the project controls analyst preparing the snapshot for the steering meeting.
objectives: Compute cost variance (CV) from earned value and actual cost at a single status point
Compute the cost performance index (CPI) and round it to two decimal places
Compute percent spent (AC/BAC) as a share of the total budget consumed
Interpret a negative CV and a CPI below 1.0 as signals of overspend against work performed
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organization or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 90000, EV = 80000, AC = 100000, BAC = 250000.

Step 1 — Cost Variance (CV). CV = EV - AC = 80000 - 100000 = -20000. The negative sign means the project has spent 20000 more than the value of the work completed so far.

Step 2 — Cost Performance Index (CPI). CPI = EV / AC = 80000 / 100000 = 0.80 (2 decimal places). Every unit spent is earning only 0.80 units of budgeted work — a clear overspend signal for the sponsor.

Step 3 — Percent Spent. Percent spent = AC / BAC = 100000 / 250000 = 0.40 (2 decimal places). Two-fifths of the total budget is already consumed, while EV / BAC shows only 80000 / 250000 = 0.32 of the work is earned.

Interpretation: with CV negative, CPI below 1.0, and budget consumption running ahead of work earned, cost efficiency is the immediate concern at this checkpoint; if this efficiency persists, the completion estimate will rise above the 250000 budget.

scenarios.title: SD-EVM-108 — Reaction Wheel Qualification: Cost Forecast Under a Rejected Change
scenarios.project_type: Satellite reaction wheel assembly qualification program
scenarios.summary: Month-6 EVM snapshot on a satellite reaction wheel qualification program: compute CV, CPI, EAC and VAC while correctly ignoring a rejected change that draft minutes wrongly show as approved.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls analyst on a qualification program for a reaction wheel assembly destined for a small-satellite bus. Six months in, thermal-vacuum cycling has slipped and rework on the bearing cartridge lot has driven spending above plan, and the sponsor wants a defensible completion forecast before the next program review. Complicating matters, a supplier-proposed scope addition of 40000 for a second vibration test axis appears as "approved" in draft meeting minutes, but the change control board actually rejected it last week, so the performance measurement baseline is unchanged.
objectives: Compute cost variance (CV) and the cost performance index (CPI) from a single EVM snapshot
Compute a CPI-based estimate at completion (EAC = BAC/CPI) and the variance at completion (VAC)
Distinguish an approved baseline change from a rejected change request when selecting the BAC for forecasting
Interpret a CPI below 1.0 as an overspend signal and explain its effect on the completion forecast
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real program, supplier, or organization.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 192000, EV = 168000, AC = 200000, BAC = 480000.

Step 0 — Baseline check. The 40000 vibration-axis change was REJECTED by the change control board, so it never enters the baseline. Use BAC = 480000 exactly as given; do not add 40000.

Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 168000 - 200000 = -32000. Negative, so the program has spent 32000 more than the value of work performed.

Step 2 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 168000 / 200000 = 0.84. Each unit of cost is earning only 0.84 units of value.

Step 3 — Estimate at completion (CPI method): EAC = BAC / CPI = 480000 / 0.84 = 571428.57. This assumes the current cost efficiency persists for the remaining work.

Step 4 — Variance at completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 480000 - 571428.57 = -91428.57. The program is forecast to overrun its budget by roughly 91.4 thousand if nothing changes.

Interpretation: with CPI = 0.84 the sponsor's concern is justified; the forecast overrun is about 19% of BAC, and the rejected change must not be used to mask it by inflating BAC.

scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 2400, EV = 2000, AC = 2500, BAC = 6000.

Step 1 — Schedule variance: SV = EV - PV = 2000 - 2400 = -400. The negative value confirms the permit delays: less work has been earned than was planned by this point.

Step 2 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 2000 - 2500 = -500. The rollout has cost 500 more than the value of the work actually completed — the overtime the sponsor is worried about is visible here.

scenarios.title: Decline Extension Under Pressure: EVM Forecast at Verrick Deep South
scenarios.project_type: Underground copper decline extension and crusher relocation
scenarios.summary: Underground copper decline extension where a rejected cable-bolting variation muddies the cost report; compute SPI, CPI, EAC and VAC from the approved figures.
scenarios.brief: Verrick Deep South is a synthetic underground copper mine sinking a new decline with a relocated underground crusher station and conveyor transfer system. At the current snapshot the ground-support cycle is running slower than planned and the sponsor is alarmed by an apparent overspend in the draft cost report. Complicating matters, a 380 variation for extra cable bolting was rejected by the change board yet still appears as a pending line in the draft report; the approved actual cost figure supplied to you already excludes it. Cut through the noise and give the steering committee a clean earned value position and completion forecast.
objectives: Compute SPI and CPI from a single-period earned value snapshot.
Forecast EAC using the CPI method and derive the Variance at Completion.
Distinguish approved actual costs from rejected change-order amounts when selecting EVM inputs.
Interpret index values and VAC sign to advise a sponsor on schedule and cost health.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; no real company, mine, project or person is represented.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 4200, EV = 3840, AC = 4460, BAC = 9600. The rejected cable-bolting variation (380) is excluded from all inputs — it was never approved, so it belongs in neither AC nor BAC.

Step 1 — SPI = EV / PV = 3840 / 4200 = 0.9143 → 0.91 (2 dp). Work is progressing at about 91% of the planned rate.

Step 2 — CPI = EV / AC = 3840 / 4460 = 0.8610 → 0.86 (2 dp). Each unit spent earns only about 0.86 of value.

Step 3 — EAC = BAC / CPI, carrying the unrounded CPI: 9600 / (3840/4460) = 9600 × 4460 / 3840 = 11150.00.

Step 4 — VAC = BAC - EAC = 9600 - 11150.00 = -1550.00.

Interpretation: SPI < 1 and CPI < 1 confirm the project is both behind schedule and over cost. The negative VAC means that at current cost efficiency the decline extension is forecast to finish 1550 over the approved budget — the sponsor's concern is justified, and it stems from genuine cost performance, not the rejected variation.

config.prompt:
You are the project controls analyst on the Verrick Deep South decline extension at an underground copper mine. The ground-support cycle is behind plan and the sponsor fears an overspend.

One twist: a variation for extra cable bolting (value 380) was REJECTED by the change control board yet still shows as a pending line in the draft cost report. The Actual Cost figure given already excludes it — do NOT add the 380 to anything. The Budget at Completion is the approved baseline.

1. Schedule Performance Index (SPI) = EV / PV
2. Cost Performance Index (CPI) = EV / AC
3. Estimate at Completion (EAC) = BAC / CPI
4. Variance at Completion (VAC) = BAC - EAC

Report SPI and CPI to 2 decimal places; carry unrounded intermediates into EAC and VAC and report both to 2 decimal places. Negative VAC means a forecast overrun.

scenarios.title: Night-Window Apron Rehabilitation: Three EACs, One Data Date
scenarios.project_type: Apron rehabilitation and stand electrification program
scenarios.summary: Expert earned value drill on a night-window airfield apron program: derive SPI, CPI, three competing EAC methods, TCPI, and the gap between percent complete and percent spent.
scenarios.brief: A mid-size coastal airport is rehabilitating an apron and electrifying aircraft stands using only the hours between the last arrival and the first departure. One unusually strong paving period has convinced the delivery team that the rest of the work will run at the budgeted rate, and they want the forecast rebuilt on that assumption. The controls file at the data date tells a colder story. The analyst must lay all three forecast methods side by side before anyone picks one.
objectives: Compute SPI and CPI from cumulative PV, EV and AC at a single data date.
Produce EAC by the CPI method, the composite SPI x CPI method, and the budget-rate method from identical inputs.
Calculate TCPI against BAC and compare it with the CPI achieved to date.
Distinguish percent complete (EV/BAC) from percent spent (AC/BAC) and quantify the gap.
Judge whether one favourable period justifies a budget-rate forecast.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic expert-level earned value and forecasting drill.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real airport, program or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (PV = 22500000, EV = 20700000, AC = 23000000, BAC = 52000000):
1. SPI = EV / PV = 20700000 / 22500000 = 0.92.
2. CPI = EV / AC = 20700000 / 23000000 = 0.90.
3. Remaining work = BAC - EV = 31300000.
4. EAC (CPI method) = BAC / CPI = 52000000 / 0.90 = 57777777.78.
5. EAC (composite) = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) = 23000000 + 31300000 / 0.828 = 60801932.37.
6. EAC (budget rate) = AC + (BAC - EV) = 54300000. This is the trap: it assumes the 0.90 cost performance simply stops on the evidence of one strong period, and it is by far the most flattering of the three.
7. TCPI to BAC = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 31300000 / 29000000 = 1.08. Remaining work must run about 20 percent more efficiently than the 0.90 achieved to date - the quantitative rebuttal to the budget-rate claim.
8. Percent complete = EV / BAC = 39.81.
9. Percent spent = AC / BAC = 44.23 - roughly 4.4 points of budget consumed beyond value earned.

scenarios.summary: Forecast the final cost of a mine dewatering pipeline that hit an overspend in month 3: compute the latest cumulative CPI, a CPI-based EAC, and the variance at completion.
scenarios.brief: Halfway through installing the in-pit dewatering pipeline at a synthetic open-cut operation, the project sponsor has flagged a persistent overspend: pump skids arrived on time, but trenching through abrasive rock chewed through drill consumables and standby labour. Interpret variance at completion (VAC = BAC - EAC) as a forecast overrun or underrun.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Read the latest cumulative figures. At month 5: EV = 288, AC = 320, and BAC = 400.

Step 2 — Final cumulative CPI. CPI = EV / AC = 288 / 320 = 0.90. Every unit spent is earning only 0.90 units of budgeted work, so the job is running about 10% over on cost.

Step 3 — Estimate at completion. Assuming the current cost efficiency continues, EAC = BAC / CPI = 400 / 0.90 = 444.44 (2 dp).

Step 4 — Variance at completion. VAC = BAC - EAC = 400 - 444.44 = -44.44. The negative sign confirms the sponsor's concern: at today's efficiency the project is forecast to finish roughly 44.44 over budget.

Context check (not asked, but visible in the data): month 2 is the worst schedule month (SPI = 80/100 = 0.80, a pump-skid delivery slip that was recovered) while month 3 is the worst cost month (CPI = 144/180 = 0.80, the abrasive-rock trenching overrun). Cost efficiency has since stabilised at 0.90 rather than returning to 1.00, which is why the CPI-based EAC still shows an overrun.

Final answers: final CPI = 0.90; EAC = 444.44; VAC = -44.44.

scenarios.project_type: Hypersonic testbed thermal protection qualification campaign
scenarios.summary: Read nine periods of cumulative PV/EV/AC on an aerospace thermal protection qualification and pin down the final indices, the CPI-based forecast, and the true worst schedule and cost months.
scenarios.brief: A reusable hypersonic flight-test vehicle is being re-qualified after its ceramic-composite thermal protection tiles failed acceptance on two prior flights. The re-tiling and arc-jet qualification campaign spans nine monthly reporting periods of cumulative planned value, earned value and actual cost. The most recent months read calmer than the middle of the campaign, and leadership wants to know whether that calm is a real turnaround or just arithmetic. Diagnose the timeline period by period and forecast the outturn.
objectives: Compute cumulative SPI and CPI for every reporting period from cumulative PV, EV and AC.
Identify the worst schedule period and the worst cost period independently rather than assuming they coincide.
Distinguish a genuine recovery from cumulative averaging that masks earlier deterioration.
Forecast EAC using EAC = BAC / CPI and derive VAC = BAC - EAC.
Report indices, forecasts and period numbers to the stated precision.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic expert-level earned value timeline drill.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, entities and events are synthetic and simplified for training and represent no real programme or cost data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - period indices (SPI = EV/PV, CPI = EV/AC):
P1 0.9500 / 0.9500; P2 0.9053 / 0.9348; P3 0.8481 / 0.9178; P4 0.8087 / 0.9073; P5 0.8226 / 0.8854; P6 0.8354 / 0.8639; P7 0.8542 / 0.8761; P8 0.8761 / 0.8903; P9 0.9077 / 0.9049.

Step 2 - final period (P9): SPI = 59000/65000 = 0.9077; CPI = 59000/65200 = 0.9049.

Step 3 - the troughs are not in the final period and do not share a period. Lowest cumulative SPI = 0.8087 in period 4 (18600/23000). Lowest cumulative CPI = 0.8639 in period 6 (33000/38200), because cost erosion kept deepening for two periods after the schedule trough.

Step 4 - EAC = BAC / CPI = 78000 / (59000/65200) = 78000 x 65200 / 59000 = 86196.61.

Step 5 - VAC = BAC - EAC = 78000 - 86196.61 = -8196.61, an overrun.

The late uptick is arithmetic: cumulative indices drift toward the mean as denominators grow, so reading health from the last row alone understates both the schedule trough at P4 and the cost trough at P6.

scenarios.project_type: renewable generation and network capital portfolio
scenarios.summary: Score five energy capital candidates on a weighted NPV/risk/fit index, including one value-destroying but high-fit pilot, then report the top score and total portfolio NPV.
scenarios.brief: A regional energy cooperative must fix its five-year capital plan and cannot fund everything its planners proposed. Five candidates sit on the table: a geothermal doublet, a tidal-lagoon pilot, a wind repowering, a hydrogen blending trial and a grid battery. The investment committee has agreed a single weighted score blending normalised NPV, strategic fit and delivery risk, so a low-risk, high-fit option can still compete with a large-NPV one. One pilot has a negative NPV and the strongest fit in the set, which is exactly where the ranking gets uncomfortable.
objectives: Normalise a set of NPVs, including a negative value, against the largest absolute NPV in the set.
Compute a weighted candidate score combining normalised NPV, strategic fit and risk using stated weights.
Identify the highest weighted score across a candidate set without relying on raw NPV ranking.
Aggregate total portfolio NPV and interpret how a value-destroying candidate affects the ranking.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an intermediate portfolio-selection skill drill; all figures constructed by the author.
scenarios.disclaimers: All entities, projects and figures are synthetic and simplified for training and represent no real organisation or investment case.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Normalisation base: largest absolute NPV = |96.0| = 96.0 (P3).

Step 2 - Apply score = 0.5 x (npv / 96.0) + 0.2 x fit - 0.3 x risk:
P1 (48.0, risk 0.55, fit 0.70): 0.2500 + 0.1400 - 0.1650 = 0.2250
P2 (-12.0, risk 0.35, fit 0.90): -0.0625 + 0.1800 - 0.1050 = 0.0125
P3 (96.0, risk 0.30, fit 0.60): 0.5000 + 0.1200 - 0.0900 = 0.5300
P4 (22.0, risk 0.65, fit 0.85): 0.114583 + 0.1700 - 0.1950 = 0.089583
P5 (60.0, risk 0.20, fit 0.45): 0.3125 + 0.0900 - 0.0600 = 0.3425

Step 3 - Highest weighted score: top_score = 0.5300 (the wind repowering). The battery ranks second at 0.3425 despite much lower NPV, because it carries the lowest risk in the set.

Step 4 - Total NPV: 48.0 + (-12.0) + 96.0 + 22.0 + 60.0 = 214.00

Answers: top_score = 0.5300; total_npv = 214.00; score_P2 = 0.0125; score_P4 = 0.0896 (0.089583). P2 stays marginally positive only because its fit contribution outweighs its negative normalised NPV at a moderate risk level.

scenarios.title: Reservoir Floating Solar — Weighted Progress Roll-Up
scenarios.project_type: 8 MW floating solar array on an irrigation reservoir
scenarios.summary: Roll up physical progress for a floating solar array using budget-weighted work packages, and see why the weighted figure differs from a simple average of package percentages.
scenarios.brief: A developer is installing an 8 MW floating photovoltaic array on a man-made irrigation reservoir. The site lead has been reporting a simple average of the five work-package percentages at the weekly review, but the anchoring and float-launch packages carry far more budget than the shore-side works. The project controls office has asked you to recompute overall progress using budget weights so the sponsor sees a defensible number.
objectives: Compute overall percent complete as a budget-weighted average of work-package progress
Compute the total weight of a work breakdown and confirm the weighting basis
Distinguish a weighted progress roll-up from a simple unweighted average of package percentages
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Total weight. Sum the budget weights of all work packages: 20 + 30 + 25 + 15 + 10 = 100. So total_weight = 100.

Step 2 — Weighted contributions. For each package, multiply weight by percent complete:
- 1.1 Anchoring and Mooring Grid: 20 x 100 = 2000
- 1.2 Float Assembly and Launch: 30 x 60 = 1800
- 1.3 PV Module Mounting: 25 x 40 = 1000
- 1.4 DC Cabling and Combiner Boxes: 15 x 20 = 300
- 1.5 Shore Inverter Station: 10 x 10 = 100
Sum of contributions = 2000 + 1800 + 1000 + 300 + 100 = 5200.

Step 3 — Overall percent complete. overall_percent = sum(weight x percent) / total_weight = 5200 / 100 = 52.00%.

Check the story's tension: the simple unweighted average is (100 + 60 + 40 + 20 + 10) / 5 = 46.00%, which understates true progress here because the heaviest packages (anchoring, float launch) are the furthest along. Weighting by budget corrects this: the defensible overall figure is 52.00%.

objectives: Compute a budget-weighted overall percent complete from work-package weights and percents
Distinguish approved-scope progress from progress claimed against a rejected change request
Interpret why an unweighted average of package percents misstates programme progress
Compute the total weighting base used for the roll-up

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Fix the correct inputs. The contractor's dashboard shows WP 1.3 (Sortation Control Software) at 65%, but that claim includes screening-lane software scope from change request CR-018, which the change board REJECTED last month — a rejected change earns no progress. The approved-scope record for WP 1.3 is 40%, and that is the figure in the table (and the figure the roll-up must use). The dashboard's quoted "58% overall" is also just an unweighted average of the five percents ((85+60+40+95+10)/5 = 58) and ignores budget weighting entirely.

Step 2 — Total weight. total_weight = 1800 + 2600 + 1200 + 900 + 1500 = 8000.

Step 3 — Weighted contributions (weight x percent):
1.1: 1800 x 85 = 153000
1.2: 2600 x 60 = 156000
1.3: 1200 x 40 = 48000
1.4: 900 x 95 = 85500
1.5: 1500 x 10 = 15000
Sum = 457500.

Step 4 — Overall percent complete = sum(weight x percent) / total_weight = 457500 / 8000 = 57.1875, which rounds to 57.19%.

Answers: overall_percent = 57.19; total_weight = 8000. Interpretation: true weighted progress (57.19%) sits below both quoted figures because the heavily weighted conveyor and commissioning packages lag, while the rejected-change claim inflated the software package.
