Report a rollup figure to two decimal places suitable for a sponsor progress review.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic weighted-progress drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All packages, weights and percentages are synthetic and simplified for training and represent no real utility asset or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Total weight = 12.5 + 23.75 + 18.25 + 14.5 + 9.75 + 7.25 = 86.00.

Step 2 - Earned weight per package (weight x percent / 100):
1.1 Surge-wall and switchyard civils: 12.5 x 100.0 / 100 = 12.5000
1.2 GIS switchgear install: 23.75 x 68.4 / 100 = 16.2450
1.3 Battery enclosure and DC blocks: 18.25 x 41.6 / 100 = 7.5920
1.4 Protection and control retrofit: 14.5 x 27.5 / 100 = 3.9875
1.5 Submarine feeder cable termination: 9.75 x 83.2 / 100 = 8.1120
1.6 Commissioning and islanding tests: 7.25 x 4.8 / 100 = 0.3480
Sum of earned weight = 48.7845.

Step 3 - Overall percent complete = sum(weight x percent) / total weight = 4878.45 / 86.00 = 56.7262, i.e. 56.73 percent (2 dp). Equivalently 48.7845 / 86.00 x 100.

Final answers: total_weight = 86.00; overall_percent = 56.73.

Sponsor note: the unweighted average of the six package percents is 54.25, so an unweighted read understates progress because the heaviest package (GIS switchgear, weight 23.75) runs ahead of the lightest ones. The real tension is that only 0.348 of the 7.25 commissioning weight is earned, so nearly all remaining scope sits in the packages that gate energisation.

scenarios.summary: Roll up ten rule-of-credit work packages on a mine tailings facility raise into a single weighted percent complete, resisting the flattering unweighted average.
scenarios.brief: The Stage 2 raise at the Kirrawee Ridge tailings storage facility must be capped and commissioned before the wet season. Four of the ten work packages are closed out at 100 percent and a fifth is all but finished, and the site superintendent is circulating a headline progress figure built from a straight average of the package percentages. The bulk-quantity packages that carry most of the weight - embankment fill and liner placement - are the ones lagging. Your job is to produce the defensible weighted roll-up.
objectives: Compute the total rule-of-credit weight of a multi-package work breakdown
Calculate weighted overall percent complete as the sum of weight times percent divided by total weight
Distinguish a weighted roll-up from an unweighted average of package percentages
Explain why completed low-weight packages can overstate headline progress
Report progress measures to a specified rounding convention
scenarios.provenance: Synthetic scenario authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; figures constructed to exercise weighted progress roll-up.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Total weight. Sum the ten package weights: 145 + 210 + 96 + 63 + 58 + 44 + 88 + 52 + 27 + 64 = 847. total_weight = 847.

Step 2 - Earned weight per package (weight x percent / 100):
1.1: 145 x 100/100 = 145.00
1.2: 210 x 48/100 = 100.80
1.3: 96 x 30/100 = 28.80
1.4: 63 x 72/100 = 45.36
1.5: 58 x 40/100 = 23.20
1.6: 44 x 100/100 = 44.00
1.7: 88 x 61/100 = 53.68
1.8: 52 x 95/100 = 49.40
1.9: 27 x 100/100 = 27.00
1.10: 64 x 100/100 = 64.00
Sum of earned weight = 581.24 (equivalently, sum of weight x percent = 58,124).

Step 3 - Weighted overall percent complete.
overall_percent = (sum of weight x percent) / (sum of weight) = 58,124 / 847 = 68.6234...
Rounded to two decimals: overall_percent = 68.62.

Step 4 - The trap. The unweighted average of the ten percentages is (100 + 48 + 30 + 72 + 40 + 100 + 61 + 95 + 100 + 100) / 10 = 746 / 10 = 74.60. scenarios.title: Tilt-Tray Sorter Drive Delay: Critical-Path Impact at Concourse D
scenarios.project_type: airport baggage screening and sorter retrofit
scenarios.summary: A late supplier shipment of sorter drive modules threatens a concourse baggage retrofit. Convert the supplier slip into critical delay, revised duration, and float consumed.
scenarios.brief: An inland regional airport is retrofitting Concourse D with an in-line hold-baggage screening loop and a replacement tilt-tray sorter, working only in overnight curfew windows. The sorter drive modules sit on the sole procurement path feeding the commissioning sequence, and that path has only a thin sliver of float left after two earlier resequences. The supplier has now issued a revised shipping notice, and the controls team must translate the slip into schedule impact before the change board meets.
objectives: Compute critical delay as the supplier slip in excess of remaining float on the driving path
Calculate the revised total project duration after absorbing the supplier slip
Determine how much remaining float is consumed by the supplier slip
Distinguish float erosion from true critical-path extension when reporting procurement impact
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic procurement drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures and entities are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real airport, supplier or contract.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: project_duration = 240 days, remaining_float = 12 days, supplier_delay_days = 27 days.

Step 1 - Float consumed. The slip first eats the float on the driving procurement path, and cannot consume more float than exists: float_consumed = min(remaining_float, supplier_delay_days) = min(12, 27) = 12 days. All float is gone and the drive-module path becomes critical.

Step 2 - Critical delay. Only the portion beyond the float pushes the finish date: critical_delay = max(0, supplier_delay_days - remaining_float) = max(0, 27 - 12) = 15 days.

Step 3 - Revised duration. new_project_duration = project_duration + critical_delay = 240 + 15 = 255 days.

Check: the 27-day slip splits into 12 days absorbed by float plus 15 days of true extension (12 + 15 = 27). Reporting the full 27 days overstates impact; reporting zero because the path "had float" understates it. Answers: critical_delay = 15, new_project_duration = 255, float_consumed = 12 (whole days).

Report all three in whole days.

scenarios.title: Cold-Chain Cross-Dock Hub: Absorbing a Reefer Supplier Slip
scenarios.summary: A reefer-unit supplier slips its delivery date on a cold-chain cross-dock commissioning project. Quantify how much of the slip the schedule can absorb and how much actually lands on the finish date.
scenarios.brief: A regional freight operator is commissioning a refrigerated cross-dock terminal that transfers temperature-controlled pallets between long-haul trailers and city vans. The commissioning schedule is baselined, and the driving path runs through installation and validation of the reefer condensing units. The nominated supplier has just issued a revised delivery notice, and the steering group has assumed the whole slip will hit go-live. As procurement lead you must separate the portion the remaining float can absorb from the portion that genuinely extends the project.
objectives: Compute critical delay as the supplier slip in excess of remaining float on the driving path
Recalculate total project duration after a procurement-driven slip is applied
Quantify float consumed by a supplier delay and distinguish it from schedule extension
Explain why a reported supplier slip does not translate one-for-one into finish-date movement
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic procurement drill; no external source data used.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, entities and schedule data are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: project_duration = 168 days, remaining_float = 6 days, supplier_delay_days = 20 days.

Step 1 - Critical delay. Only the slip beyond available float can push the finish date: critical_delay = max(0, supplier_delay_days - remaining_float) = max(0, 20 - 6) = 14 days.

Step 2 - New project duration. The extension is added to the baseline: new_project_duration = project_duration + critical_delay = 168 + 14 = 182 days.

Step 3 - Float consumed. Float is eaten only up to the amount that exists: float_consumed = min(remaining_float, supplier_delay_days) = min(6, 20) = 6 days. The path is now at zero float, so any further reefer-unit slip is day-for-day on the finish date.

Interpretation: the steering group's assumption that the full 20-day slip moves go-live overstates the impact by 6 days, but the buffer is fully exhausted - the real procurement message. Report all three values in days to two decimal places (14.00, 182.00 and 6.00 for these figures).

scenarios.title: Basalt Ridge Geothermal: Weld Crew Productivity Factor
scenarios.summary: Diagnose a geothermal weld crew that has burned fewer hours than planned yet earned far less quantity. Compute planned and actual productivity, the productivity factor, and the labour hours variance.
scenarios.brief: Phase 2 of the Basalt Ridge geothermal field is installing the steam-gathering header that ties the wellheads into the separator station. The pipe-welding crew was baselined on a fixed weld count and a fixed direct labour hour budget, and quantity is credited only once a weld is radiographed and accepted. At the reporting cut-off the crew has charged fewer hours than the baseline curve predicted, which reads as good news on the timesheet report alone. The catch is that the hour total also absorbs cut-out and re-weld effort that earns no new quantity, so the controls lead needs the productivity picture before anyone celebrates an underrun.
objectives: Compute planned productivity as planned quantity divided by planned labour hours
Compute actual productivity as earned quantity divided by actual labour hours
Derive the productivity factor as actual productivity divided by planned productivity
Calculate the signed labour hours variance and interpret it against the productivity factor
Explain why rework hours depress the productivity factor even when hours are underrun
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic productivity-analysis skill drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures, names and quantities are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Planned productivity = planned_qty / planned_hours = 1680 / 4200 = 0.400 welds per labour hour.

Step 2 - Actual productivity = earned_qty / actual_hours = 1092 / 3150 = 0.346667, rounded to 0.347 welds per labour hour. The actual hours include cut-out and re-weld time; those hours are charged to the weld account but produce no additional earned welds, so they stay in the denominator and drag the rate down.

Step 3 - Productivity factor = actual productivity / planned productivity = 0.346667 / 0.400 = 0.866667, rounded to 0.867. A factor below 1.0 means the crew needs about 15 percent more hours per weld than the baseline assumed (1 / 0.867 = 1.154).

Step 4 - Hours variance = actual_hours - planned_hours = 3150 - 4200 = -1050 labour hours. Negative means fewer hours charged than the full baseline budget.

Step 5 - Interpretation: the 1050 hour underrun is not a saving. Only 1092 of 1680 welds are earned (65 percent of scope) while 75 percent of the budgeted hours are consumed. At the demonstrated 0.347 welds per hour the remaining 588 welds need roughly 1695 hours against 1050 hours left, forecasting an overrun near 645 hours unless reject rates fall.

Final answers: planned_productivity = 0.400; actual_productivity = 0.347; factor = 0.867; hours_variance = -1050.

Timesheets show 3150 actual labour hours charged to the weld account, and that total includes all cut-out and re-weld time, which earns no additional quantity. scenarios.title: Edge Compute Hall Fit-Out: Node Racking Productivity Factor
scenarios.summary: Convert planned and earned node quantities into labour productivity rates, then judge whether an under-run on charged hours is real efficiency or hidden under-performance.
scenarios.brief: A technology contractor is building out a modular edge compute hall, where crews rack, cable and burn-in test compute nodes for a shared data hall. The estimate fixed a planned node count against planned direct labour hours, and the controls lead now reports earned nodes and the hours actually charged after the second commissioning wave. The hours charged came in under plan, which the delivery manager is reading as good news. The drill asks the learner to test that reading against the productivity numbers.
objectives: Compute planned productivity as planned quantity divided by planned labour hours.
Compute actual productivity from earned quantity and actual charged labour hours.
Derive the productivity factor as actual productivity divided by planned productivity.
Calculate the labour hours variance and explain why an hours under-run can still mask lost productivity.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab using the standard earned-quantity productivity-factor method; all figures are invented for training.
scenarios.disclaimers: All quantities, hours and organisations in this drill are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: planned_qty = 960 nodes, planned_hours = 1200 h, earned_qty = 744 nodes, actual_hours = 1080 h.

Step 1 - Planned productivity = planned_qty / planned_hours = 960 / 1200 = 0.8000 nodes per labour hour.

Step 2 - Actual productivity = earned_qty / actual_hours = 744 / 1080 = 0.6889 nodes per labour hour (0.688888... unrounded).

Step 3 - Productivity factor = actual productivity / planned productivity = 0.688888... / 0.8000 = 0.8611. A factor below 1.0 means each charged labour hour delivers less installed quantity than the estimate assumed; about 14 percent of the planned output rate has been lost.

Step 4 - Hours variance = actual_hours - planned_hours = 1080 - 1200 = -120 hours (120 fewer hours than planned).

Step 5 - Interpretation. Quantity variance = 744 - 960 = -216 nodes, a 22.5 percent shortfall against only a 10 percent hours under-run. The crews charged fewer hours because they installed far fewer nodes, so the apparent saving is a progress shortfall, not efficiency. At the current 0.6889 rate the remaining 216 nodes need roughly 314 hours, far more than the 120 hours left unspent, so the forecast at completion overruns unless the rate recovers.

scenarios.title: Valve Chamber Renewal: PERT on a 16-Day Diversion Window
scenarios.project_type: Trunk water main pressure-reducing valve renewal
scenarios.summary: Estimate the expected duration, standard deviation, and on-time probability for a four-activity valve renewal chain that must finish inside a 16-day supply diversion window.
scenarios.brief: A regional water utility is renewing a corroded pressure-reducing valve set in an underground chamber on a trunk main. Supply to the district is being fed through a temporary diversion that the network team will only sustain for 16 days, so the scheduler needs a probabilistic view of the four-activity renewal chain before committing to the outage. You have three-point (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) duration estimates for each activity, executed strictly in sequence.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from three-point estimates using (o + 4m + p) / 6
Compute the standard deviation of a chain of activities by summing activity variances
Interpret a z-score under the normal approximation to estimate the probability of meeting a deadline
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real utility, network, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A Isolate and drain chamber: (1 + 4x2 + 3)/6 = 12/6 = 2 days
B Cut out old valve set: (2 + 4x4 + 6)/6 = 24/6 = 4 days
C Install and weld new valve assembly: (2 + 4x5 + 8)/6 = 30/6 = 5 days
D Pressure test, disinfect, recommission: (1 + 4x3 + 5)/6 = 18/6 = 3 days

Step 2 — Expected chain duration: 2 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 14.00 days.

Step 3 — Activity standard deviations, sd = (p - o)/6, then sum variances:
A: (3-1)/6 = 1/3, variance 1/9
B: (6-2)/6 = 2/3, variance 4/9
C: (8-2)/6 = 1, variance 1
D: (5-1)/6 = 2/3, variance 4/9
Total variance = 1/9 + 4/9 + 9/9 + 4/9 = 18/9 = 2.00; chain standard deviation = sqrt(2.00) = 1.41 days.

Step 4 — Probability of finishing within the 16-day diversion window:
z = (deadline - expected) / sd = (16 - 14) / 1.4142 = 1.41.
From the standard normal distribution, P(Z <= 1.41) is approximately 0.9214, so prob_on_time is approximately 92.14%.

Answers: expected_duration = 14.00 days; std_dev = 1.41 days; prob_on_time = 92.14%.

config.prompt: A regional water utility is renewing a corroded pressure-reducing valve set in an underground trunk-main chamber. Using PERT three-point estimating: 1) compute the expected chain duration in days, 2) compute the standard deviation of the chain duration in days, and 3) using the normal approximation, compute the probability (as a percentage) of finishing within the 16-day diversion window. Round all answers to 2 decimal places.

scenarios.title: Potash Re-Entry Chain: PERT Analysis Against a Rejected Deadline Extension
scenarios.project_type: Underground potash mine re-entry after water inrush
scenarios.summary: Apply three-point PERT estimating to a five-activity mine re-entry chain and judge the probability of restarting production before a toll-milling window closes — using the correct, unamended deadline.
scenarios.brief: A water inrush flooded the main decline of an underground potash operation, halting hoisting. The recovery team has built a five-activity re-entry chain — dewatering, ground support rehabilitation, winder recommissioning, ventilation fan replacement, and the regulator's re-entry inspection — that must finish before day 56, when the toll-milling window at a third-party concentrator closes. The contractor's change request CR-041 asked to move the milestone to day 60; forum minutes call it "endorsed for consideration", but the change control board register shows it REJECTED. Analyse the chain against the milestone that actually stands.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from three-point (o, m, p) estimates and aggregate them along an activity chain
Compute chain variance and standard deviation by summing activity variances, not standard deviations
Interpret change-control records to select the governing deadline when a rejected change appears endorsed elsewhere
Estimate the probability of meeting a milestone using the normal approximation and communicate the schedule risk
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real mine, company, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A Decline dewatering: (8 + 40 + 14)/6 = 10.33
B Ground support rehabilitation: (10 + 48 + 20)/6 = 13.00
C Winder recommissioning: (6 + 36 + 12)/6 = 9.00
D Primary ventilation fan replacement: (12 + 60 + 24)/6 = 16.00
E Regulatory re-entry inspection: (4 + 20 + 8)/6 = 5.33

Step 2 — Expected chain duration = sum of te = 10.33 + 13.00 + 9.00 + 16.00 + 5.33 = 53.67 days.

Step 3 — Variance per activity, v = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; B: (10/6)^2 = 2.7778; C: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; D: (12/6)^2 = 4.0000; E: (4/6)^2 = 0.4444.
Chain variance = 1.0000 + 2.7778 + 1.0000 + 4.0000 + 0.4444 = 9.22.

Step 4 — Standard deviation = sqrt(9.2222) = 3.04 days. (Sum variances first, then take the square root — never sum standard deviations.)

Step 5 — Governing deadline. CR-041 (extension to day 60) was REJECTED by the change control board; the forum's "endorsed for consideration" note carries no authority. The milestone remains day 56.

Step 6 — Probability of meeting day 56:
z = (56 - 53.6667) / 3.0368 = 0.77.
P(Z <= 0.77) from the standard normal distribution ≈ 0.779, so prob_on_time ≈ 77.89%.

Interpretation: roughly a 78% chance of restarting before the toll-milling window closes — a meaningful (about 1-in-5) residual risk, driven mostly by the ventilation fan replacement (largest variance). Had the rejected day-60 deadline been used, the probability would have been overstated at about 98%.

scenarios.title: Floating Solar Pontoon Launch — PERT Window Check
scenarios.project_type: 4.5 MW floating solar array on an irrigation reservoir
scenarios.summary: Run a three-point PERT analysis on the four-step pontoon launch chain for a floating solar array and judge whether the crew can beat the reservoir drawdown deadline.
scenarios.brief: Your contractor is installing a 4.5 MW floating solar array on a farm irrigation reservoir. The launch sequence — anchor-grid survey, pontoon string assembly, module mounting, and shore-cable tie-in — must finish before the seasonal drawdown lowers the water level 17 days from now, after which the launch ramp becomes unusable. The site manager has given optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic durations for each step and wants a quick probabilistic read on the finish date.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from three-point estimates using (o + 4m + p) / 6.
Compute the standard deviation of a chain of activities by summing variances.
Interpret a normal-approximation z-score as a probability of meeting a deadline.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or site.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A Anchor-grid survey: (2 + 12 + 4)/6 = 3.00
B Pontoon string assembly: (4 + 24 + 8)/6 = 6.00
C Module mounting: (3 + 20 + 7)/6 = 5.00
D Shore-cable tie-in: (1 + 8 + 3)/6 = 2.00
Expected chain duration = 3 + 6 + 5 + 2 = 16.00 days.

Step 2 — Variance per activity, var = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A: (2/6)^2 = 0.1111
B: (4/6)^2 = 0.4444
C: (4/6)^2 = 0.4444
D: (2/6)^2 = 0.1111
Sum of variances = 1.1111.
Standard deviation = sqrt(1.1111) = 1.05 days (2 dp).

Step 3 — Probability of finishing by the 17-day drawdown deadline:
z = (17 - 16.00) / 1.0541 = 0.95 (2 dp).
From the standard normal distribution, P(Z <= 0.95) is approximately 0.8286, so prob_on_time = 82.86%.

Conclusion: the crew has roughly an 83% chance of launching before the drawdown — favourable, but not certain, so the one-day buffer deserves watching.

scenarios.title: Night-Window De-Icing Pad: PERT Handover Risk
scenarios.project_type: remote de-icing pad and glycol recovery commissioning
scenarios.summary: Expert PERT drill on an airport de-icing pad built in strictly sequential night closures: derive expected duration, variance, standard deviation and the probability of meeting the handover deadline.
scenarios.brief: A regional airport is adding a remote de-icing pad with a closed-loop glycol recovery system at the end of a taxiway stub. The controls team must turn the three-point estimates into a defensible probability of hitting the contractual handover date.
objectives: Compute PERT expected activity durations from three-point estimates using the beta approximation
Aggregate activity variances across a serial chain instead of summing standard deviations
Derive the project standard deviation from total project variance
Convert a deadline into a z-score and an on-time completion probability under the normal assumption
Identify which activity contributes the dominant share of total schedule uncertainty
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic airside construction exercise; no real project, organisation or dataset is referenced.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training and do not represent any actual airport project, contract or cost basis.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures (deadline 75 days):

1. te = (o + 4m + p)/6 per activity: A (8,10,18)=11.00; B (6,9,24)=11.00; C (12,14,22)=15.00; D (7,8,15)=9.00; E (5,6,13)=7.00; F (4,5,6)=5.00; G (6,7,14)=8.00; H (3,4,11)=5.00.

2. Serial chain, so expected_duration = 11+11+15+9+7+5+8+5 = 71.00 days.

3. var = ((p-o)/6)^2: A=2.7778; B=9.0000; C=2.7778; D=1.7778; E=1.7778; F=0.1111; G=1.7778; H=1.7778.

4. Project variance = sum of activity variances = 21.7778, reported as 21.78. Activity B alone supplies about 41 percent of it.

5. std_dev = sqrt(21.7778) = 4.6667, reported as 4.67. The trap: adding the eight standard deviations gives 12.00, which is wrong because standard deviations do not add; only variances do.

6. z = (deadline - te)/std_dev = (75 - 71)/4.6667 = 0.8571.

7. prob_on_time = Phi(0.8571) = 0.8043, i.e. roughly 80.4 percent.

Answers: expected_duration 71.00, variance 21.78, std_dev 4.67, prob_on_time 0.8043.

config.prompt: A regional airport is building a remote de-icing pad with a closed-loop glycol recovery system on a taxiway stub that must reopen before each morning departure bank. Every work package is therefore executed inside consecutive overnight closures, so the eight packages run strictly end to end with no overlap. The figures below give each package's optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations in working days, plus the contractual handover deadline in days from notice to proceed. Using the standard PERT beta approximation, and assuming activity durations are independent and the project total is normally distributed, compute the expected project duration, the total project variance, the project standard deviation, and the probability of handover on or before the deadline. Round durations, variance and standard deviation to 2 decimals; express the probability as a decimal between 0 and 1 rounded to 4 decimals.

ask.label: Probability of handover on or before the deadline (decimal, 4 dp)

scenarios.title: Decline Crew Overload: Six-Period Resource Histogram
scenarios.summary: Read a six-period crew-hour demand-versus-capacity histogram for an underground decline drive and quantify peak demand, the worst single-period overload, total over-demand and the number of overloaded periods.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic underground copper-gold operation is driving a second ventilation decline while the existing decline stays in production. The schedule loads shotcrete-and-bolting crew-hours unevenly across six two-week periods, and one period loses crew availability to a planned hoist rope change. The planning superintendent needs the overload picture quantified before any levelling or contract-crew decision is made.
objectives: Extract peak single-period resource demand from a period-by-period histogram
Compute single-period overload as demand minus capacity, floored at zero
Identify the largest single-period overload and distinguish it from the peak-demand period
Aggregate total over-demand across the horizon and count the overloaded periods
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic resource-management skill drill; no external data source.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real mine, crew roster or schedule.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Overload per period: overload(t) = max(0, demand(t) - capacity(t)).
P1: max(0, 3120 - 3400) = 0
P2: max(0, 3980 - 3400) = 580
P3: max(0, 4460 - 3400) = 1060
P4: max(0, 4150 - 2600) = 1550
P5: max(0, 3300 - 3400) = 0
P6: max(0, 2870 - 3400) = 0

Step 2 - Peak demand = max demand(t) = max(3120, 3980, 4460, 4150, 3300, 2870) = 4460.00 crew-hours, in Period 3.

Step 3 - Peak overload = max overload(t) = max(0, 580, 1060, 1550, 0, 0) = 1550.00 crew-hours, in Period 4. This is not the peak-demand period: the capacity dip to 2600 crew-hours in Period 4 opens a wider gap than the higher 4460 crew-hour demand in Period 3, which is still met by 3400 crew-hours of capacity. Overload is driven by the demand-capacity gap, not by demand alone.

Step 4 - Total over-demand = sum of overload(t) = 0 + 580 + 1060 + 1550 + 0 + 0 = 3190.00 crew-hours.

Step 5 - Overloaded periods = count of t with overload(t) > 0 = Periods 2, 3 and 4 = 3.

Final: peak_demand 4460.00; peak_overload 1550.00; total_overdemand 3190.00; overloaded_periods 3.

config.prompt: A synthetic underground copper-gold operation is driving a second ventilation decline over six two-week periods. For each period the table gives the shotcrete-and-bolting crew-hours demanded by the schedule and the crew-hours available from the resourced crews; both demand and capacity vary period to period as headings are advanced and as the main hoist is taken offline for a planned rope change. Using only the figures given, report: the peak demand in any single period, the largest single-period overload (demand above capacity), the total over-demand summed across all periods, and the number of overloaded periods. Treat any period where capacity meets or exceeds demand as zero overload. Express crew-hour values rounded to 2 decimal places and the period count as a whole number.

scenarios.title: Blade Retrofit Crew Loading on a Coastal Wind Repowering Program
scenarios.project_type: onshore wind blade-retrofit and repowering program
scenarios.summary: Level a certified rope-access crew across six fortnights of a wind repowering campaign: find peak demand, the worst single-period shortfall, total over-demand and how many fortnights are overloaded.
scenarios.brief: A coastal wind repowering program is swapping blade sets and upgrading nacelle controls across a 42-turbine array during a narrow low-wind season. All rope-access and blade-composite work draws on one pool of certified technicians, measured in crew-hours per fortnight. One fortnight loses part of that pool to a mandatory recertification block, while the retrofit sequence pushes its heaviest lifting into the middle of the window. The controls team wants the resource picture before committing to the sequence.
objectives: Compute peak resource demand across a multi-period crew-hour histogram
Calculate the largest single-period shortfall (peak overload) from demand and capacity data
Sum total over-demand across all periods to size the aggregate resourcing gap
Count the number of periods in which demand exceeds available capacity
Distinguish the peak-demand period from the peak-overload period when capacity is not flat
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as a synthetic resource-levelling skill drill; all figures invented by the author.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real project, organisation or crew.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Shortfall per period: shortfall_t = max(0, demand_t - capacity_t).
P1: max(0, 1180-1440) = 0
P2: max(0, 1520-1440) = 80
P3: max(0, 2260-1440) = 820
P4: max(0, 1980-1080) = 900
P5: max(0, 1240-1440) = 0
P6: max(0, 1600-1440) = 160

Step 2 - peak_demand = max(demand_t) = max(1180, 1520, 2260, 1980, 1240, 1600) = 2260 crew-hours (period 3).

Step 3 - peak_overload = max(shortfall_t) = max(0, 80, 820, 900, 0, 160) = 900 crew-hours (period 4). This is NOT the peak-demand period: period 4 has lower demand but capacity drops to 1080 during the recertification block, producing the worst single-period gap.

Step 4 - total_overdemand = 0 + 80 + 820 + 900 + 0 + 160 = 1960 crew-hours.

Step 5 - overloaded_periods = count of periods with shortfall_t > 0 = periods 2, 3, 4, 6 = 4.

Final: peak_demand = 2260; peak_overload = 900; total_overdemand = 1960; overloaded_periods = 4.

Interpretation: the 1960 crew-hour gap spans four of six fortnights, while slack exists only in periods 1 (260) and 5 (200). Re-sequencing alone recovers under a quarter of the gap, so added certified crew or a longer window is required.

scenarios.title: Kestrel Basin Floating Solar: EMV of the Live Risk Register
scenarios.project_type: 48 MW floating solar array on a flooded quarry reservoir
scenarios.summary: Translate a five-entry risk register for a floating solar project into expected monetary values, netting one opportunity against four threats and handling a rejected risk-transfer change request.
scenarios.brief: Kestrel Basin is a 48 MW floating solar array being installed on a flooded former quarry that feeds an existing hydro switchyard. The steering committee meets Thursday to decide whether to draw on management reserve, and the sponsor wants the live risk register expressed in expected-value terms first. A recent change request that would have transferred the utility interconnection risk was rejected, so every entry below remains the project's exposure.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value (EMV) of individual threats and opportunities as probability x impact.
Compute a register-level EMV total in which opportunity EMVs offset threat EMVs.
Distinguish a rejected risk-transfer change request from an approved one and keep the affected risk in the project register.
Interpret the sign convention of EMV results (negative = expected cost exposure, positive = expected benefit).
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or utility.
scenarios.worked_solution:
EMV of each entry = probability x impact (keep the sign: threats negative, opportunities positive).

Step 1 - Confirm the register contents. CR-014 proposed transferring R3 to the utility but was REJECTED, so R3 stays in the project register and must be included. R4 is an opportunity, so its EMV is positive and offsets the threats.

Step 2 - Compute individual EMVs:
- R1: 0.35 x (-180000) = -63000.00
- R2: 0.60 x (-95000) = -57000.00
- R3: 0.25 x (-240000) = -60000.00  -> emv_R3 = -60000.00
- R4: 0.40 x (+150000) = +60000.00  -> emv_R4 = 60000.00
- R5: 0.15 x (-70000) = -10500.00

Step 3 - Sum for the register total:
emv = -63000 - 57000 - 60000 + 60000 - 10500 = -130500.00

Final answers: emv = -130500.00; emv_R3 = -60000.00; emv_R4 = 60000.00.

Interpretation: the register carries a net expected exposure of 130500, even after the Phase 2 rebate opportunity fully offsets the switchyard slip in expectation - useful context for Thursday's reserve-drawdown decision.

scenarios.summary: Compute expected monetary value for individual risks and the full register on a small telemetry platform migration, distinguishing threats from an opportunity.

Interpret the register-total EMV as the probability-weighted net exposure of the project
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real company, project, or market data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Formula. EMV of a risk = probability x impact. Threats carry negative impacts; opportunities carry positive impacts.

Step 2 — R1 Vendor firmware delay (threat): EMV_R1 = 0.4 x (-50000) = -20000.

Step 3 — R2 Historical data rework (threat): EMV_R2 = 0.2 x (-30000) = -6000.

Step 4 — R3 Early bulk-license discount (opportunity): EMV_R3 = 0.5 x (+10000) = +5000.

Step 5 — Register total. Sum all EMVs: EMV = -20000 + (-6000) + 5000 = -21000.

scenarios.title: TVAC Go/No-Go: EMV of a Mixed Risk Register
scenarios.summary: Net out a five-entry risk register — four threats and one opportunity — for a smallsat propulsion qualification campaign, computing per-risk and total EMV before the sponsor releases the TVAC test window.
scenarios.brief: Astraline Orbital Systems is running the qualification test campaign for its 16U smallsat bus fitted with a new Hall-effect electric propulsion module. The programme sits only 2 percent under its management reserve ceiling, so the sponsor has asked for a fresh expected monetary value read of the risk register before authorising the thermal vacuum test window. The register mixes four threats with one genuine opportunity, and the sponsor wants to see whether the opportunity meaningfully offsets the threat exposure.
objectives: Compute the expected monetary value of an individual risk as probability times impact
Distinguish threats (negative impact) from opportunities (positive impact) when netting a risk register
Aggregate a mixed register into a single total EMV to inform a contingency decision
Interpret whether an opportunity's EMV materially offsets total threat exposure
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not reflect any real programme, organisation, or test facility.
scenarios.worked_solution:
EMV of a single risk = probability x impact. Threats carry negative impacts, opportunities positive impacts; the register total is the plain sum, letting opportunities offset threats.

Step 1 — per-risk EMVs:
- R1: 0.30 x (-180000) = -54000.00
- R2: 0.45 x (-60000) = -27000.00
- R3: 0.25 x (-96000) = -24000.00
- R4: 0.40 x (+75000) = +30000.00 (opportunity — keep the positive sign)
- R5: 0.15 x (-120000) = -18000.00

Step 2 — asked single values:
- emv_R1 = -54000.00
- emv_R4 = +30000.00

Step 3 — register total:
emv = -54000 - 27000 - 24000 + 30000 - 18000 = -93000.00

Interpretation: gross threat exposure is -123000; the batching opportunity offsets 30000 of it, leaving a net expected exposure of -93000. The most common error is treating R4 as a threat (subtracting 30000), which gives -153000 and overstates the contingency the sponsor must hold.

scenarios.title: Floating Wind and Electrolyser Tie-In: EMV of the Risk Register

scenarios.summary: Advanced risk drill on a six-item register for a floating offshore wind pilot feeding an onshore electrolyser. Compute the portfolio EMV and three named line-item EMVs to size the contingency ask.
scenarios.brief: A developer is building a four-unit floating offshore wind pilot whose entire output is contracted to an onshore electrolyser skid. Marine campaign windows are short, the grid connection has a fixed energisation slot, and two upside events could claw back cost. The steering group has approved a six-line quantified risk register and now wants a single expected-value figure it can defend in the contingency paper.
objectives: Compute line-item expected monetary value as probability multiplied by impact for threats and opportunities alike.
Aggregate line-item EMVs into a portfolio EMV across a mixed threat-and-opportunity register.
Apply the sign convention so opportunities offset rather than inflate total threat exposure.
Interpret the resulting EMV as a defensible contingency figure for a sponsor decision.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic risk-management drill; no external source data used.
scenarios.disclaimers: All entities, events and figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project or organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Method: line-item EMV = probability x impact, keeping the sign (negative = threat, positive = opportunity). Portfolio EMV = sum of all line-item EMVs.

R1: 0.28 x -1,840,000 = -515,200
R2: 0.42 x -1,265,000 = -531,300
R3: 0.35 x -2,410,000 = -843,500
R4: 0.22 x 1,730,000 = 380,600

R6: 0.31 x -740,000 = -229,400

Opportunity subtotal = 380,600 + 173,700 = 554,300
Portfolio EMV = -2,119,400 + 554,300 = -1,565,100

Answers: emv = -1,565,100.00; emv_R2 = -531,300.00; emv_R3 = -843,500.00; emv_R4 = 380,600.00. Reading for the sponsor: the register carries a net expected exposure near 1,565,100, and R3 is the single largest threat at about 40 per cent of the threat subtotal, so protecting the energisation slot is where mitigation money buys the most. scenarios.title: Floating Solar Array — Critical Path Under a Rejected Change
scenarios.project_type: 8 MW floating solar array on an irrigation reservoir
scenarios.summary: Run a forward and backward pass on an 8-activity floating-solar installation network, identify the critical path, and compute float — while spotting a duration change that was never actually approved.
scenarios.brief: Your contractor is installing an 8 MW floating solar array on a man-made irrigation reservoir. The site team has handed you the baseline activity network for the on-water works, but their draft log also carries change request CR-014, which proposed adding 4 days to the anchor grid installation. The change board rejected CR-014 last week, yet it still shows as "approved" in the draft. As the scheduler, you must analyse the network using only board-approved data.
objectives: Compute early/late dates for a CPM network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path of a merged activity network
Compute total float for non-critical activities
Distinguish board-approved schedule changes from rejected changes appearing in draft records
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Screen the inputs. CR-014 (add 4 days to activity C) was REJECTED by the change board, so C keeps its baseline duration of 9 days. Analyse the network exactly as given.

Step 2 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur):
A: ES 0, EF 5
B: ES 5, EF 17
C: ES 5, EF 14
D: ES 5, EF 12
E: ES 17, EF 27
F: ES = max(14, 12) = 14, EF 22
G: ES = max(27, 22) = 27, EF 33
H: ES 33, EF 37

Project duration = 37 days.

Step 3 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − dur):
H: LF 37, LS 33
G: LF 33, LS 27
F: LF 27, LS 19
E: LF 27, LS 17
D: LF 19, LS 12... LS = 19 − 7 = 12
C: LF 19, LS 10
B: LF 17, LS 5
A: LF 5, LS 0

Step 4 — Total float (TF = LS − ES):
A 0, B 0, E 0, G 0, H 0 → critical path = A–B–E–G–H.
F: 19 − 14 = 5
D: 12 − 5 = 7
(C: 10 − 5 = 5, not asked.)

Final answers: project_duration = 37; critical_path = {A, B, E, G, H}; float_F = 5; float_D = 7.

2. critical_path — the set of critical activities (zero total float).
3. float_F — total float of activity F, in days.
4. float_D — total float of activity D, in days.

Report durations and floats as whole or decimal day values; round any index-style value to 2 decimal places.

scenarios.title: Bus-Gate Apron Conversion: Critical Path Basics
scenarios.summary: Build a six-activity CPM network for converting a disused cargo apron into a seasonal bus-gate facility, then find the project duration, the critical path, and the float on the pavement repair work.
scenarios.brief: A regional airfield is converting a disused cargo apron into a seasonal bus-gate facility ahead of the summer charter peak. The works package is small but the operations team needs a firm answer on how many working days the apron must stay closed. As the scheduler, you have the six-activity logic network and durations agreed at the kickoff meeting, and the operations manager wants to know which activities drive the closure window and how much slack exists on the pavement repairs.
objectives: Compute early and late dates through forward and backward passes on a small precedence network
Determine the project duration and identify the critical path at a merge point
Compute total float for a non-critical activity and interpret what it means for the apron closure window
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real airport or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + duration, day-0 convention):
A: ES 0, EF 3. B (after A): ES 3, EF 8. C (after A): ES 3, EF 7. D (after C): ES 7, EF 10. E (after B and D, merge): ES = max(8, 10) = 10, EF 12. F (after E): ES 12, EF 14.

Project duration = 14 days.

Step 2 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − duration):
F: LF 14, LS 12. E: LF 12, LS 10. D: LF 10, LS 7. C: LF 7, LS 3. B: LF 10, LS 5. A: LF = min(LS of B, LS of C) = min(5, 3) = 3, LS 0.

Step 3 — Total float (TF = LS − ES):
A: 0. B: 5 − 3 = 2. C: 0. D: 0. E: 0. F: 0.

Critical path (zero-float chain) = A → C → D → E → F.

Answers: project_duration = 14; critical_path = {A, C, D, E, F}; float_B = 2. The pavement repairs (B) can slip up to 2 days without extending the apron closure.

scenarios.title: Cross-Dock Robotics Retrofit: Critical Path Under a Rejected Change
scenarios.summary: Run a forward and backward pass on an 8-activity cross-dock retrofit schedule, identify the critical path, and compute floats — while spotting a duration change that was never actually approved.
scenarios.brief: A regional parcel operator is retrofitting one of its cross-dock hubs with a robotic sortation spine and a new chilled-goods chamber so the site can handle grocery volumes. The planning engineer left mid-project, and the draft schedule circulating in the war room quietly includes a compression from change request CR-014 — which the change board formally rejected last week. You must rebuild the CPM analysis from the approved baseline durations before the go-live date is communicated to carriers.
objectives: Compute early and late dates for a precedence network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path in a schedule containing a merge point
Compute total float for non-critical activities and interpret schedule flexibility
Distinguish approved baseline data from unapproved changes embedded in working documents
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 0 — Apply the correct data. CR-014 (compressing C from 9 to 6 days) was REJECTED by the change board, so the approved baseline duration for C is 9 days. The draft schedule's 6-day figure must be ignored.

Step 1 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur):
A: ES 0, EF 4. B (after A): ES 4, EF 9. C (after A): ES 4, EF 13. D (after C): ES 13, EF 18. E (after B): ES 9, EF 16. F (after D,E): ES = max(18,16) = 18, EF 22. G (after E): ES 16, EF 19. H (after F,G): ES = max(22,19) = 22, EF 24.

Project duration = 24 working days.

Step 2 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF − dur):
H: LF 24, LS 22. F: LF 22, LS 18. G: LF 22, LS 19. D: LF 18, LS 13. E: LF = min(LS F, LS G) = min(18,19) = 18, LS 11. C: LF 13, LS 4. B: LF = LS E = 11, LS 6. A: LF = min(LS B, LS C) = min(6,4) = 4, LS 0.

Step 3 — Total float (TF = LS − ES):
A: 0, C: 0, D: 0, F: 0, H: 0 → critical path = A–C–D–F–H (4+9+5+4+2 = 24).
float_E = 11 − 9 = 2 days.
float_G = 19 − 16 = 3 days.

Final answers: project_duration = 24; critical_path = {A, C, D, F, H}; float_E = 2; float_G = 3.

scenarios.title: Bay 4 Seal-Verification Cutover: Critical Path and Hidden Slack
scenarios.summary: Run a full forward and backward pass on a ten-activity intermodal bay conversion with three merge points, then report the project duration, the critical path and the float on three parallel activities.
scenarios.brief: An inland intermodal transload yard is rebuilding one bay so containers can move rail-to-road through an automated seal-verification lane instead of a manual chassis swap. The sponsor has already given the anchor shipper a firm cutover date, and two work streams — the gantry/controls chain and the dock re-striping chain — converge twice before the live-run acceptance test. The planner needs to know which chain actually governs the date and how much slack the others really hold.
objectives: Perform a forward pass to derive early start and early finish dates across two converging work streams.
Perform a backward pass to derive late start and late finish dates and the total project duration.
Identify the complete critical path through a network containing three merge points.
Compute total float for named non-critical activities and distinguish genuine slack from near-critical exposure.
Explain to a sponsor which parallel chain most threatens a committed cutover date.
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; network logic and durations constructed by the author for deterministic CPM grading.
scenarios.disclaimers: All durations, logic and the yard itself are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real terminal or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur):
A: 0-12. B: 12-21. C: 12-26. D: 21-29. E: 26-32. F: 21-36.
G merges D (29) and E (32): ES 32, EF 37.
H merges F (36) and G (37): ES 37, EF 46.
J: 37-41.
K merges H (46) and J (41): ES 46, EF 49.
Project duration = 49 working days.

Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF - dur), starting LF(K) = 49:
K: LS 46. H: LF 46, LS 37. J: LF 46, LS 42. G: LF = min(37, 42) = 37, LS 32. F: LF 37, LS 22. E: LF 32, LS 26. D: LF 32, LS 24. C: LF 26, LS 12. B: LF = min(24, 22) = 22, LS 13. A: LF 12, LS 0.

Total float = LS - ES:
A 0, C 0, E 0, G 0, H 0, K 0 -> critical path A-C-E-G-H-K (12+14+6+5+9+3 = 49).
B = 13 - 12 = 1. F = 22 - 21 = 1. D = 24 - 21 = 3. J = 42 - 37 = 5.

Answers: project_duration = 49; critical_path = {A, C, E, G, H, K}; float_B = 1; float_F = 1; float_J = 5.

Sponsor reading: the B-F-H chain carries only 1 day of float, so the gantry/controls stream is effectively a second critical path — one bad shift on F puts the committed cutover date at risk even though F is formally non-critical. Only J (5 days) holds slack worth trading.

scenarios.title: Geothermal Wellfield Flow-Battery Tie-In: Resolving a Three-Merge Critical Path
scenarios.summary: Expert CPM drill on a 12-activity geothermal storage tie-in network with three merge points, a long offsite fabrication chain, and a parallel electrical branch that must be evaluated numerically.
scenarios.brief: A synthetic independent power developer is bolting a vanadium-flow storage block onto an operating geothermal wellfield so that off-peak brine output can be time-shifted into the grid. The schedule braids three streams - civil earthworks, an offsite separator skid, and the electrical and controls chain - into a single commissioning gate. Each stream carries a plausible claim on the driving path, and the merge logic at three points decides which claim survives. Resolve the network with a full forward and backward pass rather than by eye.
objectives: Perform a forward pass to compute early start and early finish across three merge points and derive total project duration
Perform a backward pass to compute late start and late finish for every activity in the network
Identify the complete critical path as a set rather than inferring it from the longest individual activity
Compute total float as LS minus ES for named non-critical activities and distinguish near-critical work from genuinely slack work
scenarios.provenance: Original synthetic network authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab; not derived from any actual project record.
scenarios.disclaimers: All activities, durations and logic are synthetic and simplified for training; they represent no real facility, contract or schedule.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Forward pass (ES/EF), each activity starting when all predecessors finish:
A 0/8; C 0/14; B 8/14; D 8/17; E 14/19; F merge max(14,14)=14 -> 14/18; G 17/28; H 19/26; J merge max(28,26)=28 -> 28/34; K 18/23; L merge max(34,23)=34 -> 34/42; M 42/48.
project_duration = 48 working days.

Backward pass (LS/LF) from LF(M)=48:
M 42/48; L 34/42; J 28/34; K 29/34; G 17/28; H 21/28; F 25/29; E 16/21; D 8/17; C 11/25; B LF=min(LS E 16, LS F 25)=16 -> 10/16; A LF=min(LS B 10, LS D 8)=8 -> 0/8.

Total float = LS - ES:
A 0, D 0, G 0, J 0, L 0, M 0 -> critical_path = {A, D, G, J, L, M}; check 8+9+11+6+8+6 = 48.
float_H = 21 - 19 = 2
float_B = 10 - 8 = 2
float_C = 11 - 0 = 11
float_K = 29 - 18 = 11

The traps: C is the single longest activity (14 days) and starts on day zero, yet its chain C-F-K-L-M totals only 37 days and holds 11 days of float. The electrical branch A-B-E-H-J-L-M totals 46 days, so B, E and H hold just 2 days of total float — a one-week switchgear slip pushes commissioning even though those activities are not critical today.

scenarios.title: Floating Solar on the Dam Reservoir: WBS Roll-up and 100% Rule Audit
scenarios.summary: Prompt shortened to meet the 500-900 character budget; all other content fields verified and unchanged. Arithmetic in worked_solution spot-checked (1470/3180/1175/385 -> 6210.00; 1450 vs 1470 -> false).
scenarios.brief: A utility is adding a floating solar array on the reservoir of an existing hydropower station to boost dry-season output. The planning engineer has drafted a work breakdown structure and rolled leaf-level estimates upward, but a deputy planner separately declared a control-account value on the Moorings & Anchoring branch before the leaf estimates were finalised. You must roll up the structure and audit it against the 100% rule before the baseline review.
objectives: Compute a WBS root total by rolling up leaf work-package values through the hierarchy
Audit a declared parent-level control-account value against the sum of its children
Interpret the 100% rule and identify when a stale declared value breaks decomposition integrity
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, organisation, or cost data.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaf work packages (nodes with no children): 1.1.1 = 620, 1.1.2 = 540, 1.1.3 = 310, 1.2.1 = 2200, 1.2.2 = 980, 1.3.1 = 760, 1.3.2 = 415, 1.4 = 385.

Step 2 — Roll up branch subtotals from the leaves:
- 1.1 children sum = 620 + 540 + 310 = 1470
- 1.2 children sum = 2200 + 980 = 3180
- 1.3 children sum = 760 + 415 = 1175
- 1.4 (leaf) = 385

Step 3 — Root total = sum of all leaf values = 1470 + 3180 + 1175 + 385 = 6210.00. Note the roll-up always uses the leaf estimates, not the stale declared branch value.

Step 4 — Apply the 100% rule: every parent that carries an explicit value must equal the sum of its children. Branch 1.1 was declared at 1450, but its children sum to 1470 (a shortfall of 20 against the declared figure). The declared value does not equal the children's sum, so the structure fails the rule.

Final answers: root_total = 6210.00; hundred_percent_valid = false.

scenarios.title: Warehouse Robotics Fleet Software Upgrade — WBS Roll-Up Check
scenarios.summary: Roll up a three-branch work breakdown structure for a robotics fleet software upgrade and verify the 100% rule where a branch owner has declared an explicit control-account value.
scenarios.brief: A fulfilment-automation vendor is upgrading the fleet-control software that steers 120 warehouse robots. The delivery lead has decomposed the release into three branches — navigation, telemetry, and rollout — and sized every work package in effort points. The rollout branch owner has also declared a fixed branch value for her control account, and the sponsor wants confirmation that the structure still rolls up cleanly before baselining.
objectives: Compute the root total of a WBS by summing leaf work-package values
Verify the 100% rule for a parent node that carries an explicitly declared value
Interpret a clean roll-up as readiness to baseline the scope structure
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not reflect any real organisation or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaf work packages and their values.
Navigation Module: Path Planning Engine = 40, Obstacle Detection Update = 35.
Telemetry Dashboard: Data Pipeline Rework = 25, Operator UI Screens = 30.
Rollout and Training: Pilot Deployment = 45, Operator Training = 25.

Step 2 — Compute root_total by summing all leaves:
root_total = 40 + 35 + 25 + 30 + 45 + 25 = 200.

Step 3 — Check the 100% rule (hundred_percent_valid).
Only one parent carries an explicitly declared value: Rollout and Training (node 1.3) is declared at 70.
Sum of its children = 45 + 25 = 70, which equals the declared 70.
No other parent declares a value, so no other check is required.
Therefore hundred_percent_valid = true.

Final answers: root_total = 200; hundred_percent_valid = true. The structure rolls up cleanly and is ready to baseline.

scenarios.title: SD-WBS-108 — Deployer Pod WBS Rollup and the 100% Rule
scenarios.summary: Roll up a nine-node WBS for a small-satellite deployer pod qualification program and test whether a declared control-account value at the structures branch honours the 100% rule.
scenarios.brief: A launch-services integrator is qualifying a new 12U deployer pod that ejects rideshare CubeSats from the upper stage. The programme office has decomposed the effort into a three-level WBS with costed work packages, but the structures lead has hand-entered a control-account value for her branch instead of letting it roll up from the work packages. Before baselining, the planning manager wants the total programme value computed from the leaves and the hand-entered branch value checked against the 100% rule.
objectives: Compute a WBS root total by rolling up costed leaf work packages through the hierarchy.
Distinguish rolled-up parent values from explicitly declared control-account values.
Interpret the 100% rule and detect a parent whose declared value does not equal the sum of its children.
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real organisation, programme, or contract.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Identify the leaf work packages (nodes with no children) and their values: Pod housing machining 1850; Release mechanism assembly 1600; Vibration fixture fabrication 900; Sequencer board build 1240; Flight software V&V 980; Thermal vacuum cycling 1510; Random vibration and shock 1130; Programme management office 640.

Step 2 — Root total. The root value is the sum of all leaves: 1850 + 1600 + 900 + 1240 + 980 + 1510 + 1130 + 640 = 9850. So root_total = 9850.00.

Step 3 — 100% rule check. The rule requires every parent that carries an explicit declared value to equal the sum of its children exactly. Element 1.1 Structures & Mechanisms is declared at 4200, but its children sum to 1850 + 1600 + 900 = 4350. Since 4200 != 4350 (a shortfall of 150), the declared value violates the 100% rule.

Step 4 — Conclusion: hundred_percent_valid = false. The structures control account must be corrected to 4350 (or a work package re-scoped) before the baseline is set.

scenarios.title: Nimbus Relay: WBS Roll-Up and 100% Rule Audit
scenarios.summary: Audit a 13-node work breakdown structure for a streaming telemetry platform rebuild: roll the work packages up to the root and test whether the declared control-account values satisfy the 100% rule.
scenarios.brief: Nimbus Relay is an internal rebuild of a streaming telemetry platform that ingests device signals for a synthetic technology firm's analytics products. The delivery lead has drafted a work breakdown structure with three control accounts and a standalone cutover package, and two of those control accounts already have effort figures published to the steering group. Before the baseline is locked, the sponsor wants the root roll-up recomputed from the work packages alone and the 100% rule audited. A control account whose published number drifts from its work packages will corrupt every downstream variance report.
objectives: Roll up a multi-level work breakdown structure from work packages to the root without double-counting summary levels
Distinguish declared control-account values from computed roll-ups when auditing a WBS
Test each declared parent node against the 100% rule and identify the account that breaches it
Report a validated root total to two decimals for baseline approval
scenarios.provenance: Authored for the PCI Project Controls Simulation Lab as an original synthetic skill drill on WBS roll-up and 100% rule validation.
scenarios.disclaimers: All organisations, figures and effort values are synthetic and simplified for training; they are not drawn from any real project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - identify the leaves (lowest-level nodes, the only ones carrying chargeable effort): 1.1.1 = 428.75, 1.1.2 = 512.40, 1.1.3 = 305.35, 1.2.1 = 640.25, 1.2.2 = 512.35, 1.3.1 = 386.90, 1.3.2 = 274.15, 1.3.3 = 198.40, and 1.4 = 517.30 (a work package sitting directly under the root).

Step 2 - roll up each branch. Branch total = sum of child leaves.
1.1 = 428.75 + 512.40 + 305.35 = 1246.50
1.2 = 640.25 + 512.35 = 1152.60
1.3 = 386.90 + 274.15 + 198.40 = 859.45
1.4 = 517.30 (leaf, no children)

Step 3 - root_total = 1246.50 + 1152.60 + 859.45 + 517.30 = 3775.85. Summary nodes are never added on top of their children, or the total would be double-counted.

Step 4 - apply the 100% rule to every node that declares a value: a declared parent must equal exactly the sum of its children.
1.1 declared 1246.50 vs computed 1246.50 - difference 0.00, compliant.
1.2 declared 1180.00 vs computed 1152.60 - difference 27.40, non-compliant. The published Streaming Feature Store figure claims 27.40 labour-hours of scope that no work package carries.
1.3 declares no value, so nothing to test.

Answers: root_total = 3775.85; hundred_percent_valid = false. The sponsor should not baseline until 1.2 is reconciled - either the declared value is corrected to 1152.60 or the missing 27.40 hours of scope is decomposed into a work package.

Does the structure satisfy the 100% rule (every declared parent value equals the sum of its children)?
